chat.eyebrow: Ask the atlas · exploratory, not official
chat.title: Ask the atlas
chat.lead: Ask a question in plain English. The answer is written only from these pages, and every sentence that states a finding is checked word for word against the passage it quotes, so you can follow it back to its page.
starters: Do patents filed without an attorney fare worse?
What did Stage 3 make of B6?
What do we know about universities and patents?

how.title: What it reads
how.text: Only these pages: the observations, the glossary, the lenses, the sources, and the pages on Stage 3, limits, what comes next and the check against IP Australia. It searches them, a small model picks the passages that bear on the question, and a larger one writes the answer from those alone.

how.title: What it may not do
how.text: Use outside knowledge; state an association as a cause (a **descriptive** or **observational** finding is never a cause); or answer the five research questions, which wait for Stage 3 to be reviewed. A question about IP Australia's or WIPO's publications belongs to the Econ chat.

how.title: The check
how.text: The model cites sentences by number and code copies them, so every quote is exact. Code then checks every quote against its passage, and that every number in a cited sentence appears in the sentences it cites. An answer that fails goes back once; one that still fails is shown flagged, never hidden.

how.title: Cost and records
how.text: Answers stop for the day when a daily spending cap is reached; the passages found are still shown. Questions and answers are recorded in the service's log so the chat can be checked and improved.

how.title: What it is
how.text: An exploratory research tool for IPAVentures, not an official IP Australia publication or advice. Read the cited page before relying on an answer.

hero.eyebrow: Stage 3 of 3 · exploratory data analysis · first pass done
hero.title: What Australia's IP data show so far, and how we know
hero.lead: This research asks how Australia's intellectual property system creates public value, and where IP Australia could add the most. Before answering, the data have been examined in three stages: every measure on its own, then every pair of measures, then the pairs that mattered with their other factors held together. These pages set out what each stage found, in plain English, and let you follow any finding back to the public data it came from.

site.banner: **Stage 1 describes; Stage 2 relates; Stage 3 tests what survives; none explains.** Stage 1's observations say what the data show. Stage 2's say which measures go together and whether the link holds in a second sample. Stage 3's say how much of each link is left once its other factors are held together, and what structure there is among places, countries, industries and institutions. None is a cause, and none answers a research question yet: anything causal needs designs that come after the exploration.
site.journey_intro: The analysis has three stages, each looking at the same data in a new way. Stage 3's first pass is done and its two tables (early signals and data gaps) await the research owner's review. Only then, with the owner's agreement, are the five questions answered.

stages.name: Each variable on its own
stages.short: What each measure looks like, how complete it is, and its quirks. 128 observations (U0 to U127).

stages.name: Pairs of variables
stages.short: Which measures move together, how strongly, and for whom. 63 observations (B1 to B63).

stages.name: Many variables together
stages.short: Whether the signals survive once other factors are held together, and what structure there is. 40 observations (M1 to M40).

stages.name: Answering the questions
stages.short: The five questions, with evidence proportionate to each claim.

featured.intro: Every observation can be followed from the published data to the finding, and a Stage 3 observation back to the Stage 2 signal it tests. This one shows how.
featured.title: Patents filed without an attorney are still granted far less often, once the factors settled at filing are held
featured.text: Stage 2 found that Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted about 36 points less often ({B6}). Holding the route, filing year, state and co-filers together, 31.2 points of the gap remain (87.2%), in both decades. The chart sets each raw gap (grey) beside the held one (blue), with its interval. Open it to see the chain from Stage 2, the reasoning, and why this is an association and not a cause.

stage3.title: What Stage 3 found
stage3.intro: Stage 3 took each signal Stage 2 carried forward and held its named third factors together in one model, to see how much of it is left. The bar counts every check by its outcome; the list gives the findings most worth knowing. All are associations or descriptions, not causes.

items.title: Filing without an attorney still goes with far fewer grants
items.text: With the route, year, state and co-filers held together, Australian individuals' patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often (35.8 raw), in both decades; trade marks and designs with no agent before the first renewal are less often in force after it. Not a cause: an application dropped early may never appoint an attorney.

items.title: Australian organisations' patents: three readings that still disagree
items.text: At the same reach they are less likely to end (hazard ratios 0.648 to 0.811), yet they reach fewer offices and are cited about 27% to 30% less at the same reach, field, route and year. None of the three is value; they must be read together.

items.title: Asking for examination sooner is not a sign of a longer life
items.text: Expedited examination's link with staying in force does not survive the filer, field and route held together, and Australian individuals' expedited patents are about a quarter more likely to end in a given year. On the wider measure IP Australia's commissioned study uses, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents), patents are more likely to end, held together (1.276 and 1.383), against the study's finding.

items.title: Some Australian invention ends up owned overseas, by two routes
items.text: Granted Australian-founded patents are more often now held only overseas, at the same reach and filer type, and so are patents filed before the firm's first registration. Inventions made here and filed from overseas come in about equal numbers from international teams and from all-Australian ones.

items.title: The same organisations file more divisionals
items.text: Divisionals doubled within the same filers (+19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones), not through a change in fields or filers.

items.title: Fees look a weak lever
items.text: Owners did not let rights go more often at the anniversary after any of nine renewal fee changes (for patents, within about 1.4 points either way), and with trend and season held most filing fee breaks do not behave as prices would.

items.title: Among firms, age, form and size go with filing; R&D spend only weakly
items.text: Older R&D claimants and public companies more often have a filing linked, held together; government suppliers that file win about two and a half times the contracts; among large employers the size gap widens within an industry. Spending above the median goes with a standard patent by only 4 to 5 points.

items.title: Places: one advantage gradient, and what lies beyond it
items.text: Advantage, income and education are mostly one measure. Beyond it, business density, manufacturing businesses and places with more degrees than their resources suggest go with filing; residents' incomes add nothing detectable; remoteness stays.

items.title: Across countries and industries, patents follow business R&D
items.text: Across OECD members, patenting at home follows business R&D at the same income and size; across industries, patents allocated per business follow business R&D at the same value added. Australia is nearest Norway, New Zealand and Sweden on non-IP indicators.

items.title: Institutions: research that patents cite goes with their own patenting; licence income does not follow patents
items.text: Across every kind of institution, with kind and size held, research that patents cite goes with more patents per work. At the same research spend, more patents are not seen to go with more licence income.

items.title: Raising the Bar's rush holds; the business cycle barely shows
items.text: With trend and season held, Raising the Bar's rush and Australians' lower level of patents after it hold, while the Designs Act's step does not stand apart from a control. With block resampling, the cycle shows only in overseas applicants' trade marks before 2008. Trade marks share a long-run path with real GDP and run a quarter ahead of it, as IP Australia's note finds, but the lead is small once GDP's own growth is held and is not detected since 2008.

stage3.page_title: What held once other factors were allowed for
stage3.lead: Stage 2 found pairs of measures that move together and named, for each, the other factors that might explain it. Stage 3 holds those factors together, signal by signal, and says how much of each is left. It also asks what structure there is among places, countries, industries and institutions. This page sets out how the test works, what its outcomes mean, and every check it made, each linked to its page.
stage3.banner: **Held is not controlled.** Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive, and none answers a research question yet. Its two tables, early signals and data gaps, await the research owner's review.
stage3.how_intro: Every Stage 3 page follows the same five steps, and shows the first three at its top as a chain: what Stage 2 found, what was held together, and what is left.

how.title: Start from a Stage 2 signal
how.sub: A pair that held in two samples
how.text: A pair of measures that went together in Stage 2, in a first sample and again in a second: for example, filing without an attorney and fewer grants ({B6}).

how.title: Name its third factors
how.text: Stage 2 named, for each signal, the other factors that could make the two measures go together: the route of filing, the year, the field, the filer's type, a place's advantage.

how.title: Hold them together
how.sub: One model, every factor at once
how.text: One model holds every named factor fixed at once, so the signal is read among rights, firms or places alike in all of them. Intervals allow a filer's many rights to be alike, or resample neighbouring quarters in blocks.

how.title: Compare raw and held
how.sub: How much of the signal is left
how.text: The raw figure (Stage 2's comparison, with nothing held) is set beside the held one. The charts show both: grey for raw, blue for held, each with its 95% interval.

how.title: Give the outcome, and check it again
how.text: Holds if at least half is left and the interval is clear of no difference; weakened if less than half is left; not detected once held if the interval includes no difference; reversed if it turns the other way. Each is read again in the second sample or period.

example.title: An example: filing without an attorney
example.intro: Stage 2 found Australian individuals' patents filed alone granted about 36 points less often ({B6}). Stage 3 held the route, filing year, state and co-filers together.
example.text: Grey dots are the raw gaps, blue the gaps with those factors held, each with its interval. For individuals 87.2% of the gap is left in FY2010 to FY2019, and 86.2% in the decade before: it holds. For Australian organisations in FY2000 to FY2009 both intervals cross the line of no difference: not detected either way.

stage3.verdicts_intro: Each outcome is a word as well as a colour. The counts are of checks: a page can check several earlier observations, and an observation can be checked by more than one page.
stage3.board_intro: Every earlier observation Stage 3 revisited, grouped by lens: what Stage 2 (or Stage 1) found, the outcome once other factors were held, and the Stage 3 page that made the check. Choose an outcome to see only those checks.
stage3.structure_intro: Besides testing signals, Stage 3 asked which measures repeat each other and whether there are distinct kinds of place or country. These are descriptive.

structure.title: Places' characteristics are mostly one advantage gradient
structure.text: Across 2,525 postal areas the first component, advantage, carries 49.5% of the variation, and IRSAD can be predicted almost entirely from the other measures. No single measure (income, education) should be read as the one that matters.

structure.title: Places form a continuum, not kinds
structure.text: The best grouping of areas has a silhouette of 0.269, short of clear segments; one group of 288 advantaged, educated city areas holds 56% of the placed standard patents.

structure.title: Countries differ along several dimensions
structure.text: Across 35 OECD members the first component carries 24.7% of the variation. Australia is low on manufacturing and exports, high on education and new businesses, and nearest Norway, New Zealand and Sweden.

structure.title: Trends dominate the monthly series
structure.text: Trade marks' and overseas applicants' series are almost all trend; seasons are strong for provisionals and Australians' trade marks; what is left of different series moves together only moderately, perhaps the calendar.

structure.title: The name match recovers most missing business numbers
structure.text: Tested on rights with a known ABN, 1.1% to 4.8% of matches name another ABN. Applied, it closes most of the recent fall in patents linked to an ABN and changes no firm finding. Adopting it is the owner's decision (OQ26).

stage3.next_intro: Stage 3 ends with two tables for the research owner's review: fifteen early signals worth investigating, each with its evidence, strength and a suggested next step, and thirteen gaps in the data with possible sources and costs.

verdict_words.holds: The same direction as the raw figure, its 95% interval clear of no difference, and at least half of the raw size left once the third factors are held together.
verdict_words.weakened: The same direction and clear of no difference, but less than half of the raw size left, so much of the signal was its third factors.
verdict_words.not detected once held: The interval with the factors held includes no difference. Not the same as no association; a moderate one may be missed.
verdict_words.reversed: Clear of no difference, but the other way round from the raw figure.
verdict_words.appears once held: The raw figure was not detected, but with the factors held an association is clear.
verdict_words.not detected either way: Neither the raw nor the held figure is clear of no difference.
verdict_words.does not replicate: Clear in one sample or period but not in the second, so not carried as a signal.
verdict_words.mixed: The page's parts differ (one group or period holds, another does not); its text says which is which.
verdict_words.refined: A description that sharpens or corrects an earlier one, rather than a test of a held signal.

stage2.title: What Stage 2 found
stage2.intro: Stage 2 measured every pair of measures in each lens and kept only those that are at least small, survive the correction for the number of pairs tested, and hold in a second period or sample. Most such pairs are how the IP system works, or one broad gradient of development running through places and countries. These are the signals left once those are set aside: associations to test in Stage 3, not explanations. Stage 3 has since tested each; every one of their pages says what was left.

items.title: Filing without an attorney goes with poorer outcomes
items.text: Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted about 36 percentage points less often, in both decades and among examined applications too. Australians' trade marks with no agent before the first renewal stay in force less often (19.1 points). The arrow may run backwards: an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney.

items.title: Some inventions made here are filed or held overseas
items.text: About one patent in seven with an inventor in Australia is filed from overseas. Australian-filed patents now held only overseas are more common among the wide and the granted, though by firm the youngest filers are not clearly different. Few of the US patents citing Australian research have an Australian party, but a citation is not use, so none of this shows where value is realised.

items.title: Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries; the signals of value disagree
items.text: Filed in the same number of countries, Australian organisations' patents more often stay in force for 10 years than overseas organisations', except those filed only in Australia. But they reach fewer countries and are cited less, mostly because of that reach. Older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete in the records, so these are read from FY2010.

items.title: Filing follows advantage and remoteness, not one firm
items.text: Each step of area advantage goes with 1.7 to 1.9 times the standard patent rate, and the gradient holds with remoteness allowed for and with each area's largest filer taken out. Areas that gained graduates or income over a decade were not seen to gain filing, so it looks like a standing difference between places.

items.title: Among firms, filing goes with company form, age and, among large employers, size and industry
items.text: R&D spend goes with patenting only weakly, even within size bands. About half of R&D claimants have no IP filing linked to their business number, mostly private companies of 3 to 10 years. Counting every large employer, the largest are 24.3 points more likely than the smallest to have a filing linked, and industry sorts patenting far more than size.

items.title: Across countries, IP follows R&D and income
items.text: Across OECD members, patenting rises with business R&D almost one for one, and Australia filed about what its business R&D predicts in 2016 to 2020. Within a decade, changes in R&D were not seen to go with changes in patenting. Few of Australia's researchers work in business (31st of 37 members).

items.title: Policy changes broke series as the law required; few breaks show behaviour, and fee changes rarely moved filing
items.text: Seven of eight policy changes moved a series further than any comparison month, but most of those breaks were certain by law. The rush before Raising the Bar is the clearest sign of applicants' behaviour. Of the changes in fees to obtain a right, only one break went the way a price would; of the changes in renewal fees, only one (trade marks, July 1993) survives every check.

items.title: Women's share among inventors varies by field more than by filer
items.text: From 4.2% in civil engineering to 26.9% in biotechnology, an order that holds across decades. On provisional applications, Australian organisations' inventors include more women than Australian individuals'.

items.title: Across industries, the patents allocated by technology follow R&D once services are counted
items.text: Industry counts are applications allocated by what they protect, not what each industry's businesses file. Through the crosswalk with services, patents allocated per business follow business R&D per business. A division's share of innovating businesses showed no clear pattern with patenting in three surveys.

items.title: Institutions whose research US patents cite more also patent more
items.text: Larger, more cited universities file more patents per work. Across institutions, disclosures go with patents and patents with licence income, partly because every measure is divided by the same research spend. No association was detected between industry-partnered grants and joint filing, though a moderate one is not ruled out.

site.ten_intro: Read together, Stage 1's observations point to a handful of patterns. Each is descriptive: a shape in the data worth testing, not an explanation. The numbers link to the observations behind them.

ten.title: Patents are mostly filed from overseas; trade marks mostly from home
ten.text: About nine in ten standard patents filed in Australia come from overseas (the United States alone 43.6%), while Australians file 59.19% of trade marks. China now files as many patent applications here as Australians do, and three-quarters of Australians' own applications are made abroad.

ten.title: Almost everything is concentrated
ten.text: The top 1% of filing firms filed 55.3% of firms' standard patents; the tenth of postal areas with the most patents filed 72.5% of them with 29.2% of the people; five attorney firms handle 63.96% of standard patents; the Group of Eight hold two-thirds of ARC and NHMRC funding.

ten.title: Places differ far more than chance would make them
ten.text: 68.2% to 72.5% of areas file below what chance allows around the national rate, and 6.7% to 15.5% above it, in small areas and pooled ones alike. Later stages must model this spread rather than assume it away.

ten.title: Australians, above all individuals, often file without an attorney
ten.text: Overseas filers use an attorney for 99.0% of standard patents, Australian filers for 85.4%, and Australian individuals file 62.4% of their trade marks alone.

ten.title: Provisional applications doubled in FY2026
ten.text: 10,069 against 4,143 to 5,047 a year before, mostly from individuals but from organisations too, both broadly and through a few heavy filers. It is in the filings, not the recording. Why is a question for IP Australia.

ten.title: Around some policy changes, filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses
ten.text: Rushes to file before a rule changed (Raising the Bar, 4.41 times Australians' usual month; the innovation patent's closure, 4.31 times), steps, and pauses when new Acts began; around other changes nothing stands out. These timings are the raw material for the natural experiments the later questions need.

ten.title: Later standard patents more often stay in force; about half of trade marks are still in force after ten years
ten.text: Standard patents' median time in force rose from 10.6 years (granted in the 1980s and 1990s) to 13.5 (2000s and 2010s). These are shares still on the register, not value; the research owner adopted years in force as a working measure for Stage 2, alongside other signals.

ten.title: US patents often cite Australian research, and R&D spending has fallen
ten.text: US patents often cite Australian research institutions' work; 93.6% of those citations come from patents with no Australian applicant or inventor, as most US patents have none. A citation is not use. Australia's R&D spending rose to 2008 as a share of GDP and has fallen since, below the OECD median.

ten.title: The register's history shapes what it can say
ten.text: Early years hold only the rights that survived until records were computerised; some events were dated in batches; patent ownership history starts in FY2003. Each is handled, but each limits comparisons over time.

ten.title: Links between datasets are the weakest point
ten.text: Firms' IP counts are lower bounds; IP RAPID links fewer recent filers to a business number (IP Australia's register restores most for trade marks and designs); only large employers have an industry; half the universities' patents carry a postcode that is not a place where people live.

reading.intro: Every observation page has the same parts, and each part looks different, so that a finding is never confused with the reasoning, assumptions or limits around it.

parts.title: The observation
parts.text: The finding itself, in a green box with its number (U0 to U127 in Stage 1, B1 to B63 in Stage 2, M1 to M40 in Stage 3). Only this is a finding.

parts.title: Reasoning steps
parts.text: How the data lead to the finding, one step at a time, in dashed grey. Steps are not findings.

parts.title: Assumptions
parts.text: Where the analysis takes something as given. Marked in amber, so you can judge them.

parts.title: Limits
parts.text: What the observation cannot tell you, in rose.

parts.title: Explainers
parts.text: Statistical or technical terms, explained in blue beside the text, and on any dotted word.

reading.strength_intro: The research goal asks every claim to say how strong its evidence is. There are four levels. Everything in Stage 1 is the first; most of Stages 2 and 3 is the second.

strengths.name: Descriptive
strengths.text: What the data show. How much, how often, for whom. No claim about why.

strengths.name: Observational
strengths.text: Things go together, even with other factors held. There may be other explanations. Stages 2 and 3 produce these.

strengths.name: Causal
strengths.text: One thing causes another. Needs a design, such as a natural experiment, that this exploration does not have.

strengths.name: Projected
strengths.text: An estimate of the future, with its assumptions stated. Belongs to Question 5.

site.observations_intro: Every observation from the three stages, grouped by lens and the notebook's sections, which open and close. Stage 1's (U numbers) describe one measure at a time; Stage 2's (B numbers) relate two measures and say whether the link held in a second sample; Stage 3's (M numbers) hold a Stage 2 signal's other factors together and say what is left. Filter by lens, question, stage or Stage 3's outcome, or search; an earlier observation that Stage 3 tested shows the page that tested it.
site.storage_text:
**Kept as published.** Each publisher's file is downloaded and kept exactly as released (the "raw" copy), so any number can be traced back to the original.

**Tidied, not changed.** Each raw file is converted into tidy tables in a standard format (Parquet), one row per record, with the publisher's values kept. Where a source had to be repaired, the repair is written into code and recorded in a decision record, and the raw file still holds the original.

**Fingerprinted.** Every file gets a fingerprint (a SHA-256 hash: a code that changes if a single character of the file changes), its size, rows and location, in the project's manifest. Tests check the files against the fingerprints.

**Stored in two places.** Small tables are kept in the GitHub repository itself. Large ones (IP RAPID's events, the business register and others) are kept in a private cloud storage bucket (Cloudflare R2), because they are too big for GitHub; the manifest records them in the same way.

lenses_page.intro: A lens is an analysis-ready table with one row per thing being described: an IP right, a firm, a place, a country in a year, a month, an industry in a year, or a research institution in a year. Every source in the corpus is attached to at least one lens.
lenses_page.why: Two measures can only be compared if they describe the same thing. A patent count and a population cannot be set side by side until both are counted for the same place. So every table is brought to a lens's unit by a stated join or sum, and each lens keeps one row per unit (a test checks). Where two sources measure the same thing, one is the main measure and the other a labelled comparison; they are never added together.

questions_page.intro: The research asks five questions, from what public value the IP system creates to what interventions could achieve. Stages 1 and 2 do not answer them. They find out what the data can and cannot say about each, and which measures go together, so that the answers, when they come, rest on sound ground.
questions_page.caution: Each observation names the questions it moves closer to and says how. Those links are the analyst's guide, not findings: an observation about patents filed from overseas does not, on its own, say anything about who benefits.

data_page.intro: Every number on these pages starts in data that a public body published: IP Australia, the ABS, the ATO, the World Bank, WIPO, the OECD and others. Nothing is typed in by hand. This page follows a number from its publisher to an observation, and lists every source with its licence and where it is kept.
data_page.sources_intro: The source register (54 sources). Observation {U0} describes the corpus as profiled on 4 November 2026 (54 sources, 194 tables). Thirteen were added after the first profiles: the research institutions' register (ROR), IP Australia's own register, and the fee history, the Reserve Bank's rates, the national accounts, the ATO's statistics by postcode, WGEA's employers and others while filling the data gaps Stage 2 found. Open a source to see its tables, their size, where each is kept and its fingerprint.

journey.title: Published
journey.sub: A public body releases the data
journey.text: A publisher releases data on its website or an open data portal, under a licence (most here are Creative Commons, which allow reuse with credit).

journey.title: Copied as published
journey.sub: The raw file is kept unchanged
journey.text: The project downloads the file and keeps it exactly as released, with the date it was copied. Nothing is retyped.

journey.title: Tidied into tables
journey.sub: One row per record, values kept
journey.text: Code (one module per source, in the repository) reads the raw file into tidy tables. Values are not changed; where a source needed repair, the repair is in code and recorded.

journey.title: Fingerprinted and stored
journey.sub: In GitHub, or cloud storage if large
journey.text: Each table's fingerprint, rows and location go into the manifest. Small tables live in the repository; large ones in a cloud storage bucket.

journey.title: Built into a lens
journey.sub: One row per right, firm, place…
journey.text: The build code joins the tables into seven lenses, one row per unit. Every derived column is defined in one file, so anyone can check exactly how it was made. Lenses are rebuilt in minutes, never edited by hand.

journey.title: Profiled in the notebook
journey.text: A notebook runs a query on a lens, and saves its output (a table or chart) with the notebook, so it can be read on GitHub without running anything. Stage 1's notebook profiles each measure; Stage 2's relates pairs; Stage 3's holds several together in one model.

journey.title: Written as an observation
journey.text: The analyst writes the observation directly under the output, quoting its numbers. If a number is not on the page, it is not a finding. These pages are checked against the notebook in the same way.

limits.intro: The three stages are groundwork. They are honest about what they are: a careful description of each measure on its own, then of which measures go together, then of how much of each link is left once its other factors are held. This page gathers what they cannot do, the assumptions they make, where the data are weakest, and the mistakes found and corrected on the way.
limits.cannot_title: What the three stages cannot tell you

cannot.title: Why
cannot.text: Stage 1's observations are descriptive and Stage 2's are associations. Stage 3 holds the measured third factors together, which is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain a link, and some links may run backwards (an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney, {B6}, {M1}). Causal claims need designs, such as natural experiments, that come after the exploration.

cannot.title: What "not detected" means
cannot.text: When Stage 3 says a link is not detected once held, its interval includes no difference. That is not evidence of no link: with 19 industries, about 40 universities or 36 countries, a moderate link can go undetected. Only for patents' renewal at each anniversary is the null precise (within about 1.4 points, {M28}).

cannot.title: Value
cannot.text: Counts of rights, lifetimes, reach and citations are measures of activity and private value, not of public value. The research goal treats them as indicators, never as success.

cannot.title: People from places
cannot.text: Stage 2's pairs across postal areas and countries describe the areas and countries, not the people or firms in them. Areas with more graduates file more; that does not show the graduates are the filers.

cannot.title: Small units
cannot.text: Industries (19 divisions), OECD members (36 to 38) and research institutions (about 40 universities, 60 to 84 institutions) are few, so their intervals are wide and their results are leads at most; a second period of the same units is a stability check, not a replication.

cannot.title: Everyone
cannot.text: The firms lens holds businesses found in an IP, R&D, procurement or tax source, not all businesses, so shares of large employers that file are taken over every employer ({B50}). Individuals in IP RAPID are pseudonymised, so their gender cannot be estimated; only inventors' can, from names, and reliably only for inventors in Australia.

cannot.title: Small firms
cannot.text: Size and industry are known only for employers of 100 or more (WGEA). Without the ABS's BLADE (linked business data, ruled out for now), small firms' size, industry, growth and survival are out of reach (OQ20). This limits how far Questions 3 and 5 can be answered.

cannot.title: The present
cannot.text: The latest months of some records are incomplete because the register records them late (trade mark and design cessations, recent ABN links, perhaps priority claims, {B38}). Each observation says which years are safe to compare.

assumptions: Public data are taken to be what their publishers say they are. Where checks found otherwise (placeholder dates, mislabelled countries, numbers counted twice), the data were repaired and the repair recorded; elsewhere, the publisher's values stand.
A business is identified by its ABN. Related companies in a group have different ABNs and are counted apart.
A place is a postal area, reached through the postcode recorded on an application or in the business register. A registered address may be a head office or an adviser's, not where the work is done.
An industry is reached through what a right protects (its technology or goods classes), by published probabilities, because few firms in the corpus have an industry.
Gender is estimated from first names and countries, as a probability summed over many people; it says nothing about any one person, and is read only for inventors in Australia.
Money is shown as recorded (nominal) unless a page says otherwise; fees are also shown in June 2026 dollars, adjusted with the quarterly Consumer Price Index.
Where a series begins with only the survivors of an earlier system, or with partial records, those years are left out rather than estimated.

Stage 2 measures every pair on one scale from 0 to 1 and calls a pair a lead only if it reaches 0.1, survives the correction for the number of pairs, holds in a second period or sample, and is not two versions of one measure (ADR 0030).

Stage 3 calls a signal held if, with its third factors held together, it keeps its direction, its 95% interval is clear of no difference and at least half of its raw size is left (ADR 0046). A filer's rights are one source of evidence (clustered by the filer's party), and quarterly changes are resampled in blocks.
limits.weak_intro: The binding limit on what this research can say is how well its datasets link together. These are the links the two stages found weakest.

weak.title: Firms
weak.text: Firms reach IP only through business numbers on applications, so firms' IP counts are lower bounds; IP RAPID's recent filings carry fewer, and IP Australia's register restores most for trade marks and designs ({U41}, {U45}, {U100}). A name match recovers most of the rest and changes no firm finding, but is kept apart from the counts ({M12}). Size and industry reach only employers of 100 or more ({U112}), the main third factor every firm signal lacks.

weak.title: Industries
weak.text: Industries reach patents only through a crosswalk; the recommended one leaves out services, so a second one with services sits beside it ({U75}, {U114}).

weak.title: Places
weak.text: Places reach IP only through postcodes, and half the universities' patents carry a postcode where no one lives ({U49}, {U87}).

weak.title: Institutions
weak.text: Research institutions reach their IP through a reviewed list of names and business numbers that someone in the sector has yet to check ({U81}, OQ11).

weak.title: Inventors and families
weak.text: Inventors' countries are known mostly for patents also filed abroad, gender only as an estimate that holds for Australia ({U95}, {U97}), and older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete before FY2010 ({B55}, OQ21).

limits.corrections_intro: The record corrects its own mistakes when they are found, in the notebooks and in the summaries. These are the corrections made during the three stages and in building these pages.

corrections.what: The policy register said the Patents Act 1990 brought in 20-year patents.
corrections.now: Its term was 16 years until 1 July 1995; the change is now the 17th policy event ({U23}).

corrections.what: Charts of trade marks before 1983 and designs before 1986 showed survivors without saying so.
corrections.now: Corrected in {U5} and {U10}; the series start where records are complete.

corrections.what: The World Bank's trade mark series was described as applications.
corrections.now: It counts classes, as WIPO's do ({U67}).

corrections.what: Five figures differed slightly between builds of the lenses, because two ties were broken arbitrarily.
corrections.now: The ties are fixed, two builds agree row for row, and the figures are corrected ({U48}, {U49}, {U52}, {U53}).

corrections.what: Three more figures depended on how ties fell (the share of people in the top tenth of areas; universities' postcodes).
corrections.now: Corrected ({U52}: 29.2% and 32.8% of people; {U87}: UNSW's 210, not 216).

corrections.what: Observation {U0} still gave the first corpus profile (152 tables from 38 sources) when the output above it gave the later one.
corrections.now: The notebook's text now follows its output (162 tables from 41 sources), found while building these pages.

corrections.what: {B11} left open whether the fall in Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia (73.0% to 40.68%) was a change in practice or in the records.
corrections.now: Mostly the records. Older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete ({B55}), so family measures for Australian applicants are read from FY2010.

corrections.what: Firms that file were counted from IP RAPID's own records, which miss the business numbers IP Australia's register links.
corrections.now: One flag now counts any linked filing; sole traders' and R&D claimants' shares moved, and "never filed" became "no filing linked" ({U42}, {U54}, {B23}).

corrections.what: An application's origin and type were the current holder's.
corrections.now: They are the filer's, IP Australia's definition of a resident application; most shares moved by a point or less ({U7}, {U13}, {U67}).

corrections.what: Firms' first filings were read as their entry into the system, and changes of holder as transfers.
corrections.now: They are first observed filings and two endpoints, filing and today ({U101}, {U18}, {B19}).

corrections.what: Lifetimes counted every right from the start of its term, and were described as renewal.
corrections.now: Each right is counted from its grant or registration, and read as the share still in force; expedited patents' link with lifetime reversed ({U36}, {B8}, {B10}, {B13}).

corrections.what: Policy and fee breaks were read without controls, and against placebo dates as if those were probabilities.
corrections.now: Each break is classed by kind and set beside series it should not have moved; most were certain by law ({B37}, {B47}, {B49}).

corrections.what: A final review of both stages found 68 of 186 observations reading further than their numbers, or quoting a figure the output did not give.
corrections.now: Each is restated in the notebook with the earlier wording kept. The largest change: shares of large employers that file are taken over every employer, not only those in the firms table (48.6% to 72.9% by size, not 70.4% to 82.5%; {U112}, {B50}). Weak links are no longer written as absences, same-unit samples as replications, industry allocations as filing, or US patent citations as use ({B39}, {B32}, {B41}, {U85}, {B46}).

corrections.what: These pages had fallen behind the notebooks for 131 observations, and four charts no longer matched the data.
corrections.now: Every page was brought into line with its notebook, the charts now use the filer's origin and the current survival method, and 40 more pages have a chart (178 of 186).

corrections.what: A review of all three stages found that Stage 3's first pass had left eighteen of Stage 2's carried signals untested, with renewal at each right's anniversary, while its table said all were taken up.
corrections.now: Each now has its test ({M26} to {M38}); two figures were corrected where they stood ({M1}'s verdict, {M16}'s lowest silhouette), and the labour market and the IP judgments, planned for the timeline, were attached ({U124}, {B63}).

corrections.what: Stage 3's helper for yes or no outcomes returned a meaningless interval, silently, when two held factors picked out the same rows.
corrections.now: It drops the repeated factor before fitting (a test covers it); the notebook was re-run in full and no earlier figure changed.

corrections.what: These pages were frozen while Stage 3 ran, so 53 earlier observations that Stage 3 tested still read as Stage 2 left them.
corrections.now: Every Stage 3 observation has a page, and each earlier page it tested says what was left once other factors were held, with a link to the test.

corrections.what: Observation {U0} still described the corpus as profiled on 25 October (162 tables from 41 sources), though 13 sources had been added since, and the review against IP Australia still read as it did on 27 October.
corrections.now: The corpus was profiled again and {U0} follows it (194 tables from 54 sources). The review's page now says where each of its findings stands: IP Australia's register settled the designs of unknown origin and sided with IP RAPID on 2018's trade marks.

corrections.what: The review against IP Australia's published figures covered only Stage 1's first 99 observations, so the later ones and Stages 2 and 3 had not been checked the same way.
corrections.now: The same check was made of the 130 since ({U99} to {U127}, {B1} to {B63}, {M1} to {M38}): 13 more published figures agree, and none of the 130 is disputed or contradicted. The review's page shows both passes.

next.intro: The three stages have prepared the ground: every measure described, every pair related, and each pair that mattered tested with its other factors held together. Stage 3 ends with two tables for the research owner's review: early signals worth investigating and gaps in the data. Nothing here answers a research question; that comes only after the owner's review, with designs proportionate to each claim.

stages.name: Stage 2, pairs of variables
stages.asks: Which pairs of measures move together, in what shape, how strongly, and for whom?
stages.how: Within each lens, every pair of variables was screened on one scale. A pair counted as a lead only if it was at least small, survived the correction for the number of pairs tested, and held in a second period or sample; the planned pairs were then measured in plain units, with intervals.
stages.example: Postal areas with more advantaged residents file 1.7 to 1.9 times as many standard patents per person for each step of advantage, and the gradient is not one firm's ({B29}, {B30}).
stages.adds: The first **observational** evidence: associations that bear on who benefits (Q2) and on the conditions for value (Q3), each with its candidate third factors.
stages.done: Every pair within each lens screened; each lead with its size and interval, past the correction and held in a second sample.

stages.name: Stage 3, many variables together
stages.when: First pass done (3 November 2026); tables await the owner's review
stages.asks: Do the signals survive once other factors are held together? What structure and groups exist?
stages.how: Each signal Stage 2 carried was modelled with its named third factors held together, and its raw and held figures compared (holds, weakened, not detected once held, reversed). The methods the final review asked for were used throughout: intervals that allow a filer's rights to be alike, block resampling of quarterly changes, citations counted at a fixed age, industry comparisons through the crosswalk with services, and research spend as a base. Places' and countries' characteristics were reduced to a few components, and places grouped to see whether they form kinds.
stages.example: Is an area's patent rate still linked to advantage once its business mix and education are allowed for? Yes, but weaker: 35% to 39% of the ratio is left, and business density and degrees beyond resources matter too ({M14}).
stages.adds: Separates signals that hold from ones explained by something else, and produces two tables: fifteen early signals, with their evidence and strength, and thirteen data gaps, with possible sources and costs.
stages.done: When the owner has reviewed the two tables and decided on the name match (OQ26).

stages.name: Answering the questions
stages.when: After the owner's review, with the owner's agreement
stages.how: Analyses designed for each question: descriptive where that suffices, and natural experiments or other designs wherever an additional benefit is claimed.
stages.example: Using Raising the Bar as a natural experiment, following who rushed and what their rushed applications became, to estimate what a policy actually changed ({M25}).
stages.adds: Answers with evidence proportionate to each claim, as the research goal requires.
stages.done: When the owner adopts the findings.

next.signals_title: Early signals that warrant further investigation
next.signals_intro: Stage 3's first table, for the research owner's review (section 8 of the Stage 3 notebook). Each signal is an association that survived its third factors held together, in both samples unless marked; none is a cause, and adopting any as a conclusion is the owner's decision.

signals.signal: Filing alone goes with far fewer grants (Australian individuals' standard patents, about 31 points), and no agent before the first renewal with fewer trade marks and designs in force after it, with the factors settled at filing held
signals.next: A design that separates the choice of an attorney from the outcome: the same filers' applications with and without one, or a change in what representation costs

signals.signal: Within the same reach, Australian organisations' patents are less likely to end, yet reach fewer offices and are cited less at the same field, route and year
signals.next: Validate each as a sign of value against licensing, litigation or sale; read the three together, never one alone

signals.signal: Expedited examination is not a sign of a longer life once the filer, field and route are held; for Australian individuals it goes with a shorter one
signals.next: Separate work-sharing requests from applicants' own (OQ25); ask what individuals expedite for

signals.signal: Granted Australian-founded patents are more often now held only overseas, at the same reach and filer type; so are patents filed before the filing firm's first registration (+5.40 and +6.21 points)
signals.next: Dated ownership changes and the holders' identities, to read moves rather than endpoints

signals.signal: Women among inventors: on provisionals more on organisations' than individuals'; on standard patents the field accounts for the filer gap
signals.next: Women by field within filers; the provisionals' recent coverage (OQ17)

signals.signal: Among R&D claimants, older firms, higher spenders and public companies more often have a standard patent linked, held together; among suppliers, company form, age and a city address (not the postcode's advantage); suppliers that file win more contracts and value; among large employers the size gap widens within industry; large taxpayers that file report no more income
signals.next: Firm size and industry for small firms (OQ20); the timing of filing against contracts and claims

signals.signal: Filing concentrates in advantaged, educated city areas, and beyond the advantage gradient goes with business density, degrees and R&D claimants beyond what resources predict, and manufacturing's share of businesses (where Stage 2 saw none); remoteness stays; most attached indicators are the gradient
signals.next: Where filers work against where they are registered; universities' postcodes ({U49}, {U87})

signals.signal: Across OECD members, residents' patents follow business R&D at the same income and size, as do research effort's other measures among the attachments; Australia sits near the line, among Norway, New Zealand and Sweden on the non-IP indicators
signals.next: Use the nearest members as the comparison set for Australia's IP system

signals.signal: Patents allocated per business follow business R&D across divisions at the same value added; three survey items (ideas from within the business, work methods, small firms' focus on costs) and fewer business exits go with IP per business at the same size and value added
signals.next: A second year of business R&D and of the survey items; firm-level industry for the filers themselves

signals.signal: At the same research spend, more patents are not seen to go with more licences or licence income; across every kind of institution, research that patents cite goes with the institution's own patenting, kind and size held
signals.next: The sector review of the institutions link (OQ11); commercialisation data by field

signals.signal: Raising the Bar's rush, and Australians' lower level of standard patents after it, hold with trend and season held; the Designs Act's overseas step does not stand apart from a rise in a control
signals.next: A design for Q5 around Raising the Bar (who rushed, and what their rushed applications became)

signals.signal: Divisionals doubled among organisations' standard patents, within the same filers (Australian +19.18 points, overseas +10.97)
signals.next: How long divisionals keep claims pending, and how they relate to their parents' examination (IP Australia's examination records)

signals.signal: Inventions made in Australia and filed from overseas are, in about equal numbers, international teams' and all-Australian teams'; fewer since FY2010 with the team held
signals.next: Who the overseas filers of all-Australian teams are (subsidiaries, buyers); Australian inventions filed only abroad

signals.signal: Owners did not let rights go more often at the anniversary after a change in its renewal fee (rises of 11% to 33%, a 10% cut); for patents the intervals rule out more than about 1.4 points; the national cessation series' steps are not seen at each right's anniversary
signals.strength: Observational, a precise null for patents
signals.next: Owners' payment dates (early payment at the old fee), and the fee's share of a patent's cost of keeping, to read fees as a lever

signals.signal: FY2025's fall in provisionals followed up within 12 months is in new and heavy individual filers; filers seen before followed up about as often
signals.next: IP Australia on when priority claims are recorded (OQ18), and PCT follow-ups at national phase, about 30 months on

next.recorded: The business cycle ({B52}, {B56}, {B63}, {M36}): with block resampling only overseas applicants' trade marks before 2008 move with it. A third factor for before-and-after comparisons, not a signal.
next.gaps_intro: Stage 3's second table: the gaps in the data that limit the signals above, with a possible source and cost for each. Sourcing any that cost money or need an account is the owner's call.

data_gaps.gap: Size and industry for small firms
data_gaps.why: The main third factor every firm signal lacks ({M8}, {M9}, {M11}, {M29})
data_gaps.source: ABS DataLab (BLADE; ruled out, OQ9), or industry estimated from each firm's IP classes and name (OQ20)
data_gaps.cost: A fee and an approval; or free, as an estimate

data_gaps.gap: The ABNs IP RAPID leaves out
data_gaps.why: Recent counts of firms by year; the name match closes most of the fall but links only 17.7% to 35.3% of the unlinked rights ({M12})
The name match uses ABN main names and ASIC company names only
data_gaps.source: ASIC's business names register (bulk data, free)

data_gaps.why: Ownership is read at two endpoints only ({M6}, {M30}); who files all-Australian teams' patents from overseas ({M27})
Reach and citations are read from FY2010 only ({M3}, {M4}, {B55})
Shared shocks across monthly series may be calendar effects ({M20})

data_gaps.gap: A review of the institutions link
data_gaps.why: Every institutions result rests on it ({M23}, {M24}, {M38})

data_gaps.gap: Business R&D by division in more than one year
data_gaps.why: The industry results rest on FY2024 alone ({M22}, {M37})
Whether owners paid early at the old fee, which the anniversary test cannot see ({M28})
Whether divisionals keep claims pending longer ({B15}, {M26})
data_gaps.source: IP RAPID's links with examination events; IP Australia

data_gaps.why: The IP judgments end with the corpus ({U124}, OQ22)

data_gaps.gap: The CER's and AusTender's monthly series in the timeline
data_gaps.why: Planned timeline attachments not built (both sources are in other lenses, so every source still reaches a lens)

next.puzzles_intro: Things the analysis has found but cannot yet explain. They are kept in view, not explained away. Several are closed or narrowed: IP RAPID's innovation patents in 2016 ({U67}), by the review against IP Australia; the trade mark expedite fall of November 2018 ({U34}), by IP Australia's own register ({U103}); most of the fall in Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia ({B11}), by a gap in older records ({B55}); and about half of the recent fall in first patent filers, by the name match ({M12}).
puzzles: Australians' direct filing of standard patents rose to 28.3% in FY2026 ({U90}), and provisionals filed in FY2025 were followed up less often, mostly by new and heavy individual filers ({B38}, {M35}); both could be priority claims recorded late (OQ18).
The share of divisional applications about doubled among both Australian and overseas organisations, within the same filers ({B15}, {M26}); why is not in the data.
Firms with a first observed patent fell from 1,167 (FY2021) to 810 (FY2024); innovation patents closed in August 2021 ({U45}). About half of the later fall is linking ({M12}).
Plant breeder's rights applications were the decade's lowest in FY2025 and FY2026, which may be real or a delay in recording ({U6}).
The World Bank's share of the labour force with advanced education steps up around 2010 ({U65}).
Plant breeder's rights change hands more often in recent years ({U17}).
Petty patents filed in FY1986 to FY1988 mostly have no acceptance recorded ({U32}).

Patent cessations stepped up after September 2002 in the national series, but not at each patent's own anniversary ({M34}, {M28}); and why a 2% rise would move trade mark cessations in 1993 is not shown.
next.open_intro: Some questions only the research owner, or IP Australia, can answer. They are listed so that nothing depends on an unstated guess.
owner: **Review Stage 3's two tables**: the fifteen early signals and thirteen data gaps above, before the questions are answered.
**The name match** (OQ26): whether to adopt the matched business numbers into the firms' counts, or keep them beside the counts ({M12}).
**A sector check of the institutions link** (OQ11): a half-hour review by someone who knows the sector, which every institutions result rests on ({M23}, {M24}, {M38}).
**Firms' size and industry for small firms** (OQ20): known only for employers of 100 or more; small firms need a paid or requested source.
**Older Australian patent families** (OQ21): repair the links from the EPO's patent family service (free, but an account in your name), or read family measures from FY2010 only.
**Court judgments after March 2025** (OQ22) and ABS TableBuilder (OQ4, on hold).
ipa: What evidence supports IP Australia's reading that digital tools, including AI, drove the rise in provisional applications, and are the few very heavy filers part of it? (OQ5, {U8}, {M35})

IP Australia's register records "Examination expedited" for nearly every trade mark claiming an overseas filing date, and for a growing share of other marks where no one asked; IP RAPID stopped publishing the event in November 2018. What does it mean where no one asked, and could IP RAPID publish it? (OQ6, {U34})
IP Australia's register holds a business number for most of the recent applications that have none in IP RAPID. Why does IP RAPID leave them out, and could it publish them? (OQ7, {U45}, {M12})
What does IP Australia's figure of 55.6% of resident applications filed by individuals in 2022 count? (OQ12, {U13}, {U48})
IP Australia's own register, IP RAPID and WIPO agree on 2018's trade marks, about 2,000 fewer than IP Australia's report: what did the report's 2018 count include? (OQ13, {U5})
IP Australia's register holds the owner's country for most designs IP RAPID leaves without one. Could IP RAPID publish it? (OQ14, {U7})
Are inventors added to a provisional application later, or no longer recorded for some? (OQ17, {B18})
When does IP RAPID record a patent application's priority claims: when it is filed, or later? (OQ18, {B38}, {M35})
Can IP RAPID tell applicants' own requests for expedited examination from work-sharing requests (the Patent Prosecution Highway)? (OQ25, {M5})
after: The research owner reviews Stage 3's early signals and data gaps, and decides on the name match (OQ26).
Source the data worth adding for the gaps (free first; any cost proposed with an estimate).
Only then design the analyses that answer the five questions, with natural experiments wherever an additional benefit is claimed.

site.glossary_intro: Every technical term used on these pages, in plain English. Dotted words anywhere on the site open the same explanations.

glossary_groups.data: Data and how it is handled

corpus.name: The corpus

facts.label: sources, every one in the register

corpus.description: Before any lens, the project gathered public data from 54 sources into one place, its **corpus**: IP Australia's registers, business registers, R&D and procurement records, the ABS, international panels and research databases. Observation {U0} describes the corpus as a whole. Everything else is read through a lens.
limits: The number of rows a source has measures how much it records, not how much it matters to the questions.

rights.name: IP rights

facts.label: patents, trade marks, designs and plant breeder's rights
columns, after seven attachments, the register's fills and Stage 3's name match

rights.description:
Every patent, trade mark, design and plant breeder's right in IP Australia's open register, IP RAPID, from the first application in February 1904 to October 2026. Each row says what the right is, who filed it and who holds it now, where they are, how it reached Australia, what happened to it (examination, grant, opposition, assignment, lapse) and, for patents, how widely the invention was protected abroad, how often later inventions cite it and where its inventors live.

Seven **attachments** add those last groups of columns from other tables: the parties (who filed, who holds, who represents them), the events (each milestone and the right's lifetime), the links (the route into Australia), Google Patents (the worldwide family), the inventors, and IP Australia's own register with its record of provisional applications' inventors. The register fills what IP RAPID leaves out (business numbers, design owners' countries, the inventors of provisional applications), in columns beside IP RAPID's, never replacing them. Origin and applicant type are the filer's, IP Australia's definition of a resident application (ADR 0037). Stage 3 added one column: an ABN found by matching the filer's name to the business register, for Australian organisations' rights with none, kept apart and never added to the counts ({M12}, {U126}).

repairs.what: Where a right's applicants have no country recorded, its origin is "unknown", not "overseas".
repairs.why: Counting the unknowns as overseas had added 517,145 old patents to the overseas side.

repairs.what: Standard patents, provisional applications and second-tier (innovation and petty) patents are counted apart everywhere, and headline figures use standard patents.
repairs.why: They are different rights. A provisional is a cheap placeholder that is never granted; a second-tier patent is a cheaper, shorter right. Adding them together hides what each is doing.

repairs.what: Two placeholder dates are emptied (an end date of 1 January 1970 on 1,282 rights, and one registration before the register began).
repairs.why: 1 January 1970 is the "zero" of computer dates, standing in for an unknown date, not a real one.

repairs.what: Trade marks registered before 1986 have no "days to registration".
repairs.why: The register holds only their filing date, so their recorded time to registration is almost always zero.

repairs.what: The "technology area" is kept for patents only.
repairs.why: For every trade mark and design it simply repeated the class of goods, so it measured nothing new.

repairs.what: An attorney counts only if the agent on record is not the applicant itself.
repairs.why: The register's "agent" is the address for service, which is often the applicant's own; counting it said every trade mark had an attorney.

repairs.what: A missing Australian state is taken from the applicant's postcode.
repairs.why: The register left out the state for 34.96% of recent Australian standard patents, though the postcode was there, and postcode and state agree for over 99% of rights where both exist.

repairs.what: The business or person who **filed** a right is kept beside the one who **holds** it now.
repairs.why: "Who files, and from where" and "who holds it now" are different questions; rights are often sold.

repairs.what: Each right's milestones come only from events the register still holds as standing (not later reversed), with placeholder and impossible dates left out.
repairs.why: A lapse that was later reversed did not end the right.

repairs.what: A patent priority's office is read from the number itself, not from the register's country label.
repairs.why: The register labels 93.88% of international (PCT) numbers, and many other offices' numbers, as Australian.

repairs.what: The two tie-breaks in the build (a filer with two same-day postcodes, an agent with several names) are fixed.
repairs.why: Without them a few figures changed slightly every time the table was rebuilt.

limits: The register holds only the rights that survived until it was computerised for trade marks before 1983, designs before 1986 and provisional applications before September 1985 ({U23}).
Ownership history for patents starts with those filed in FY2003 ({U17}).
Inventors' countries are known mostly for patents also filed abroad ({U95}).

timeline.name: Australia over time
timeline.unit: One row per month, January 1904 to September 2026

facts.label: monthly series of applications and events
official fee columns, from every version of the fee regulations
columns, with the labour market and IP judgments added in the review

timeline.description:
IP Australia's whole register month by month: applications of each type from Australian, overseas and unknown applicants; what happened to rights (grants, lapses, cessations, expiries, oppositions, sales, extensions of term) as counts of events; the Consumer Price Index each quarter; and the month each of 17 IP policy changes took effect.

Added after Stage 2: the official fees in force each month (and each change to them), the Reserve Bank's cash rate and exchange rates, GDP and each state's final demand from the national accounts, and the PBS's monthly cost with Section 100. Added in the review of 3 November 2026: the Labour Force Survey (employment, unemployment, participation and owner-managers) and the courts' IP judgments, January 1995 to February 2025 ({U124}).

repairs.what: Each series starts only where its records become continuous and complete; earlier months are empty, not zero.
repairs.why: Before that, the register holds survivors, partial records or events dated in batches, so a month's count is not what happened that month. Fifteen series were started by hand for this reason.

repairs.what: The rise of the standard patent term from 16 to 20 years (1 July 1995) was added as the 17th policy change.
repairs.why: Patent expiries all but stop for four years from that month; the change was missing from the policy list.

repairs.what: Trade mark registrations are counted by the date they were entered, and each event is counted once.
repairs.why: A trade mark is registered "as from" its filing date, so counting by that date measured filings, not registrations.

limits: Months before each series' start are empty on purpose; a long series is not complete back to 1904.

Comparisons of months around a policy change in Stage 1 do not allow for trends or seasons ({U28}); Stage 2's placebo months do ({B37}), and Stage 3 holds each series' trend and season with control series beside it ({M25}, {M34}).
Quarterly changes are alike from one quarter to the next, so they are worth fewer independent observations than they number; Stage 3 resamples them in blocks ({M19}, {M36}).

firms.name: Firms

facts.label: ABNs found in one of six sources
columns, with Stage 3's four counts found by name

firms.description: Every Australian Business Number that appears in IP RAPID, IP Australia's register, IPLORD, the R&D Tax Incentive, AusTender (government contracts) or the ATO's tax transparency reports, with what the business is, where it is registered, how old it is on the record, the IP it filed and holds, its R&D claims, its large-company income and its contracts. It is the businesses found in those sources, not every business in Australia, so a share of all businesses, or of all large employers, is taken over a wider count ({B50}). For employers of 100 or more, WGEA's reports add a size band and an industry; smaller firms have neither. Stage 3 added four counts of filings found by matching the filer's name to the business register, read beside the counts by ABN and never added to them ({M12}, {U126}).

repairs.what: Applications are credited to the business that filed them, not the one that holds them now.
repairs.why: Otherwise a firm's filing record would change whenever it bought or sold rights.

repairs.what: The ABNs that only IPLORD links to IP are flagged, and IPLORD's own counts are kept out.
repairs.why: IPLORD counts differently from IP RAPID; adding the two would mix measures.

repairs.what: Each contract counts once, at its latest value; R&D uses each firm's latest (amended) report.
repairs.why: Summing every amendment counted the same contract many times ($7,585.9 billion against $1,258.5 billion).

repairs.what: Age is "years since the earliest public registration", with a flag where the record may start late.
repairs.why: ABNs and GST began in 1999-2000, so a business first seen then may be much older.

limits: IP counts are lower bounds ({U41}); IP RAPID links fewer recent filers to an ABN, and IP Australia's register restores most for trade marks and designs ({U45}, {U100}).
Only large employers have an industry (from WGEA): the business register extract holds none.
Small firms' growth and survival are out of reach without the ABS's BLADE, which is ruled out.

regions.name: Places

facts.label: more sources in the companion table of area values

regions.description: Every Australian postal area (the ABS's version of a postcode) with its people, businesses, remoteness, socio-economic indexes, Census medians, the IP filed from it over FY2017 to FY2026, its R&D claimants and its government contracts. A long companion table holds every value of seven more area sources: the Census, Data by Region, business counts (CABEE), PHIDU's health and social atlas, the Clean Energy Regulator, the ATO's statistics by postcode and the Census time series (2011, 2016 and 2021).

repairs.what: Applications are counted at the filer's postcode, not the current holder's.
repairs.why: A right sold to a firm elsewhere should stay where it was filed.

repairs.what: A rate is shown only where 10 or more applications would be expected at the national rate.
repairs.why: A count of 10 has a 95% range of about 5 to 18 by chance alone; below that, an area's rate is mostly noise.

repairs.what: Small areas can be pooled into 335 larger ones (SA3s).
repairs.why: So that every area's filings count somewhere, even where its own rate is too uncertain to show.

repairs.what: Values published for other kinds of area are moved to postal areas by their 2021 residents.
repairs.why: A count can be split by where people live; a median or rate is averaged, weighted by the people shared.

limits: About one standard patent in eighteen comes from a postcode that is not a postal area, half of universities' patents among them ({U49}, {U87}).
An address is where a business is registered, not where it works.

national.name: Australia and other countries
national.unit: One row per country, year and indicator

facts.label: attached values (GII, OECD, WIPO and more)

national.description: Thirty indicators for every country, 1960 to 2025: IP filings, royalties, R&D, researchers, GDP and exports from the World Bank; filings by residents of each country at every office from WIPO; and the OECD's R&D intensity. A long companion table holds every value of the Global Innovation Index 2026, 24 OECD datasets, WIPO's other tables, Measuring What Matters and Closing the Gap, with supplementary values for four GII indicators blank for Australia, kept apart from the GII's own.

repairs.what: WIPO's filings by residents of former states (such as the Soviet Union) and of unknown origin are kept, with a column saying what each place is.
repairs.why: They had been dropped silently, losing 9.65% of WIPO's patent applications by origin.

repairs.what: Two sources were reprocessed (Closing the Gap's Australian Government column, Measuring What Matters' stacked tables).
repairs.why: 85 values sat in a side column, and 45 cells shared a key.

limits: Before 1995 WIPO cannot say where most applicants come from ({U64}).
Counts grow with a country's size; fair comparisons need ratios to people or GDP (Stage 2).

industries.name: Industries
industries.unit: One row per ANZSIC industry division and financial year

facts.label: patent crosswalks, without services (the main one) and with

industries.description: The 19 divisions of the Australian and New Zealand industry classification: IP applications assigned to industries through published crosswalks, businesses and their entries and exits, business R&D, wages and the creative industries' value added, value added by division from the national accounts, and three business surveys of innovation. Few firms in the corpus have an industry, so IP reaches industries only through what it protects: a patent's technology classes and a trade mark's classes of goods and services.

repairs.what: Each right is split over industries by probabilities (an "expected count"), so a division's count is a sum of shares.
repairs.why: A patent's technology can belong to several industries; the crosswalks give the chance of each.

repairs.what: 26 patent classes the crosswalk did not know (new or retired ones) are mapped to their predecessors.
repairs.why: Otherwise 12,143 class marks fell out of every count.

repairs.what: The step between two industry classifications no longer splits weight over partial links.
repairs.why: It had sent half of pharmaceuticals' patents to textile finishing and inorganic chemicals.

limits: The patent crosswalk in the corpus leaves out service industries, so patents reach only goods-producing ones ({U75}).
Business counts cover four recent years and business R&D one, so comparisons are of patterns, not models.

institutions.name: Research institutions
institutions.unit: One row per research institution and calendar year
institutions.description: Australia's research institutions, each identified by its Research Organization Registry (ROR) record: their research output and citations, the citations US patents make to their work, their ARC and NHMRC grants, the IP they file in Australia, those patents' families abroad and their government contracts. The link from an institution to its rights, grants and contracts is a reviewed list of names (including commercialisation companies) and ABNs. The National Survey of Research Commercialisation adds disclosures, licences, start-ups and licence income for 2000 to 2015.

repairs.what: Institutions are linked to rights, grants and contracts through a reviewed list of 116 extra names and 146 ABNs.
repairs.why: Universities file under former names, predecessors' names and their commercialisation companies' names.

repairs.what: An institution's works and citations are its own, never added across institutions or from a child to its parent.
repairs.why: A paper with authors at two institutions counts for both.

limits: Whether the reviewed list is complete has not yet been checked by someone in the sector (OQ11).
Research output is available only from 2010.

questions.title: What public value does the IP system create?
questions.text: The economic, social, technological and environmental outcomes that go with patents, trade marks and designs; the costs of getting, keeping and enforcing rights; the costs to consumers, competitors and later innovators; and what the evidence can say about the system's net contribution to public welfare.
sub: What economic, social, technological and environmental outcomes are associated with different forms of IP protection?
Under what circumstances do patents, trade marks and registered designs support innovation, commercialisation, investment, competition or knowledge diffusion?
What are the costs of obtaining, maintaining, licensing and enforcing rights?
What are the potential costs to consumers, competitors, follow-on innovators and the broader public?
What can existing evidence establish about the system's net contribution to public welfare?
reach: Counts of rights, lifetimes and citations measure activity and private use, not public value. The research goal treats them as indicators, never as success.

The costs to consumers and competitors are not in the data yet. Official fees, the most direct cost to applicants, are now in the timeline from every version of the fee regulations ({U108}); attorneys' fees are not recorded.

questions.title: Who benefits, and who is underserved?
questions.text: Which businesses, industries, regions and groups get the most from IP protection; who faces barriers to using it; and how outcomes differ between startups, small firms, large firms and research institutions, and by gender, place and circumstance, where reliable data exist.
sub: Which businesses, industries, regions and population groups derive the greatest benefits from IP protection?
Which groups face disproportionate barriers to understanding, accessing or using the system?
Are there underserved groups with substantial unrealised innovation potential?
How do outcomes differ between startups, SMEs, established businesses, research institutions and larger enterprises?
How do outcomes vary by gender, geography, socioeconomic circumstances and other relevant characteristics?
reach: Individuals in IP RAPID are pseudonymised, so their gender cannot be estimated; only inventors' can, and reliably only for inventors in Australia ({U97}).
Without the ABS's BLADE, small firms' growth and survival cannot be followed, and size and industry are known only for employers of 100 or more ({U112}).

questions.title: What determines whether IP protection produces value?
questions.text: The business, institutional and market conditions that let rights holders benefit from their IP: finance, skills, management, market access and collaboration; whether registering changes access to investment, licensing, procurement or overseas markets; and when alternatives such as trade secrets or open licensing work better.
sub: Which business, institutional and market conditions enable rights holders to commercialise or otherwise benefit from their IP?
How important are complementary capabilities such as finance, skills, management, market access and collaboration?
Does formal registration change access to investment, licensing, procurement, partnerships or international markets?
When do alternative approaches, such as trade secrets, open licensing, collaborative research or public funding, produce better outcomes?
What distinguishes successful use of registered IP from registration that produces little observable benefit?
reach: Firm-level outcomes (growth, survival, productivity) for small firms need BLADE, which is ruled out for now.
Alternatives to registration (trade secrets, open licensing) leave almost no trace in these data.

questions.title: Where are the greatest opportunities for intervention?
questions.text: The barriers that stop valuable innovation happening or reaching the market, which of them IP Australia could influence, and where funding, services, regulatory change, partnerships or better access to expertise could add public value; and where IP Australia should act itself, collaborate or advocate.
sub: Which barriers prevent potentially valuable innovation from occurring or reaching the market?
Which barriers could IP Australia materially influence?
Where might targeted funding, new services, regulatory changes, partnerships or improved access to expertise generate additional public value?
Which interventions could address market failures or institutional gaps that existing arrangements do not adequately address?
Where should IP Australia focus its own efforts, and where would collaboration or advocacy be more appropriate?
reach: Stages 1 to 3 can point to where use is uneven and what goes with it, even with other factors held; they cannot say that changing it would add value. That needs designs such as natural experiments, for any claim of additional benefit.

questions.title: What outcomes could interventions produce?
questions.text: The size, spread and timing of the benefits an intervention could bring; how much would be additional to what would happen anyway; its costs; how sensitive the results are to assumptions; and what evidence would justify scaling, changing or stopping it.
sub: What is the expected magnitude, distribution and timing of the benefits?
How much would be additional to what would occur without intervention?
What are the likely financial, administrative and opportunity costs?
How sensitive are expected results to assumptions about participation, effectiveness, economic conditions and implementation?
