What evidence would be needed to justify scaling, modifying or discontinuing an intervention?
reach: Additionality (what happens because of an intervention, compared with what would have happened anyway) needs causal designs that come after Stage 3. The policy changes in the timeline ({U28}, {B37}) are the raw material for them; most of their breaks were certain by law, and few show applicants' behaviour. With trend and season held, Raising the Bar's rush and lower level hold ({M25}), and owners did not let rights go more often after renewal fee changes ({M28}).

median.title: Median
median.short: The middle value: line everything up from smallest to largest, and the median is the one halfway along. Half are below it and half above.
median.more: Unlike the average (mean), the median is not dragged up by a few very large values, so it describes the typical case when a handful of firms or places are far larger than the rest. That is why these pages use it so often.

mean.title: Mean (average)
mean.short: The ordinary average: add everything up and divide by how many there are.
mean.more: When a few values are huge, the mean is pulled towards them and stops describing a typical case. Compare it with the median.

percentile.title: Percentile
percentile.short: The value below which a given share of things fall. The 90th percentile is the value 90% of cases are below; the 99th, the value all but the top 1% are below.
percentile.more: The median is the 50th percentile. The "middle half" runs from the 25th to the 75th.

middle-half.title: Middle half (interquartile range)
middle-half.short: The range that holds the middle 50% of values, from the 25th to the 75th percentile. A quarter of cases are below it and a quarter above.

long-tail.title: Long tail (skew)
long-tail.short: A spread where most cases are small and a few are very large. The few large ones stretch out a long "tail" to the right of a chart.
long-tail.more: In a long-tailed spread, averages mislead and shares held by the top 1% or 10% are large. Skewness is a number that measures how lopsided a spread is: 0 for a symmetric one, larger for a longer right-hand tail.

log-scale.title: Log scale
log-scale.short: An axis where each step is ten times the last (1, 10, 100, 1,000) instead of adding the same amount. It lets very small and very large values be seen on one chart.
log-scale.more: On a log scale, equal distances mean equal ratios. A spread that falls in a near-straight line on two log scales is a sign of a long tail.

concentration.title: Concentration curve
concentration.short: A line that shows how much of a total the top x% hold. Line everyone up from largest to smallest; the curve rises steeply if a few hold most of it, and follows the diagonal if everyone holds the same.
concentration.more: Read it by picking a point on the horizontal axis (say, the top 1%) and reading up to the curve: that is the share of the total they hold.

lower-bound.title: Lower bound
lower-bound.short: A number the true value is at least as large as. A firm's IP count is a lower bound because some of its rights cannot be linked to it.

nominal.title: Nominal and real dollars
nominal.short: Nominal dollars are as recorded at the time. Real dollars are adjusted for inflation, so that amounts from different years can be compared fairly.
nominal.more: Money is shown as recorded unless a page says otherwise; the official fees are also shown in June 2026 dollars, adjusted with the Consumer Price Index ({U30}, {U109}).

share-of-known.title: Share among known values
share-of-known.short: A percentage worked out only over the cases where the answer is recorded, leaving out the unknowns. It is shown only where unknowns are few, or with the unknown share beside it.

survival-curve.title: Survival curve (Kaplan–Meier)
survival-curve.short: A chart of the share of rights still in force after each number of years. It counts rights that are still in force as "unfinished", rather than dropping them or treating them as ended.
survival-curve.more: Simply averaging the lifetimes of rights that have ended would leave out every right still running, which are often the longest-lived. The Kaplan–Meier method uses each right for as long as it has been observed, so recent rights still count for the years they have lived.

unfinished.title: Unfinished (censored) cases
unfinished.short: Cases whose end has not happened yet, such as a patent still in force. Their full length is unknown, but they are known to be at least as long as they have run so far.

cohort.title: Cohort
cohort.short: A group that started at the same time, such as all patents filed in the 2000s. Comparing within a cohort is fair because everyone has had the same time to change.

funnel-plot.title: Funnel plot
funnel-plot.short: A chart of each area's rate against its size, with two curved lines showing how far from the national rate an area could fall by chance alone. Small areas swing widely by chance, so the lines flare out like a funnel.
funnel-plot.more: If differences between areas were only chance, about 95% would sit inside the 95% lines. Many points outside the lines mean the areas really do differ.

chance-limits.title: 95% limits (range due to chance)
chance-limits.short: The range a count or rate would fall in 95 times out of 100 if nothing but chance were at work. A value outside it is unlikely to be chance alone.

poisson.title: Poisson model
poisson.short: A standard model of counts of rare, independent events (such as patent filings in an area). It assumes the counts vary only by chance around one rate.

negative-binomial.title: Negative binomial model
negative-binomial.short: A model of counts that allows more spread than chance alone would give. Used when areas differ far more than a Poisson model expects, as they do here ({U53}).

expected-count.title: Expected count
expected-count.short: A count made by adding up probabilities rather than whole items. If a patent is 70% likely to belong to one industry and 30% to another, it adds 0.7 and 0.3 to their counts.

correlation.title: Correlation
correlation.short: How closely two measures move together, from −1 (one rises as the other falls) through 0 (no pattern) to +1 (they rise together). Spearman's version compares ranks rather than values.
correlation.more: A correlation is a pattern, not a cause. Stage 1 uses it only to check that two sources agree; Stage 2 uses Spearman's version to measure how strongly pairs of measures go together. As a rough guide, 0.1 is small, 0.3 moderate and 0.5 or more strong.

ratio.title: Ratio (as a check)
ratio.short: One count divided by another. A ratio of 1.000 between two sources' counts of the same thing means they agree exactly; 1.05 means the first is 5% higher.

rolling-total.title: 12-month total
rolling-total.short: The sum of the last 12 months, recalculated each month. It smooths out the seasons, so a trend is easier to see.

seasonal.title: Seasonal pattern
seasonal.short: A rise or fall that comes back at the same time each year, such as fewer filings in January. Shown as each month against an ordinary month (100).

variation.title: Variation (relative)
variation.short: How much a series moves from month to month, as a share of its average. 0.08 means a typical month is within about 8% of the average; above 1 means the series is very uneven.

outlier.title: Outlier
outlier.short: A value far from the rest. Here, usually one more than one and a half times the middle half's width beyond it (the "box-plot rule"), or a month at least three times, or under a third of, the months around it.

effect-size.title: Effect size and interval
effect-size.short: How big a difference or link is (not just whether it exists), with a range showing how sure we can be. With millions of records almost everything is "significant", so size and range matter more.

multiple-testing.title: Correction for many tests
multiple-testing.short: When hundreds of pairs are tested, some will look linked by luck. A correction raises the bar so that chance findings are not mistaken for real ones.

placebo.title: Placebo date
placebo.short: A date when nothing happened, tested as if a change had. If a "change" shows up there too, the real one may be a trend or a season, not the policy.

natural-experiment.title: Natural experiment
natural-experiment.short: A real event, such as a policy change, that affects some people and not others (or at one time and not another), so that comparing them can show what the change itself did.

additionality.title: Additionality
additionality.short: The benefit that happens because of a right, policy or service, compared with what would have happened without it. The research goal puts it ahead of simple attribution.

descriptive.title: Descriptive evidence
descriptive.short: What the data show: how much, how often, for whom, since when. No claim about why. Every Stage 1 observation is descriptive.

growth-rate.title: Average yearly growth
growth-rate.short: The steady yearly rise that would take a count from its starting value to its ending value over the years between them (compound growth).

standard-patent.title: Standard patent
standard-patent.short: The usual patent: examined in full before it is granted, and lasting up to 20 years (25 for some medicines). Headline patent figures here are for standard patents.

provisional.title: Provisional application
provisional.short: A cheap placeholder that secures a filing date for 12 months while an invention is developed. It is never granted itself; the applicant must follow it with a full application.

second-tier.title: Second-tier patent
second-tier.short: A cheaper, shorter patent for smaller steps: the petty patent (1979 to 2001) and the innovation patent (2001 to 2021). They are counted apart from standard patents.
second-tier.more: An innovation patent was granted after a check of its formalities only, and examined only if "certified" later, so its grant rate and time to grant say nothing about examination. No new ones could be filed after 25 August 2021.

trade-mark.title: Trade mark
trade-mark.short: Protection for a brand (a name, logo, sound and so on) for particular goods or services. It can be renewed indefinitely, every 10 years.

design.title: Registered design
design.short: Protection for how a product looks: its shape, pattern or ornamentation. Up to 10 years.

pbr.title: Plant breeder's right
pbr.short: Protection for a new plant variety.

pct.title: PCT (international patent application)
pct.short: The Patent Cooperation Treaty lets an inventor file one international application and later enter the countries they choose (the "national phase"), usually about 30 months after first filing.

national-phase.title: National phase
national-phase.short: The step at which an international (PCT) application enters a country. In IP RAPID, a PCT application's date is when it entered Australia.

priority.title: Priority
priority.short: An earlier filing an application relies on for its date, often abroad within the past 12 months (6 for designs), or an Australian provisional.

madrid.title: Madrid system
madrid.short: The international system for trade marks: one application, through WIPO, can cover many countries. Australia joined in 2001.

divisional.title: Divisional application
divisional.short: A new application split off from an earlier one, keeping its date. It often protects a different part of the same invention.

patent-family.title: Patent family
patent-family.short: Every application for the same invention, in every country's office. How many offices a family reaches is a common sign of how much its owner expects it to be worth.

citations.title: Forward citations
citations.short: Later patents that cite a patent as earlier work. Being cited often is a common sign that later inventions build on it; it is not a measure of value on its own.

lapse.title: Lapse
lapse.short: An application that ended before it was granted or registered, for example because fees were not paid. No lapsed right was ever granted.

cease.title: Cessation
cease.short: A granted or registered right that its owner let go, usually by not renewing it.

expiry.title: Expiry
expiry.short: A patent reaching the end of its full term (20 years for a standard patent filed since 1979).

renewal.title: Renewal
renewal.short: Paying to keep a granted right in force. A patent is renewed every year from its fourth anniversary; a trade mark every 10 years; a design once, at 5 years.

grace-period.title: Grace period
grace-period.short: Extra time after a renewal fee falls due during which the owner can still pay (six months for trade marks and designs). A right ceases on the record only after its grace period, so the latest months are incomplete.

examination.title: Examination
examination.short: IP Australia's check that an application meets the law (new, inventive, distinctive and so on). Patent applicants must ask, and pay, for it.

expedited.title: Expedited examination
expedited.short: Examination brought forward at the applicant's request, for example because an invention is being copied.

unprompted-request.title: Unprompted request for examination
unprompted-request.short: A request to examine a patent application made before IP Australia directs the applicant to ask. An applicant has five years to ask; IP Australia can direct one sooner, after which it has two months. IP Australia's commissioned study counts an unprompted request as one way of speeding examination up.

acceptance.title: Acceptance
acceptance.short: The decision that an application meets the requirements. It is advertised, and others may then oppose it before grant or registration.

opposition.title: Opposition
opposition.short: A formal challenge by someone else to an application being granted or registered.

assignment.title: Assignment
assignment.short: A recorded transfer of ownership of a right, for example when it is sold.

extension-of-term.title: Extension of term
extension-of-term.short: Up to five extra years for a standard patent on a pharmaceutical substance, to make up for time lost waiting for approval to sell it.

attorney.title: Attorney (representation)
attorney.short: A professional who files and manages applications for others. Here, an agent counts as an attorney if it acts for five or more different applicants; an agent with fewer is "another agent", and no agent but the applicant is "self".

filer.title: Filer and holder
filer.short: The filer is the person or business that applied for a right (its "founding applicant"). The holder is whoever owns it now. They differ when a right is sold.

nice.title: Nice class
nice.short: One of 45 international classes of goods and services that trade marks are filed in (class 35, for example, is advertising and business services).

ipc.title: IPC and technology fields
ipc.short: The International Patent Classification sorts patents by technology. WIPO groups its classes into 35 technology fields, such as medical technology or computer technology.

raising-the-bar.title: Raising the Bar
raising-the-bar.short: Reforms that tightened Australia's patent law from 15 April 2013. Applicants rushed to file and request examination under the old rules.

grant-rate.title: Grant rate
grant-rate.short: The share of a year's applications that were eventually granted or registered. Recent years look low because many are still being examined.

lens.title: Lens
lens.short: An analysis-ready table with one row per thing being described: an IP right, a firm, a place, a country in a year, a month, an industry in a year or a research institution in a year.

corpus.title: Corpus
corpus.short: All the public data the project has gathered, from 54 sources, before it is organised into lenses.

attachment.title: Attachment
attachment.short: Extra columns or a companion table joined to a lens from another source, such as each right's events or each area's Census values.

iprapid.title: IP RAPID
iprapid.short: IP Australia's open data on every patent, trade mark, design and plant breeder's right since 1904, updated weekly.

register.title: IP Australia's register
register.short: The live records behind IP Australia's search sites, read through its trade mark, patent and design APIs. IP RAPID is a weekly copy of it, with some fields left out.
register.more: Checked against IP RAPID on 27 October 2026, the register agreed with it for nearly every record of a random sample, and held what IP RAPID leaves out: owners' business numbers, design owners' countries and its own record of fast-tracked examination. Those fill the gaps here, beside IP RAPID's own values.

filled.title: Filled (from the register)
filled.short: A value that keeps IP RAPID's where it has one and takes IP Australia's register's where IP RAPID has none. IP RAPID's own value is kept beside it.

design-shell.title: Design shell
design-shell.short: A design record with nothing in it but its number and status: no date, owner or class in IP RAPID or in IP Australia's register. 11,098 of them, numbered 1973 to 1982, are left out.

iplord.title: IPLORD
iplord.short: An older IP Australia research dataset (to 2020) that links applicants to business numbers. Used here only as a check, because it counts differently.

manifest.title: Manifest
manifest.short: The project's register of every file: its fingerprint, size, rows and where it is kept.

fingerprint.title: Fingerprint (SHA-256)
fingerprint.short: A long code worked out from a file's contents. If one character of the file changes, the code changes, so it proves a file is the one recorded.

r2.title: Cloud storage (R2)
r2.short: A private storage bucket (Cloudflare R2) for tables too large to keep in GitHub. The manifest records them like any other file.

placeholder-date.title: Placeholder date
placeholder-date.short: A false date entered where the real one is unknown, such as 1 January 1970 (the "zero" of computer dates). Such dates are found and emptied.

survivors.title: Survivors (in old records)
survivors.short: When records were computerised, only the rights still on the register were entered. Before that point the data hold the survivors, not every application, so they understate filings and failures.

batch-dates.title: Batch dating
batch-dates.short: Events recorded on a few days a year, in bulk, so that some months show none and others several months' worth.

crosswalk.title: Crosswalk (concordance)
crosswalk.short: A published table that translates one classification into another, such as patent technology classes into industries, often with a probability for each link.

pseudonymised.title: Pseudonymised
pseudonymised.short: Names replaced by codes to protect privacy. IP RAPID does this for individual applicants.

perturbation.title: Perturbation (Census)
perturbation.short: Small random changes the ABS makes to small Census counts to protect privacy, so parts need not add exactly to totals and counts of 1 or 2 are unreliable.

gender-estimate.title: Gender estimate
gender-estimate.short: A probability that a first name in a given country is a woman's, from WIPO's name dictionary. Summed over many inventors it gives an expected number of women; it says nothing about any one person.

adr.title: Decision record (ADR)
adr.short: A short, dated note of a decision and why it was made, kept in the repository (docs/adr). Every repair to the data has one.

abn.title: ABN (Australian Business Number)
abn.short: The number that identifies a business to government. It is how this project links IP to the business register, R&D claims and government contracts.

abr.title: ABR (Australian Business Register)
abr.short: The register of every ABN, with each business's type, status, state and postcode.

gst.title: GST registration
gst.short: Registration for the goods and services tax, required once turnover reaches about $75,000 a year. A rough sign of an active, trading business.

entity-group.title: Entity group
entity-group.short: The kind of business: private company, public company, trust, sole trader, partnership, government body and so on.

postal-area.title: Postal area
postal-area.short: The ABS's version of a postcode, built from small Census areas. Post office boxes and postcodes with no residents are not postal areas.

sa3.title: SA3
sa3.short: A larger ABS area (335 in Australia), used here to pool small postal areas so that every area's filings count somewhere.

remoteness.title: Remoteness
remoteness.short: The ABS's five classes of how far a place is from services, from major cities to very remote.

irsad.title: Advantage (SEIFA, IRSAD)
irsad.short: The ABS's index of relative socio-economic advantage and disadvantage. Areas are ranked and cut into tenths (deciles): 1 is the most disadvantaged tenth of areas, 10 the most advantaged.
irsad.more: A tenth of areas is not a tenth of people: small and large areas count the same.

census.title: Census
census.short: The ABS's count of every person in Australia, every five years. Here, the 2021 Census.

cabee.title: CABEE
cabee.short: The ABS's Counts of Australian Businesses, including Entries and Exits, by industry, size and area.

rdti.title: R&D Tax Incentive
rdti.short: The government's main support for business research, through tax offsets. The ATO publishes who claims and how much.

austender.title: AusTender
austender.short: The Australian Government's register of contracts it awards, with each supplier's ABN and the contract's value.

gerd.title: GERD and BERD
gerd.short: Gross and business expenditure on research and development: all R&D spending in a country, and the part spent by businesses, usually as a percentage of GDP.

oecd-median.title: OECD median
oecd-median.short: The middle value among the 38 OECD member countries: half are above and half below.

gii.title: Global Innovation Index (GII)
gii.short: WIPO's yearly ranking of economies on 79 indicators of innovation inputs and outputs. A rank reflects WIPO's choice of indicators and weights.

wipo.title: WIPO
wipo.short: The World Intellectual Property Organization, the UN agency that runs the PCT and Madrid systems and publishes IP statistics for every country.

anzsic.title: ANZSIC
anzsic.short: The Australian and New Zealand Standard Industrial Classification, with 19 broad industry divisions such as manufacturing or construction.

ror.title: ROR
ror.short: The Research Organization Registry, an open list that gives every research institution one identifier.

openalex.title: OpenAlex
openalex.short: An open database of research publications and their citations.

go8.title: Group of Eight
go8.short: Australia's eight leading research-intensive universities (Melbourne, Sydney, Monash, UNSW, Queensland, ANU, Adelaide and Western Australia).

commercialisation-company.title: Commercialisation company
commercialisation-company.short: A company a university owns to manage its inventions, such as NewSouth Innovations (UNSW) or UniQuest (Queensland). Many patents are filed in its name.

cpi.title: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
cpi.short: The ABS's measure of how prices change over time, used to adjust dollar amounts from different years for inflation.

bcs.title: Business Characteristics Survey
bcs.short: An ABS survey of businesses' innovation, barriers and finance, published by industry and size.

screen.title: Screen (of every pair)
screen.short: Stage 2's first step in each lens: every pair of measures is measured on one scale from 0 (unrelated) to 1 (perfectly related), whatever kind of measure each is, so that nothing is chosen by hand before it is looked at.
screen.more: Two numbers are compared by Spearman's rank correlation, a number and a category by a rank version of the correlation ratio, and two categories by a corrected Cramér's V. For a yes/no measure all three give the same answer, so their strengths can be set side by side (ADR 0030).

lead.title: Lead
lead.short: A pair of measures worth following up. In Stage 2 a pair is a lead only if it passes four tests: it is at least small (a strength of 0.1), survives the correction for the number of pairs tested, holds again in a second period or sample, and is not two versions of one measure.
lead.more: A lead is a pattern to explain, not an explanation. Stage 3 tests whether it survives other factors.

halves.title: Halves (first and second half)
halves.short: Where a lens has no years to split by (firms, places, institutions' rights, the GII's economies), its rows are split at random into two halves: patterns are found in the first half and checked in the second, which played no part in finding them.
halves.more: The split uses a fixed scramble of each row's key (a hash), so every run puts each firm or area in the same half. Results are given for both, first half then second: "0.114; 0.126" means 0.114 in the first half and 0.126 in the second. Since 2 November 2026 every analysis uses the same rule (ADR 0041).

replication.title: Replication (a second sample)
replication.short: Checking a pattern again on different units: rights filed a decade earlier, or the other random half of the firms or places. A pattern that appears in one sample only may be chance or a quirk of that period.
replication.more: Where a lens has few units (19 industry divisions, about 110 research institutions, 36 OECD members), the second look is at the same units in another period. That is a [[stability-check|stability check]], not a replication.

stability-check.title: Stability check
stability-check.short: A second look at the same units at another time: the same countries a decade earlier, the same 19 industry divisions a year later, mostly the same research institutions seven years earlier. Units keep their traits, so agreement is expected whatever the relationship. It shows a pattern is stable, not that it holds in an independent sample.

no-association.title: No association detected
no-association.short: The wording used when a link between two measures is weak, or does not pass the correction for many tests: the data cannot tell it from chance at this sample size. It is not evidence that there is no link, unless an interval rules out any link that would matter.

interval.title: Interval (95%)
interval.short: A range around a number that shows how precisely it is known. If the study were repeated many times, ranges built this way would hold the true value 95 times in 100. A narrow interval means a precise estimate.
interval.more: Stage 2 uses intervals suited to each measure: Wilson's for a share, Newcombe's for a difference between two shares, Greenwood's for a survival curve, and the bootstrap for medians and correlations.

bootstrap.title: Bootstrap
bootstrap.short: A way to find an interval by resampling: draw the data again many times at random (with replacement), recompute the number each time, and see how much it moves. Stage 2 resamples whole patents or firms, not single records.

percentage-point.title: Percentage point
percentage-point.short: The difference between two percentages. A grant rate of 40.8% against 4.9% is a gap of 35.9 percentage points ("points"), not 35.9%.

third-factor.title: Third factor (confounder)
third-factor.short: Something else that could make two measures go together without one causing the other. Firm size could explain why firms with IP also win larger contracts. Stage 2 names the candidates; Stage 3 holds them steady.

simpsons-paradox.title: Simpson's paradox
simpsons-paradox.short: When a pattern in pooled data disappears or reverses within every group, because the groups' mix changed. Expedited patents look longer-lived overall only because more of them came from the filers who keep patents longest.

ecological.title: Between places, not people (ecological)
ecological.short: A link measured across areas or countries describes the areas, not the people or firms in them. Areas with more graduates file more, but that does not show that graduates are the ones who file.

standard-deviation.title: Standard deviation
standard-deviation.short: A measure of how spread out values are around their average. About two-thirds of areas lie within one standard deviation of the average advantage score, so "per standard deviation" means a typical step up or down.

rate-ratio.title: Rate ratio
rate-ratio.short: How many times higher one rate is than another. A rate ratio of 1.7 per step of advantage means each step goes with 1.7 times as many filings per person; 1 means no difference.

log-change.title: Change in logs
log-change.short: A way to measure proportional change: a change of 0.1 in logs is about a 10% rise, and -0.1 about a 10% fall. It makes a change of the same proportion the same size in a large series and a small one.

prediction-interval.title: Prediction interval
prediction-interval.short: The range within which a single new case (one country) would be expected to fall, given the pattern across the others. It is wider than the interval for the pattern itself, because single cases vary.

held-together.title: Held together (raw and adjusted)
held-together.short: A comparison made inside one model with several third factors at once, so that each is held fixed while the others are too. The raw figure is the plain comparison Stage 2 made, with nothing held; the difference between the two is how much of the raw figure those factors account for.
held-together.more: Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive.

verdict-words.title: Holds, weakened, not detected once held, reversed
verdict-words.short: Stage 3's words for what is left of a signal once its third factors are held together. Holds: the same direction, its 95% interval clear of no difference, and at least half of the raw size left. Weakened: the same direction and clear, but less than half left. Not detected once held: the interval includes no difference. Reversed: the other direction, and clear.
verdict-words.more: Where the raw figure was not itself detected: appears once held (the held one is clear) or not detected either way. "Does not replicate" marks a result seen in one sample but not the second; "mixed", a page whose parts differ; and "refined", a description that sharpens an earlier one. Ratios are compared on a log scale (ADR 0046). Not detected is not the same as no association: a moderate one may be missed.

average-marginal-effect.title: Average difference in points (average marginal effect)
average-marginal-effect.short: How a model of a yes or no outcome (granted or not, a filing linked or not) is reported here: the difference, in percentage points, between the predicted chance of the outcome with the signal and without it, averaged over every row with its other factors as they are.

clustered.title: Clustered intervals
clustered.short: Intervals that allow the rows of one group (the rights of one filer) to be alike. A firm with thousands of applications then counts as one source of evidence, not thousands, and the intervals widen accordingly.

filers-party.title: Filer's party
filers-party.short: The applicant IP RAPID records as giving a right its origin and type (the first founding applicant in Australia, else the first with a known country), identified by its party number. Stage 3 groups a filer's rights by it.

hazard-ratio.title: Hazard ratio
hazard-ratio.short: From a model of how long rights stay in force: how much more or less likely a right in one group is to end in any given year than one in another, with other factors held. 0.8 means 20% less likely to end, so more often still in force; 1 means no difference.
hazard-ratio.more: Stage 3 uses a proportional hazards (Cox) model and counts each patent from its grant, as Stage 2's survival curves do (delayed entry).

principal-components.title: Principal components
principal-components.short: A way to summarise many related measures in a few combined ones. Each component is a weighted mix of all the measures, and the first carries as much of the variation as any single mix can; the weights show what it stands for.

variance-inflation.title: Variance inflation
variance-inflation.short: How far one measure can be predicted from the others. Above about 5 to 10, the measures repeat one another, so holding them all at once, or reading any one alone, can mislead.

silhouette.title: Silhouette (how distinct groups are)
silhouette.short: A score from -1 to 1 for a grouping of places or units: how much closer each is to its own group than to the next. Stage 3 reads groups as distinct only at 0.5 or more, and as some structure from 0.25.

partial-correlation.title: Partial rank correlation
partial-correlation.short: The correlation of two measures' ranks once what the held factors explain has been taken out of both. It reads an association beyond those factors without assuming straight lines, for small sets of units such as countries, industries or institutions.

cointegration.title: Cointegration
cointegration.short: Two series that each wander over time but keep a stable distance from each other in the long run: they share a path. A test of it (Engle-Granger, here) asks whether the gap between them keeps returning to its usual size.

block-resampling.title: Block resampling (moving-block bootstrap)
block-resampling.short: A bootstrap for series over time: resamples are built from runs of consecutive periods (8 quarters, say), so that alike neighbouring periods stay together. Its intervals are wider, and more honest, than resampling single periods.

effective-sample.title: Effective sample size
effective-sample.short: How many independent observations a series of dependent ones is worth: 68 quarters that each resemble the last may carry the information of 23 independent ones.

exposure.title: Exposure (in a model of counts)
exposure.short: What a count is a rate of: an area's residents, a university's works, an institution's research spend. The model then compares rates without dividing every measure by the same number, which can make unrelated measures look linked.

fixed-age.title: Compared at a fixed age
fixed-age.short: Citations counted over the same span for every work or patent (within five years of priority, or against works of the same publication year), since an older one has had longer to be cited.

within-filers.title: Within the same filers
within-filers.short: A comparison made inside each filer and then averaged: each filer's own average is taken out first, so the result says how the same filers changed, not how the mix of filers did.

stl.title: Trend, season and the rest (STL)
stl.short: A way to split a monthly series into a slowly changing trend, a pattern that repeats each year, and what is left. Its strength measures (0 to 1) say how much of the series each accounts for; above about 0.6 is strong.

interrupted.title: Interrupted time series
interrupted.short: A before-and-after reading of a series around a change (a new law, a fee change): the series' trend and season are held, and the model measures a rush before the change, a step in level after it and a change in slope, set beside series the change should not have moved.

newey-west.title: Newey-West interval
newey-west.short: An interval for a model of a series over time that allows neighbouring months to be alike (here, over 12 months), so that it is not too narrow.

trend-either-side.title: Trend either side
trend-either-side.short: A before-and-after comparison that fits a straight-line trend on each side of a change, each with its own slope, so that a gradual drift is not read as a jump at the change.

let-go.title: Let go (at an anniversary)
let-go.short: A right whose owner did not pay the fee due at an anniversary, so that it ceased: for patents, a cessation dated 3 to 12 months after the anniversary (the six-month grace period ends first); for trade marks and designs, one dated at the anniversary.

gamma.title: Gamma model
gamma.short: A model for positive amounts that are skewed (a few very large contract values or incomes), reported as a ratio of averages.

tweedie.title: Tweedie model
tweedie.short: A model for amounts that are often zero and otherwise skewed, such as an institution's licence income.

name-match.title: Name match (to the business register)
name-match.short: An ABN found for an Australian organisation's right that has none, by matching the filer's name to the ABR's main names and ASIC's company names, kept only if exactly one ABN has the name in the filer's state. Tested on rights with a known ABN; kept apart from the counts, never added to them (ADR 0045, 0047).

observational.title: Observational evidence
observational.short: Two things are seen to go together in data that were not designed to test a cause. Other explanations remain possible. Most of Stage 2's observations are of this kind.

official-fees.title: Official fees
official-fees.short: The fees IP Australia charges to file, examine, register and renew a right, set in regulations. They do not include attorneys' fees, which are often larger.

cash-rate.title: Cash rate
cash-rate.short: The interest rate on overnight loans between banks, which the Reserve Bank of Australia targets to steer the economy. It rises in booms and falls in downturns, so it tracks the business cycle.

gdp.title: GDP and value added
gdp.short: Gross domestic product: the value of everything produced in Australia in a period. Value added is the same measure for one industry. "Real" or "chain volume" figures remove the effect of rising prices.

wgea.title: WGEA
wgea.short: The Workplace Gender Equality Agency. Employers of 100 or more report to it each year, and it publishes each one's size band and industry by ABN: the only free source of firms' size and industry.

nsrc.title: National Survey of Research Commercialisation (NSRC)
nsrc.short: A survey of universities, research agencies and medical research institutes, 2000 to 2015: invention disclosures, patents, licences, start-ups and licence income.

asic.title: ASIC
asic.short: The Australian Securities and Investments Commission, which registers companies. Its register gives a company's registration date, one of the dates used to estimate a firm's age.

observations.headline: The corpus holds 194 tables from 54 sources, and three sources hold two thirds of its rows
observations.statement: When the corpus was last profiled, on 4 November 2026, it held 194 tables from 54 sources, 335,184,272 rows in all. Three sources hold 66.11% of the rows: IP RAPID (29.93%), TM-Link (23.57%) and the OECD's panels (12.61%).

sources

points: Row counts measure how much a source records, not how much it matters to the research questions. So the analysis is organised by unit of analysis (rights, firms, places, countries), not by the size of a source.

**Corrected on 4 November 2026.** The observation still gave the profile of 25 October (162 tables, 41 sources, 317,792,796 rows, three sources 69.73%), though 13 sources had been added since, with 29 tables, and eight tables rebuilt (the ABN spine from 398,450 to 463,279 rows, for one). The profile was re-run and the observation now follows it.

**Corrected on 27 October 2026.** The observation's text had kept the first corpus profile (152 tables, 38 sources, 314,742,745 rows, three sources 70.4%), while the output above it had the later one. The text now follows the output, as every observation must.

questions.how: Sets out the raw material every later answer will rest on, and warns that size is not importance.

prep.what: A profile of the corpus lists every processed table with its source, rows, columns and where it is kept.
prep.why: A single list makes it possible to check what the analysis can draw on.

steps: Read the corpus profile, one line per table.
Check that every table opens and that its rows match the manifest.
Count the tables and the distinct sources, and add up the rows.
Rank the sources by rows and work out each one's share of all rows.
assumptions: The profile was made on 4 November 2026, and covers every processed table the corpus's manifest lists that day. Every table opened, and its rows matched the manifest.
limits: Rows are a poor guide to importance. The World Bank's few thousand values for Australia matter as much to some questions as millions of trade mark records.
observations.next: Every later stage reads the corpus through the lenses. The profile is re-run whenever a source is added.

#### Observation U0 (descriptive; a worked example of the format)

- **Size.** The corpus holds 194 tables from 54 sources: 335,184,272 rows in all.
- **Concentration.** Three sources hold 66.11% of the rows: IP RAPID (29.93%), TM-Link (23.57%) and the OECD panels
  (12.61%).
- **Correction (4 November 2026).** This observation said 162 tables from 41 sources (317,792,796 rows; three sources
  69.73%: IP RAPID 31.57%, TM-Link 24.86%, the OECD 13.3%), from the profile of 25 October, though the corpus had
  grown since. 13 sources were added with 29 tables (among them `ror`, IP Australia's register and API harvests,
  `ipa_provisionals`, the fee history, the Reserve Bank, the national accounts and the ATO's postcode statistics);
  three tables were added to existing sources (two concordances with services, and the PBS's monthly series); and
  eight were rebuilt (among them the ABN spine, 398,450 to 463,279 rows, and the policy register, 16 to 56 events).
  The profile was re-run on 4 November and the two cells above re-run alone; every table opens and its rows match the
  manifest. The chart's source line, which gave the first profile's date (22 October), now gives this one.
- **Correction (27 October 2026).** This observation said 152 tables from 38 sources (314,742,745 rows, three sources
  70.4%): the first corpus profile, of 23 October. The output above reads the profile re-run on 25 October, which
  adds `abs_labour`, `abs_prices` and `google_patents_inventors`. Sources added since (`ror`, and the WIPO
  tables of ADR 0022) are not in either profile.
- **What this means for the EDA.** Row counts measure how much a source records, not how much it matters to the
  research questions. This notebook is therefore ordered by unit of analysis (rights, firms, places, countries), not
  by size, and the largest sources enter through the lenses built from them.

observations.headline: Five problems in the register were repaired before anything was measured
observations.statement: Profiling found five quirks: a false end date (1 January 1970) on 1,282 rights; one trade mark registered before the register began; 121,207 old trade marks "registered" on the day they were filed; a "technology area" that only repeated the class for trade marks and designs; and an attorney flag that counted applicants as their own attorneys. Each was repaired.

figures.label: rights with a false end date of 1 January 1970
trade marks before 1986 dated as registered when filed
Australian trade marks with an attorney, before and after the repair

points: **The false end date.** 1,279 trade marks and 3 designs "ended" on 1 January 1970, though they were filed from 18 July 2013 and 3 March 2020. That date is the zero of computer clocks, standing in for an unknown date.
**Registered on filing.** Of 122,980 trade marks registered before 1986, 121,207 (98.6%) were registered the day they were filed: the register holds only their filing date.
**A class, not a technology.** For all 2,335,057 trade marks and 248,748 designs with a "technology area", it equalled the class of goods.

**Attorneys.** The register's "agent" is the address for service, often the applicant itself. Counting only an agent who is not the applicant, attorney use by Australian applicants (FY2017 to FY2026) is 57.02% for trade marks, 71.65% for designs, 82.62% for patents and 41.21% for plant breeder's rights, instead of 100%, 100%, 93.31% and 52.22%.
Counting only agents who act for five or more applicants gives 49.52% for Australian trade marks, so the repaired flag may still include some agents who are not attorneys.

questions.how: Who uses an attorney is a question about access and cost; the unrepaired flag would have said everyone does.
Reliable attorney use is needed before asking whether professional help is a barrier IP Australia could ease.

prep.what: The four repairs shown here are made in the code that builds the table, with the evidence kept in the notebook from IP RAPID's own tables.
prep.why: So that anyone can see both the problem and the fix, and the original data are never altered.

steps: Look for dates that cannot be true (before the register began, or a computer's default date).
Compare trade marks' registration dates with their filing dates before 1986.
Compare the "technology area" with the class for every type of right.
For each right, check whether its agent is one of its own applicants, by identity number or by name.
Recount attorney use without those self-agents.
assumptions: An agent with the same name as the applicant (ignoring case and punctuation) is the applicant acting for itself.
limits: The repaired attorney flag may still count some agents who are not professional attorneys, such as a related company (up to about 8 points for Australian trade marks).
observations.next: Every later observation uses the repaired columns. Stage 2 uses attorney use with bounds for trade marks ({U20}).
observations.section: 1.0 Data overview and sanity checks
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U2 (descriptive). Five repairs, made before the profiles below (ADR 0012).** The evidence for each is in IP RAPID's
own tables above (the state's is in 1.7).
1. **A placeholder end date.** 1,282 rights (1,279 trade marks and 3 designs) "ended" on 1 January 1970, though the
   earliest of them was filed on 18 July 2013 (trade marks) or 3 March 2020 (designs). It is the zero of computer
   dates standing in for an unknown date, so it is now empty.
2. **A registration before the register began.** One trade mark is registered before 1904, earlier than the
   register's first application (13 February 1904). Now empty.
3. **Trade marks registered at filing.** Of the 122,980 trade marks registered before 1986, 121,207 (98.6%) were
   registered on the day they were filed: IP RAPID holds only their filing date, as the timeline found (ADR 0010).
   Their days to registration, almost always 0, are now empty; the registration date itself is kept.
4. **A technology area that was really a class.** For all 2,335,057 trade marks and 248,748 designs with a
   "technology area", it equals the main class: the Nice or Locarno class, repeated. It is now kept for patents only.
5. **Attorneys.** IP RAPID's "agent" is the *address for service*. It names one for 100% of trade marks and of
   Australian applicants' designs, but for Australian applicants it is often the applicant itself. Counting only an
   agent who is not one of the right's applicants, attorney use by Australian applicants (FY2017 to FY2026) is 57.02%
   for trade marks, 71.65% for designs, 82.62% for patents and 41.21% for plant breeder's rights. For overseas
   applicants it barely changes (96.27% to 98.69% for trade marks, designs and patents). Counting only agents who act
   for five or more different applicants gives 49.52% for Australian trade marks, so the repaired flag may still
   include some agents who are not attorneys (a director, say, or a related business): up to about 8 points for
   Australian trade marks.

observations.headline: The busiest filing days came just before rules changed, and 50,763 old rights cannot be placed in time
observations.statement: The most common application date is 12 April 2013 (1,856 rights), the Friday before the Raising the Bar reforms took effect. The most common earliest filing date is 25 August 2021 (1,342 rights), the day before innovation patents closed. 50,763 rights have no application date: 50,711 patents, 45 designs, 6 plant breeder's rights and 1 trade mark.

figures.label: rights filed on 12 April 2013, the busiest day
earliest filings on 25 August 2021
rights with no application date

points: Applications run from 13 February 1904 to 17 October 2026.
14 end dates fall after the corpus was built (22 October 2026), the latest on 27 April 2029; they are left as recorded.

Of the 50,711 undated patents, 50,488 are standard patents, almost all of unknown origin (50,442) and unknown status (49,737); 203 were ever registered (202 of them second-tier). They are old records that cannot be placed in time, so counts by year leave them out: 2.9% of patents. 11,098 design records with nothing in them are dropped ({U104}).

questions.how: A rush before a rule change shows applicants responding to policy, which is what interventions rely on.
Dated rushes are the starting point for the before-and-after comparisons that later estimate what a policy did.

prep.what: Each date column is checked for its range, its most common day and any day after the corpus was built.
prep.why: Odd dates reveal placeholders, data entry patterns or real events.

steps: For each date column, find the earliest and latest date and the day with the most rights.
Compare the busiest days with the dates of policy changes in the policy register.
Count rights with no application date, and what else is known about them.
assumptions: The busiest days are linked to the rule changes by their timing alone; Stage 1 does not test the link.
limits: A rush shows timing, not why individual applicants filed.
observations.next: Stage 2 measures the rushes against trends and seasons, with placebo dates ({U28}).

observations.headline: Standard patent applications held steady over the last ten years, while trade marks and designs rose
observations.statement: In FY2017 to FY2026 there were 28,798 to 32,960 standard patent applications a year. Trade marks rose from 72,652 (FY2017) to 98,189 (FY2026), designs from 7,727 to 10,388, and plant breeder's rights fell from 413 to 255. Second-tier patents peaked at 7,150 in FY2021, the year innovation patents closed, then fell to 52 (FY2026).

figures.label: standard patent applications in FY2026
trade mark applications in FY2026
provisional applications in FY2026, double the usual

points: Provisional applications ran at 4,143 to 5,343 a year in FY2017 to FY2025, then doubled to 10,069 in FY2026 ({U8}).

In the chart, standard patents of "origin unknown" give way to "overseas" ones between about 1975 and 1990; from FY1990 at most 0.45% a year are of unknown origin (FY1993). The change is in what the register records, not necessarily in who filed.

**Corrected.** Before 1983 for trade marks, 1986 for designs and September 1985 for provisional applications, the register holds only the rights still alive when it was computerised, so those early counts understate filings ({U23}).

questions.how: The volume of each kind of right over time is the basic measure of activity the later questions build on.
Sudden changes (the second-tier closure, the provisional rise) mark where policy or behaviour shifted.

prep.why: IP Australia and the government report by financial year.

prep.why: It is a part year, and would look like a fall.

prep.what: Origin has three values (Australian, overseas, unknown).
prep.why: Treating unknowns as overseas had inflated overseas filing for old patents (ADR 0009).

steps: Count applications by financial year, type of right and the applicants' origin.

observations.headline: About nine in ten standard patents come from overseas; most trade marks come from Australians
observations.statement: Among applications whose origin is known, Australian applicants filed 11.3% of standard patents in FY1990 and 12.4% in FY1995, then about 8% to 11.5% (9.3% in FY2026). They filed 55.9% to 62.8% of trade marks in the years shown since FY2018, and 91.8% to 98.1% of provisional applications.

of trade marks filed by Australians in FY2026

points: **Who counts as Australian.** An application is Australian if an applicant who filed it was in Australia, IP Australia's definition of a resident application. Counting the current owner instead moves the shares by at most 0.7 points for standard patents, 1.6 for designs and 4.4 for plant breeder's rights.

**Second-tier patents** were 79.2% to 87.4% Australian in FY1990 to FY2010, down to 16.2% in FY2021, when overseas applicants filed before the closure, and 61.8% to 75% in FY2024 to FY2026, on 52 to 123 filings a year.
**Plant breeder's rights:** 41.7% to 52% Australian since FY1995.

**Designs:** origin is unknown for 20.2% to 25.1% in FY1990 to FY2000 and 4.0% to 6.3% since FY2018, so a share can be given only in a few recent years (27.6% to 35.5% in FY2018 to FY2022). With IP Australia's register filling the gaps ({U102}), designs filed FY2017 to FY2026 are 32.64% Australian, with 0.083% of unknown origin.
**Decision.** Australian shares are compared from FY1990, and a design share is always shown with its unknown share.

A patent system used mostly from overseas raises different questions about public value from one used mostly at home.

prep.what: An application is Australian if a founding applicant (one named when it was filed) was in Australia, IP Australia's definition of a resident application; overseas if none was and at least one has a known country; unknown otherwise.
prep.why: Three values keep the unknowns out of both groups (ADR 0009), and the filer's origin does not change when a right is sold or assigned (ADR 0037).

prep.what: A share is shown only in years when fewer than 5% of that type's applications are of unknown origin.
prep.why: With many unknowns, a share of the known ones could be badly off.

steps: Count each type's applications by year and origin.
Work out the share of unknown origin for each year.

assumptions: An applicant's recorded country is where it is based.

observations.headline: Provisional applications doubled in FY2026, mostly from individuals but from organisations too
observations.statement: FY2026 had 10,069 provisional applications, against 4,143 to 5,047 a year in FY2022 to FY2025. In 5,510 the first applicant named at filing was an individual, against 1,413 to 1,986 a year before; in 4,558 it was an organisation, against 2,751 (FY2024) and 3,060 (FY2025). The rise began in early 2025, peaked in March and April 2026, and had eased by September 2026.

figures.label: provisional applications in FY2026
of them with an individual as first applicant
with an organisation as first applicant, up from 3,060

points: **When.** 345 in March 2024, 481 in March 2025, 1,274 in March 2026 and 1,231 in April 2026, then 750 by September 2026, still about twice March 2024's level.
**Broad.** Individuals who filed a single provisional rose from 1,538 (FY2025) to 2,507 (FY2026).
**And concentrated.** 54 individuals filed 10 or more each (1,528 between them), against 9 who filed 183 in FY2025; one filed 375. 45 organisations filed 10 or more (1,258), against 24 (566).

**Businesses cannot be told apart yet.** Provisionals with a filer's business number rose only from 2,270 to 2,610, and distinct business numbers stayed at 1,342 to 1,415 a year. But the latest filings carry fewer business numbers than earlier ones ({U45}), so this does not show that businesses' provisionals held steady.

questions.how: A sudden change in who files provisionals is something IP Australia would want explained. Possible reasons (a new filing channel, a change in cost, new drafting tools) are not in these data; they are for IP Australia and later stages to test.
Individuals are the group most likely to file without help; who they are matters for who the system serves.

prep.what: Provisional applications are counted apart from standard patents, by the type of the first applicant named when each was filed (its founding applicant, ADR 0037).
prep.why: A provisional is a placeholder, and individuals and organisations use it differently. Counting by the current applicant instead moves the counts only slightly.

prep.what: Each founding applicant's provisionals in a year are counted, to see whether the rise is broad or from a few.
prep.why: Many single filers and a few heavy filers point to different explanations.

steps: Count provisional applications by month since July 2021, split by individual or organisation.
Count them by year, with the number of distinct business numbers and those from overseas, and set the business numbers beside how completely the latest filings record them ({U45}).
For FY2025 and FY2026, count founding applicants by how many provisionals each filed (1, 2 to 9, 10 or more).
assumptions: The rise is in filing, not in recording. The owner confirmed that the register keeps provisionals once they are claimed (ADR 0010).
limits: The data show who and when, not why. That is a question for IP Australia (OQ5).
Whether businesses' provisionals rose cannot be read while recent filings lack business numbers (OQ7).
observations.next: Stage 2 lines the months up against policy and fee events, with IP Australia's own published figures as the benchmark.
observations.section: 1.2 Applications over time (`filing_fy`)
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U8 (descriptive). The rise in provisional applications is real, broad and partly concentrated.**
- **When.** In March 2024 there were 345 provisionals (105 with an individual as first founding applicant). The rise
  starts in early 2025 (481 in March 2025) and peaks in March and April 2026 (1,274 and 1,231, of which 756 and 733 by
  individuals). By September 2026 it has eased to 750 (333 by individuals), still about twice March 2024's level.
- **How much.** FY2026 had 10,069 provisionals, against 4,143 to 5,047 a year in FY2022 to FY2025. 5,510 had an
  individual as first founding applicant, against 1,413 to 1,986.
- **Mostly from individuals, but not only.** Provisionals whose first founding applicant is an organisation rose
  too, from 2,751 (FY2024) and 3,060 (FY2025) to 4,558 (FY2026), against individuals' 1,413, 1,986 and 5,510.
  Distinct filers' ABNs stayed flat (1,372 in FY2026; 1,342 to 1,415 before), and provisionals with a filer's ABN
  rose only from 2,270 to 2,610; but IP RAPID's latest filings carry fewer filers' ABNs than earlier ones (U45), so
  the flat count does not show that businesses' provisionals did not rise.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** this bullet was headed "Not from businesses", though organisations' provisionals rose by about
  half in FY2026.
- These are the filers (founding applicants, ADR 0037); first given by the current applicants, which moves them by up
  to 111 (5,399 individuals' provisionals in FY2026 by the current first applicant).
- **Broad.** Individuals who filed a single provisional rose from 1,538 (FY2025) to 2,507 (FY2026).
- **And concentrated.** 54 individuals filed 10 or more each (1,528 between them), against 9 who filed 183 in FY2025;
  one filed 375. 45 organisations filed 10 or more (1,258), against 24 (566).
- Why is outside these data. Stage 2 lines the months up against the policy and fee events, and IP Australia's own
  published figures are the benchmark (the plan's item 4).

later.what: Individuals with 10 or more provisionals that year followed up 5.46% in FY2025 against 22.38% before: the heavy filers behind the surge follow up much less.

observations.headline: "Lapsed" and "ceased" mean different things, and 408,957 old patents have no known outcome
observations.statement: Under 0.01% of lapsed patents, trade marks and designs were ever registered, against 99.93% of ceased patents, 100% of ceased trade marks and 98.27% of ceased designs: a lapse is an application abandoned, a cessation a registered right let go. 408,957 patents filed before FY2000 have the status "unknown", with no registration or end date.

figures.label: old patents with an unknown status
of expired patents have a grant date (all were granted)
of standard patents are in force today

points: "Unknown" patents were filed between FY1904 and FY1999 (median FY1961): 27% of standard patents.
Only 68.9% of expired patents have a grant date, though only a granted patent can expire, so old grants are under-recorded.

Where rights stand today (all years): trade marks 41% in force, 26% ended before registration and 28% after; designs 26% in force and 64% ended after registration; standard patents 12% in force and 7% pending; provisional applications 90% ended before grant, as they are meant to.

questions.how: How often rights are granted, kept or let go is basic to any measure of their value.

prep.what: IP RAPID's 27 statuses are grouped into stages (pending, in force, ended before grant, ended after grant, other, unknown).
prep.why: Six stages can be compared across types; 27 statuses cannot. The grouping is by status name, and the table in the notebook shows how well it holds.

steps: For each status, work out how often its rights were ever registered and have an end date.
Group statuses into stages and work out each type's share in each.
assumptions: A status's name describes its rights; the registration check confirms this for lapsed and ceased.
limits: For old patents the register does not know what happened, so rates involving them understate grants.
observations.next: Lifetimes are measured from each right's end date with survival curves ({U36}).
observations.section: 1.3 Status and how rights end
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U9 (descriptive). How rights end.**
- **"Lapsed" and "ceased" differ, as the lead said.** Under 0.01% of lapsed patents, trade marks and designs were ever
  registered, against 99.93% of ceased patents, 100% of ceased trade marks and 98.27% of ceased designs. A lapse is an
  application abandoned; a cessation is a registered right let go.
- **"Unknown" is old patents.** 408,957 patents have the status "unknown". All were filed between FY1904 and FY1999
  (median FY1961), and none has a registration or end date: the register does not know what became of them. They are
  27% of standard patents (393,027) and 6% of provisional applications (15,930).
- **Old grants are under-recorded.** Only 68.9% of expired patents have a grant date, though only a granted patent can
  expire (they were filed FY1904 to FY2025, median FY1993). So "ever registered" understates grants among old patents.
- **Where rights stand today (all years):** trade marks 41% in force, 26% ended before registration and 28% after;
  designs 26% in force and 64% ended after registration; standard patents 12% in force and 7% pending; provisional
  applications 90% ended before grant, as they are meant to. (Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043): the
  designs' shares were given as 24% and 66%; the table's 65,831 and 165,274 of 257,684 are 25.5% and 64.1%.)

observations.headline: The share of standard patent applications granted fell to 54.4% for FY2008's, then recovered
observations.statement: 74.6% of FY1990's standard patent applications were granted and 75.5% of FY2000's, but only 54.4% of FY2008's; then 61.4% (FY2010), 69.0% (FY2015) and 65.4% (FY2019). Trade marks rose from 52.1% registered (FY1990) to 80.7% (FY2019).

figures.label: of FY2008's standard patent applications were granted
of FY2019's trade mark applications were registered

points: **Designs:** 78.3% (FY1990) and 79.8% (FY2000), then about 95% from FY2010.
**Second-tier patents:** 90.0% to 98.4% from FY2008 to FY2024. This is not a pass rate: an innovation patent was granted after a check of formalities only.
**Still pending:** standard patents 2.0% of FY2021's applications, 12.2% of FY2022's and 49.1% of FY2024's.
**Decision.** Rates are compared only for years whose applications are nearly all decided: to FY2021 for standard patents, FY2024 for trade marks.

questions.how: How often applications succeed is part of what the system costs applicants and what it delivers.
Changes in grant rates may follow changes in law or practice, which IP Australia controls.

prep.what: The share registered is worked out for each financial year of filing, among all that year's applications.
prep.why: Following each year's applications to their outcome avoids mixing old and new applications.

steps: For each type and filing year, count the applications ever registered or granted.
Divide by all of that year's applications; separately, count those still pending.
Mark the recent years whose applications are still being examined.
assumptions: An application with a registration date was registered; a missing date means it was not (except for old patents, {U9}).
limits: Recent years look low only because many are still being decided.
Before 1983 (trade marks) and 1986 (designs) only survivors are recorded, so their rates look too high ({U23}).
observations.next: Stage 2 compares grant rates by origin, applicant and representation, within decided years.

observations.original:
**U10 (descriptive). Grant and registration rates by year of application.**
- **Standard patents:** 74.6% of FY1990's applications and 75.5% of FY2000's were granted, but only 54.4% of FY2008's;
  then 61.4% (FY2010), 69.0% (FY2015) and 65.4% (FY2019).
- **Trade marks:** 52.1% (FY1990), 63.2% (FY2000), 70.1% (FY2010) and 80.7% (FY2019).

- **Second-tier patents:** 90.0% to 98.4% from FY2008 to FY2024. This is not a pass rate: an innovation patent was

- **Still pending:** standard patents 2.0% of FY2021's applications, 12.2% of FY2022's and 49.1% of FY2024's; trade

observations.headline: A standard patent takes a median 980 days to grant; a trade mark 223 days to register
observations.statement: For applications filed FY2010 to FY2019, standard patents took a median 980 days (about 2.7 years) to grant, the middle half 681 to 1,318 days. Trade marks took a median 223 days, with a sharp peak at about 222 days; WIPO gives IP Australia's average time from filing to registration in 2016 as 222 days ({U70}), so the peak matches the office's usual path.

figures.label: median time to grant a standard patent
median time to register a trade mark
median for plant breeder's rights

points: 99% of standard patents are granted within 2,156 days; 99% of trade marks within 1,081, with a long tail.
Designs take a median 33 days and second-tier patents 21; an innovation patent was granted after a check of formalities only, so its 21 days are not compared with standard patents'.
57 values remain negative (registered before filed), down from 1,497 before the repairs. They are left as recorded.

questions.how: Time to protection is part of the cost of using the system, and something the office can influence.
Differences in waiting time by applicant group would bear on who is well served.

prep.what: Only applications filed FY2010 to FY2019 and since registered are used.
prep.why: By 2026 at most 0.1% of them are pending, so the times are not cut short by applications still in examination.

steps: Take every application filed FY2010 to FY2019 that was later registered or granted.
Work out the days from application to registration for each.
Summarise each type's spread (median, middle half, 99th percentile), and check the shape at several bin widths.
assumptions: The registration date is when protection was granted, as recorded.
limits: These are the times of successful applications only.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares times by origin, applicant and attorney use, within decided years.
observations.section: 1.4 Time to registration (`days_to_registration`)
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U11 (descriptive). How long registration takes, for applications filed FY2010 to FY2019.**
- **Standard patents:** median 980 days (about 2.7 years); the middle half take 681 to 1,318 days, and 99% are granted
  within 2,156. The shape is one hump, slightly skewed to the right (skew 0.50), at every bin width.
- **Trade marks:** median 223 days; the middle half take 211 to 298, with a long tail to the right (99% within 1,081
  days; skew 3.7). A sharp peak at about 222 days holds the most common value of the whole column (222 days, 3.9% of
  values, in the overview). It looks like the shortest path through examination and the opposition period: first a
  lead; WIPO gives IP Australia's average time from filing to registration in 2016 as 222 days (U70), so the peak
  matches the office's usual path (pointer added 2 November 2026, pass 8).
- **Designs** take a median 33 days, **second-tier patents** 21, and **plant breeder's rights** 1,296 (about 3.5
  years), with the widest spread (the middle half 868 to 1,932 days). An innovation patent was granted after a check
  of its formalities only, so its 21 days are not a time to examination and are not compared with standard
  patents'.
- 57 values remain negative (53 trade marks, 3 patents and 1 design), down from the 1,497 noted while building the
  lens, after repair 3. They are left as recorded.

prep.what: The median wait is worked out for each financial year of filing, FY1990 to FY2021.
prep.why: Later years are still being examined, so their medians would be too short.

steps: For each type and filing year, take the median days from application to registration, among those registered.
Convert to years and plot over time.
assumptions: Changes in the median reflect changes in processing and applicants' choices together; Stage 1 does not separate them.

observations.headline: About nine in ten standard patents filed in FY2017 to FY2026 came from overseas, 43.6% from the United States
observations.statement: Of standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026 with a known origin, 8.745% came from Australian filers, so 91.3% came from overseas. By the country of the first filer, the United States accounts for 43.6% of all standard patents, Australia 8.6%, China 6.9% and Japan 5.2%. Australians filed 59.19% of trade marks and 94.62% of provisional applications.

figures.label: of standard patents came from overseas
had a first filer in the United States
of trade marks came from Australians

points: **Designs:** 30.44% Australian, with 5.058% of unknown origin. With IP Australia's register filling the gaps ({U102}), 32.64% are Australian, with 0.083% of unknown origin.

**Individuals.** An individual is the Australian filer on 21.43% of Australian standard patents, against 4.3% of overseas ones; on 41.05% of Australian provisional applications, 43.1% of second-tier patents and 24.96% of trade marks.

**Business numbers.** 69.28% of Australian standard patents carry a filer's ABN in IP RAPID, as do 87.35% of those filed by Australian organisations and 78.6% of Australian organisations' trade marks. So 13% to 21% of organisations' applications have no ABN in IP RAPID; for trade marks and designs, IP Australia's register fills most of them ({U99}, {U100}). Plant breeder's rights carry no ABN.

**Agents.** Australian filers named an agent other than themselves (usually an attorney) on 86.81% of standard patents, 70.9% of designs, 66.66% of second-tier patents, 57.08% of trade marks and 41.47% of plant breeder's rights; overseas filers on 89.95% to 99.13%. Filing without an agent is common among Australians, above all for trade marks, and rare from overseas.
81,404 rights have no founding applicant recorded, all of unknown origin (5.305% of standard patents and 1.571% of designs, all years).

questions.how: The basic profile of who files: countries, individuals against organisations, with and without help.
A patent system used mostly by overseas applicants raises its own questions about where its benefits flow.

prep.what: The ten latest complete years, FY2017 to FY2026, are used.
prep.why: A recent decade describes the system as it is now.

prep.what: Who applied is the filer, the applicants named when the application was filed (its founding applicants). Origin and type are taken from one of them, the first in Australia, or else the first with a known country (ADR 0037).
prep.why: The filer does not change when a right is sold or assigned, and an application with an Australian founding applicant is what IP Australia counts as a resident application.

steps: For each type, work out the Australian share among applications of known origin.
Count standard patents by the country of the first founding applicant.
Among Australian filers, work out the shares that are individuals, that carry a filer's ABN, and that name an agent other than themselves.
assumptions: The first founding applicant's country stands for the application's country when countries are ranked.
limits: Counts by the first filer leave out co-applicants from other countries.
Shares are of applications, not of distinct filers, so a frequent filer counts many times.
Counting the current holder instead of the filer moves the shares only slightly (standard patents 8.675% Australian rather than 8.745%).

observations.original:
**U13 (descriptive). Who applied, FY2017 to FY2026.** Who applied is the filer: the founding applicants, with origin
and type taken from one party (`filer_group`: the first founding applicant in Australia, else the first with a known
country; ADR 0037). Shares are of applications, not of distinct filers.
- **Australian share (known origin):** standard patents 8.745%, so 91.3% came from overseas; trade marks 59.19%;
  designs 30.44% (with 5.058% of unknown origin); second-tier patents 33.86%; plant breeder's rights 44.3%;
  provisional applications 94.62%.
  Restated with the register (U102): designs 32.64% Australian, with 0.083% of unknown origin.
- **The first founding applicant's country, standard patents** (the chart): the United States 132,926 (43.6%),
  Australia 26,347 (8.6%), China 20,962 (6.9%), Japan 15,847 (5.2%), Germany 13,303 (4.4%), the United Kingdom 13,077
  (4.3%) and Switzerland 11,589 (3.8%).
- **Individuals.** The Australian filer is an individual on 21.43% of Australian standard patents, against 4.3% of
  overseas ones; on 41.05% of Australian provisional applications, 43.1% of second-tier patents and 24.96% of trade
  marks.
- **ABNs.** 69.28% of Australian standard patents have a filer's ABN in IP RAPID, and 87.35% of those filed by
  Australian organisations; for Australian organisations' trade marks, 78.6%. So 13% to 21% of Australian
  organisations' applications have no filer's ABN in IP RAPID; for trade marks and designs the register fills most of
  them (U99, U100). Plant breeder's rights carry no ABN at all.
- **Agents.** Australian filers' applications had an agent other than the applicant for 86.81% of standard patents,
  70.9% of designs, 66.66% of second-tier patents, 57.08% of trade marks and 41.47% of plant breeder's rights;
  overseas filers' for 89.95% to 99.13%. Most such agents are attorneys (1.8.1 separates them). Filing alone is common among
  Australians, above all for trade marks, and rare from overseas.
- **Founding applicants per right.** 85.42% to 98.84% of each type's rights (all years) have one; 21.92% of
  second-tier patents filed in FY2017 to FY2026 have two or more (7.354% of standard patents).
- 81,404 rights have no founding applicant recorded, all of unknown origin: 5.305% of standard patents and 1.571% of
  designs (all years).
- **Restated (2 November 2026, ADR 0037):** first given by the current applicants (the holder) and, for type, the first
  current applicant, whatever its country: standard patents 8.675% Australian, individuals 20.59% of Australian ones.

observations.headline: Health technologies lead standard patents; advertising and business services lead trade marks
observations.statement: In FY2017 to FY2026, medical technology (11.7%), pharmaceuticals (10.7%) and biotechnology (9.6%) together made up 32.0% of standard patents. Trade marks were led by advertising and business services (class 35, 11.7%), then education and entertainment (6.3%) and clothing (6.3%).

figures.label: of standard patents in medical technology, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology
of trade marks in advertising and business services

points: **Designs:** means of transport 8.7%, recording and computing equipment 8.0%, furnishing 7.6%.
**Plant breeder's rights (all years):** roses 8.4%, stone fruit 7.5%, potatoes and tomatoes 4.4%.
Every provisional application has no class, and so do most standard patents filed before 1920; from the 1980s to the 2010s under 1% lack one.

questions.how: What is protected shapes what public value might follow, from medicines to brands.
Technology is one of the conditions that may decide whether protection produces value.

prep.what: Each standard patent is placed in one of WIPO's 35 technology fields by its main patent class.
prep.why: The fields group thousands of classes into readable areas.

prep.what: Trade marks and designs use their main class of goods or product, with WIPO's headings shortened.
prep.why: Their "technology area" in the register only repeated the class ({U2}).

steps: Count FY2017 to FY2026 rights by field or class, and take the largest.
Count rights with no class by decade, and the number of classes per right.
assumptions: A right's main class describes what it mainly protects.
limits: Many patents span several fields; only the main one is counted here.
observations.next: The industries lens turns classes into industries ({U75}); Stage 2 compares value signals by field.

prep.what: A missing state is taken from the applicant's postcode.

steps: Take rights filed FY2017 to FY2026 with a founding applicant (one named at filing) in Australia.
