observations.original:
**U53 (descriptive). Areas differ far more than chance would make them; rates are shown where they mean something.**
- **The funnels:** at the national rate (18.69 trade marks and 0.99 standard patents a year per 10,000 people), chance
  would put 2.5% of areas above and 2.5% below the 95% limits. Instead 15.0% are above and 71.4% below for trade marks,
  6.7% and 68.2% for standard patents. Most areas file less than the nation, and a few file far more.
- **Pooled into 335 SA3s** the pattern holds (15.5% above, 72.5% below for standard patents), so it is not small-area
  noise. Stage 2 models these counts with room for that spread (negative binomial, not Poisson).
- **Rates shown** (ADR 0017): standard patents per person for 850 areas (82.73% of people), trade marks for 2,094
  (99.46%), designs for 812 (81.16%); per business, 650, 2,048 and 608. 324 of the 335 SA3s would expect 10 or more standard
  patents (99.8% of people).
- **Medians and extremes:** trade marks a median 8.48 a year per 10,000 people (90th percentile 32.61) and 4.35 per
  1,000 businesses. The highest per person is 2000, Sydney's centre (712.6, with 27,940 residents and 70,543
  businesses); per business it is 26.4 there. For standard patents 2113 is highest (61.8 per 10,000 people).

observations.headline: About half of R&D claimants have no filing linked to their business number, and claimants are rarer outside the cities
observations.statement: Of 17,627 active R&D Tax Incentive claimants placed in a postal area, 48.3% have no IP filing linked to their business number, and 44.7% have no link to IP of any kind. Neither shows that a claimant never filed. There are 5.6 claimants per 1,000 businesses in major cities, 2.4 in inner regional, 1.8 in outer regional, 1.3 in remote and 0.6 in very remote areas.

figures.label: of R&D claimants have no IP filing linked to their ABN
claimants per 1,000 businesses, major cities against very remote

points: Claimants in outer regional and remote areas more often have no filing linked (57% and 56.5%, against 48% in the cities); inner regional areas are close to the cities (49.4%), and very remote areas hold only 11 claimants.
Firms with a filing linked: 63.3 per 1,000 businesses in the cities, against 24.7 to 38.3 elsewhere.
**Why "no filing linked" is not "never filed".** A firm can file without its business number being recorded, or under a related company.
These are counts by registered address, often a head office, not necessarily where the R&D is done.

questions.how: Firms doing R&D with no filing linked are a group worth asking about later, for barriers IP Australia could ease; some of them may file under another entity.
R&D without IP is one of the alternatives to registration Q3 asks about.

prep.what: Firms are placed by their business register postcode. "No filing linked" means no application is linked to the claimant's ABN by IP RAPID's filer's ABN or IP Australia's register (ADR 0036); "no link to IP" means also no right held, no other IP record and no IPLORD link.
prep.why: Filing is credited to the business that filed (ADR 0016), and a count of linked filings can only show what the records link.

steps: Count active claimants and firms with a filing linked in each postal area.
Count claimants with no filing linked, and with no link to IP of any kind.
Group by remoteness and divide by businesses.
assumptions: A claimant's own ABN is the one its filings would carry; filings under a related company's ABN, or with no ABN, are missed.
limits: A lower bound on IP use: firms' IP counts are lower bounds ({U41}).
observations.next: Stage 2 studies claimants with no filing linked, by place and by firm ({B23}, {B27}).

observations.chapter: 3. Lens: Places (one row per postal area)
observations.original:
**U54 (descriptive). About half of R&D claimants have no filing linked to their ABN, and claimants are rarer outside
the cities.**
- 17,627 active claimants are placed in a postal area; 48.3% have no filing linked to their ABN by either rule
  (`ip_record`, ADR 0036), and 44.7% no link to IP of any kind (no right held, no IP RAPID or register record, no
  IPLORD link). Neither shows that a claimant never filed: a firm can file without its ABN being recorded, or under
  another entity. The claimants are in 1,436 areas; the tenth of areas with the most hold 69%.
- **By remoteness:** 5.6 claimants per 1,000 businesses in major cities, 2.4 in inner regional, 1.8 in outer regional,
  1.3 in remote and 0.6 in very remote areas; firms with a filing linked 63.3 per 1,000 in the cities against 24.7
  to 38.3 elsewhere. Claimants in outer regional and remote areas more often have no filing linked (57% and 56.5%,
  against 48% in the cities; with no link to IP, 53.6% and 54.3% against 44.3%); inner regional areas are close to the
  cities (49.4%), and very remote areas hold 11 claimants (27.3%). (Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043): this read "claimants
  outside the cities", from outer regional areas alone.)
- These are counts by the ABR's main business address: a head office, not necessarily where the R&D is done (U47).
- **Restated (1 November 2026, ADR 0036):** first counted from IP RAPID's own panel, which misses the register's
  ABNs, this read "50.7% have never filed IP" (8,939 claimants) and 49.7 IP-filing firms per 1,000 businesses in the
  cities.

observations.headline: Seven area sources add 28,960,234 values, nearly every one for nearly every postal area
observations.statement: The companion table holds 28,960,234 values: 11,379 indicator-periods from seven sources. The first five (the Census, Data by Region, PHIDU's social health atlas, business counts and the Clean Energy Regulator) hold 22,511,923; the ATO's postcode tables (2012-13 to 2023-24) and the Census time series (2011 to 2021) were added after Stage 2. The median indicator reaches 2,634 to 2,641 of the 2,641 postal areas.

figures.label: attached values
indicator-periods, from seven sources

points: ATO postcode tables: 4,602,252 values, 1,806 indicator-periods. Census time series: 1,846,059 values, 699 indicator-periods.
Values are what was taken from each source's selected tables, not everything the source publishes.

Census: 2,993 cells of 14 tables (2021). Data by Region: 774 items in 12 years. PHIDU: 2,368 indicators over 22 periods. CABEE: 260 business counts for June 2023, 2024 and 2025. Clean Energy Regulator: 11 series over 26 years.
0.05% of Data by Region's values and 0.11% of PHIDU's are empty.

questions.how: Gives Stage 2 a wide range of local conditions (education, health, industry, income) to compare with filing.

prep.what: Values published for SA2s or PHIDU's areas reach postal areas through their 2021 residents; Census and Clean Energy Regulator values are used directly.
prep.why: A count can be split by where people live; a level (a median or rate) is averaged, weighted by people shared (ADR 0018).

steps: Count values, indicators and periods by source.
For each indicator and period, count the postal areas it reaches.
assumptions: People are spread evenly enough within small areas for residents to be a fair basis for splitting.
limits: A value split from a larger area is an estimate for the postal area.
observations.next: Stage 2 uses one indicator and period at a time.

observations.headline: Values split from larger areas track direct counts; CABEE counts a quarter fewer businesses than the business register
observations.statement: Data by Region's 2021 population, split from larger areas, is within 10% of the direct count for 99.34% of postal areas of 1,000 people or more. CABEE's June 2025 business count is 0.742 of the register's active GST businesses, but ranks areas almost alike (a rank correlation of 0.988): they count different things.

figures.label: of areas within 10% of the direct population count
CABEE's count as a share of the register's

points: The Census's count (25,369,823) is the geography's count (25,365,506) to within 0.02%, the gap being the ABS's privacy adjustment.
CABEE counts businesses actively trading; the register counts registrations. So a CABEE count is never compared with a register count.

questions.how: Confirms the method for placing other data in postal areas, and which business count to use.

prep.what: The same quantity is taken from two routes and compared, area by area.
prep.why: Agreement shows the splitting method works; disagreement shows the measures differ.

steps: For each area, compare the Census and split population with the geography's count.
Compare CABEE's split business count with the register's.
Work out ratios of totals and rank correlations.
assumptions: Where two routes agree, the method is sound for other indicators split the same way.
limits: Agreement for people does not prove agreement for every indicator.
observations.next: Business counts by postal area come from the register; CABEE gives size and industry.
observations.section: 3.5 Attachments
observations.chapter: 3. Lens: Places (one row per postal area)
observations.original:
**U56 (descriptive). Split values track the direct ones; CABEE counts a quarter fewer businesses than the ABR, in the
same order.**
- **People:** the Census's count (25,369,823) is the ASGS count (25,365,506) to within 0.02%, the gap being the ABS's
  perturbation. Data by Region's 2021 estimated resident population, split from SA2s, is 1.3% higher in total (it
  adds people the Census missed), and within 10% of the ASGS count for 99.34% of postal areas of 1,000 people or more
  (Spearman 0.9999).
- **Businesses:** CABEE's June 2025 count (2,713,177) is 0.742 of the ABR's active GST-registered ABNs (3,657,678);
  the median area's ratio is 0.749 and only 2.96% of areas are within 10%, but the two rank areas almost alike
  (Spearman 0.988). They count different things (businesses actively trading, against registrations), so a CABEE
  count is never compared with an ABR count. Its employment and turnover tables give the same total (ratio 1.000).
- **So** the residents-weighted split is sound for people. For businesses by postal area, the ABR (`active_gst_abns`)
  is the count; CABEE's value is its split by size and industry, which the ABR lacks.

observations.headline: Many Census cells are small, and parts do not add exactly to totals
observations.statement: Half of the industry-by-age-by-sex cells (G54) are 0 (51.1%), as are 39.4% of the field-of-study cells and 37.4% of the occupation cells. Males plus females equal persons exactly in only 10.9% of postal areas, because the ABS adjusts small cells at random to protect privacy.

figures.label: of industry-by-age-by-sex Census cells are zero
of areas where males plus females equal persons exactly

points: 3.0% to 8.3% of each table's cells are 1 to 4. The summary tables are larger (median cells 153 and 221).
So Stage 2 uses Census shares of whole groups, never single small cells.

questions.how: Census characteristics will be compared with filing; this says how to use them safely.

prep.what: Every cell of 14 Census tables is kept, by postal area.
prep.why: Every dataset is kept whole; how to use it is decided here.

steps: For each table, work out the share of cells that are 0 and 1 to 4.
Check whether males plus females equal persons in each area.
assumptions: The ABS's privacy adjustment is random and small, as it says.
limits: Small cells cannot be used on their own.
observations.next: Stage 2 uses shares of whole groups.

observations.chapter: 3. Lens: Places (one row per postal area)
observations.original:
**U57 (descriptive). Many Census cells are small, and parts do not add exactly to totals.**
- The detailed tables are mostly small numbers: half of the industry-by-age-by-sex cells (G54) are 0 (51.1%, median
  0), 39.4% of the field-of-study cells (G50) and 37.4% of the occupation cells (G60); 3.0% to 8.3% of each table's
  cells are 1 to 4. The summary tables are larger (G01 median 153, G43 221).
- **Perturbation:** males plus females equal persons exactly in only 10.9% of postal areas (the largest gap 10). The
  ABS adjusts small cells at random to protect privacy, so Stage 2 uses Census shares of whole groups, never single
  small cells, and never checks parts against totals exactly.

observations.statement: Solar water heaters fell from 122,312 installations in 2009 to 18,505 in 2025. Solar panels went from 62,831 in 2009 to 360,423 in 2011, 370,287 in 2020 and 272,395 in 2025. Batteries first appear in the records in 2025: 207,305 that year and 339,457 in 2026 to September.

A local measure of take-up that Stage 2 can set beside filing in green technologies.

prep.what: Monthly installations are summed to calendar years, by postal area.
prep.why: Years match the other sources; 2026 runs to September.

steps: Add up installations by year and technology.

limits: It counts installations, not their size.

observations.headline: Government contracts go mostly to suppliers registered in a few places, above all the ACT
observations.statement: Contracts first published in FY2017 to FY2026 went to 54,798 suppliers in 2,015 postal areas; the top 1% of areas hold 68.4% of the value. The ACT has 27.0% of the contracts and 20.5% of the value, against 1.3% of businesses.

A supplier's postcode is often its head office, so this is where contracts are addressed, not where work is done.

questions.how: Procurement is a government lever; where its money goes matters for who it could reach.

prep.what: Each contract counts once at its latest value, by the supplier's postcode on the contract.
prep.why: Summing every amendment counted the same contract many times (ADR 0010, 0011).

observations.headline: Thirty indicators cover 229 places from 1960, but Australia's records of R&D staff end early
observations.statement: The core table holds 30 indicators for 229 places from 1960 to 2025 (135,597 values). Australia's series are complete except for R&D: researchers end in 2010 and technicians in 2008, and the World Bank's R&D spending ends in 2021 (the OECD's runs to 2023).

figures.label: values in the core table
the last year of Australia's count of researchers

points: Over 2000 to 2024 Australia has 20% of the years for R&D technicians, 24% for researchers and 40% for tertiary enrolment, against 44.2%, 81.4% and 82.8% of OECD member-years.
The World Bank supplies 113,147 values (217 countries), WIPO 19,296 and the OECD 3,154.

questions.how: International comparison is how Australia's IP system can be judged against others; gaps limit it.
Missing R&D workforce data is itself a gap worth noting for policy evidence.

prep.what: One row per country, year and indicator, from the World Bank, WIPO and the OECD.
prep.why: A country in a year is the unit of international comparison.

prep.what: The OECD's R&D series sit beside the World Bank's, never spliced.
prep.why: They differ where they overlap (2021, 1.66% against 1.86%), so they are compared, not joined (ADR 0010).

steps: For each indicator, count the countries, the years, and Australia's years.
Compare Australia's coverage over 2000 to 2024 with the OECD members'.
assumptions: The World Bank's and OECD's figures for Australia come from the ABS and are comparable across countries.
limits: Recent Australian R&D workforce figures are missing from these series. The ABS's own R&D survey gives an approximate recent figure, kept apart from them ({U120}).

observations.original:
**U63 (descriptive). The core holds 30 indicators for 229 places from 1960 to 2025; Australia's series are complete
except for R&D people and spending.**
- **Rows:** 135,597. The World Bank's 113,147 (217 countries), WIPO's 19,296 (201 countries, 6 former states and the
  unknown origin) and the OECD's 3,154 (47 countries).
- **Australia's gaps:** researchers in R&D end in 2010 and technicians in 2008; the World Bank's R&D spending ends in
  2021 (the OECD's runs to 2023); tertiary enrolment starts in 2015. Over 2000 to 2024 Australia has 20% of the years
  for technicians, 24% for researchers and 40% for tertiary enrolment, against 44.2%, 81.4% and 82.8% of OECD
  member-years. These are the published series' gaps; Australia's own R&D survey gives an approximate recent
  researchers-per-million figure and business funding share, kept apart from these series (U120).
- **Across the OECD,** the least complete series are technicians in R&D (44.2% of member-years), trade mark
  applications (65.8%) and new business registrations (68.2%).

observations.headline: Before 1995, WIPO cannot say where most patent applicants come from
observations.statement: Of WIPO's patent applications by origin, 34.35% had an unknown origin in 1980, 29.02% in 1990 and 32.24% in 1993, then 9.0% in 1994 and 1.12% in 2024. observations.original:
**U64 (descriptive). Before 1995 WIPO cannot say where most applicants come from, so its counts by country are
floors.**
- Of WIPO's patent applications by origin (all offices), 34.35% had an unknown origin in 1980, 29.02% in 1990 and
  32.24% in 1993, then 9.0% in 1994 and 1.12% in 2024. Former states held 22.59% in 1980 (the Soviet Union 1,729,188
  applications to 1991).
- **Australia's own series show the gap.** Australians' applications at every office were barely more than those at
  home until 1993 (1,723 against 1,712 in 1990), then 4,351 in 1994; WIPO's patent grants to Australian residents were

observations.headline: Australia's R&D spending rose to 2008 as a share of GDP and has fallen since, below the OECD median; manufacturing's share fell twice as fast as the median member's
observations.statement: Gross R&D spending was 1.26% of GDP in 1990, 2.24% in 2008, 1.87% in 2015 and 1.68% in 2023, against an OECD median of 1.85% in 2023. Business R&D was 1.37% of GDP in 2008 and 0.91% in 2023 (median 1.18%). Manufacturing fell from 13.7% of GDP in 1990 to 5.32% in 2025, down 61%, against 30% for the median member.

figures.label: gross R&D as a share of GDP, 2008 to 2023
manufacturing's share of GDP since 1990

points: **IP royalties:** Australia pays more for others' IP than it earns from its own in every year shown: payments $826 million (1990) to $12.4 billion (2025), receipts $162 million to $7.4 billion (current US dollars).

**Patents:** non-resident applications in Australia rose from 13,278 (1990) to 29,014 (2023) while the median member's fell from 2,416 to 479 (European offices hand much of that work to the European Patent Office). Resident applications rose from 1,712 to 2,511 against a falling median (1,868 to 1,028).
**Two breaks to read past:** the share of the labour force with advanced education steps up to 86.33% in 2010, and net foreign investment was −3.6% of GDP in 2005, a single year.

questions.how: The national context in which the IP system works; falling R&D and a shrinking manufacturing base matter for what patents can do.
Shows where Australia sits against peers, a starting point for where intervention might matter.

prep.what: Each indicator is compared with the OECD members' median in the same year, where 10 or more report.
prep.why: The median member is a fair benchmark; with fewer reporting, it moves with who reports.

steps: Take Australia's value for each indicator and year.
Work out the OECD members' median and middle half for the same year.
Compare at chosen years.
assumptions: Indicators are measured the same way across countries, as the publishers intend.
limits: Each value is a ratio of the whole economy; it does not say why R&D fell.

observations.statement: In its latest year, Australia ranks 2nd of 30 OECD members for new businesses registered and 5th of 38 for patent applications from non-residents (27,945, against a median member's 425). It ranks 34th of 35 for exports (23.24% of GDP, median 45.37%) and 31st of 32 for manufacturing (5.32%, median 12.79%). It is below the median for business R&D (26th of 35) and gross R&D (21st of 35).

Counts rank by size: Australia's population is 14th of 38 and its GDP 13th, so its counts of filings, articles and royalties sit around the 60th to 75th percentile, about where its size alone would put them.

Low business R&D and exports are possible areas where IP policy works with others.

observations.headline: IP RAPID's counts of Australia's patent applications agree with WIPO's and the World Bank's; the World Bank's trade mark series counts classes
observations.statement: From 1989 to 2024, IP RAPID's count of standard patents with a founding applicant in Australia is a median 1.011 times the World Bank's count for Australian residents (0.931 in 2008 to 1.027): about 1% more, because WIPO counts a resident by the first-named applicant. For overseas applicants the ratio is 0.981 to 1.019. The World Bank's count is WIPO's exactly. For trade marks the World Bank counts classes: IP RAPID's Australian classes are 0.943 to 1.011 of its figure.

figures.label: median ratio of IP RAPID's count to the World Bank's, Australian filers
innovation patents against WIPO's utility models in 2016, a lead

points: Counted by the first founding applicant's country, WIPO's own rule, the median ratio is 1.001 (0.924 in 2008 to 1.015).
Before 1989 IP RAPID's overseas count falls short (0.072 of the World Bank's in 1980), because it records few overseas applicants' countries then ({U7}).
IP RAPID's trade mark applications are 0.546 to 0.667 of the World Bank's "applications", which are really classes. The project's source register now says so.

questions.how: An independent check that the core counts of the IP system are right.

prep.what: The three sources are compared by calendar year of application.
prep.why: International sources count by calendar year.

steps: Count standard patents by year and origin from the register.
Take the World Bank's and WIPO's counts for Australia.
Divide one by the other, year by year.
assumptions: WIPO's statistics are compiled from offices' own reports, so agreement shows that IP RAPID is consistent with what IP Australia reports; it is not an independent count.
limits: The 2016 innovation patent gap is unexplained (a question for IP Australia).
Resident counts differ slightly by definition (any founding applicant in Australia, or the first-named one).
observations.next: Trade marks are compared across countries as class counts.
observations.section: 4.3 The same counts by three routes
observations.chapter: 4. Lens: Australia and other countries (one row per country, year and indicator)
observations.original:
**U67 (descriptive). IP RAPID, the World Bank and WIPO count Australia's patent applications alike; the World Bank's
trade mark series count classes, not applications.**
- **Standard patents, 1989 to 2024:** with a founding applicant in Australia (IP Australia's definition of a
  resident, ADR 0024, 0037), IP RAPID's count is a median 1.011 of the World Bank's for Australian applicants (0.931
  in 2008 to 1.027): about 1% more, since WIPO counts a resident by the first-named applicant, and a right with an
  Australian co-applicant named second is a resident's for IP Australia only. Counted by the first founding
  applicant's country, the median is 1.001 (0.924 in 2008 to 1.015). For overseas applicants it is 0.981 to 1.019.
  The World Bank's count is WIPO's exactly (ratio 1 in every year). Before 1989 IP RAPID's overseas count falls short (0.072 of the
  World Bank's in 1980, 0.427 in 1985, 0.906 in 1988), because it records few overseas applicants' countries then
  (U7: they are "origin unknown").
- **Innovation and petty patents** against WIPO's utility models: median ratio 1.013, but 1.331 in 2016: a lead.
- **Trade marks:** IP RAPID's Australian applications are 0.546 to 0.667 of the World Bank's "trade mark applications,
  resident, by count", but its classes are 0.943 to 1.011 of it: the World Bank counts classes, as WIPO does. The
  register now says so.
- **So** the lenses agree with the international sources, and comparisons of trade marks across countries use class
  counts on both sides. Where a comparison must match WIPO's residents exactly, the first founding applicant's
  country is the nearer definition.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, ADR 0037):** first counted by the current holder (median 1.002, 0.907 in 2008), which
  matched the World Bank as closely, but describes who holds a right, not who filed it.

observations.headline: Australia ranks 20th of 139 economies in the Global Innovation Index 2026, 13th on inputs and 24th on outputs
observations.statement: In the GII 2026, Australia is 20th of 139: 13th on innovation inputs and 24th on outputs. Its pillars run from 9th (human capital and research) to 29th (infrastructure). WIPO's strengths for Australia are education and universities; its weaknesses are outputs and trade.

figures.label: of 139 economies overall
inputs against outputs

points: Pillars: human capital and research 9th, institutions 12th, market sophistication 17th, business sophistication 23rd, knowledge and technology outputs 26th, creative outputs 26th, infrastructure 29th.
Strengths: school life expectancy (2nd), university, industry and international engagement (4th).
Weaknesses: ICT services exports (99th), low-carbon energy use (91st), graduates in science and engineering (90th), labour productivity growth (85th).
A rank reflects WIPO's choice of indicators and weights; the indicators beneath it are the evidence.

questions.how: The gap between strong inputs and weaker outputs frames the question of what the system turns into value.
Points to where Australia lags its peers, as context for choosing interventions.

prep.what: Every GII value is kept, with WIPO's strength and weakness flags.
prep.why: The indicators are the evidence; the rank is a summary (ADR 0019).

steps: Take Australia's rank on the index, sub-indices and pillars.
List the indicators WIPO marks as strengths and weaknesses.
Count missing and outdated indicators against the median economy.
assumptions: WIPO's choice of indicators and weights is taken as published.
limits: A composite rank can move because of method changes; 6 of Australia's 79 indicators are missing and 8 outdated. Four of the six are filled approximately from Australia's own statistics, beside the GII and never in its scores ({U120}).
observations.next: Stage 2 works with the indicators, not the rank.

observations.original:
**U69 (descriptive). Australia ranks 20th of 139 economies in the GII 2026: 13th on innovation inputs and 24th on
outputs.**
- **Pillars:** human capital and research 9th, institutions 12th, market sophistication 17th, business sophistication
  23rd, knowledge and technology outputs 26th, creative outputs 26th and infrastructure 29th.
- **WIPO's strengths for Australia** are education and universities: school life expectancy (2nd), university,
  industry and international engagement (4th), the QS university ranking (4th), tertiary inbound mobility (5th) and
  cluster development (5th). **Its weaknesses** are outputs and trade: ICT services exports (99th), low-carbon energy
  use (91st), graduates in science and engineering (90th), labour productivity growth (85th), and production and
  export complexity (72nd). Against other high-income economies, patent families per dollar of GDP (29th) and public
  research and industry co-publications (38th) are weaknesses too.
- **Completeness:** 6 of Australia's 79 indicators are missing and 8 are outdated (the median economy: 6 and 9). The
  missing include researchers per million people (the series that ends in 2010, U63), GERD financed by business and
  utility models by origin. These blanks are the GII's own; four of the six are filled approximately, beside the GII
  and never in its scores, from Australia's own statistics (U120).
- A rank on a composite index reflects WIPO's choice of indicators and weights; the indicators beneath it are the
  evidence, and each is in `national_indicators`.

observations.headline: The United States files about four in ten patent applications at IP Australia; China now files as many as Australians
observations.statement: Of patent applications at IP Australia, the United States filed 41.2% in 1995, 45.6% in 2004 and 41.9% in 2024. Australians filed 12.7%, 11.2% and 8.3%; China 0.0%, 0.3% and 8.3%. Three-quarters of Australians' own applications (76.1% in 2024) are made abroad.

figures.label: of applications at IP Australia from the United States (2024)
China and Australia, 2024
of Australians' applications made abroad

points: IP Australia beside other OECD offices (2024): 405 patent examiners (median office 83.5); 347 days from an examination request to the first action (median 210); trade marks 37 days to the first action (median 30).

WIPO gives IP Australia's average time to register a trade mark as 222 days (2016), the peak found in IP RAPID ({U11}). So the peak is consistent with the office's usual path to registration; WIPO's figure is an average, and IP RAPID's mean for FY2010 to FY2019 is 286.5 days.
Australian residents' applications at every office were 4,389 (1995), 10,631 (2005) and 10,633 (2024), against 1,784, 2,555 and 2,542 at IP Australia.

questions.how: Who files where shows whose inventions the Australian system protects, and where Australians seek protection.
Australians filing abroad is a measure of reaching international markets.

prep.what: Applications at IP Australia by origin come from WIPO's office tables.
prep.why: An independent view of the same filings, by every country.

steps: Take WIPO's patent applications at IP Australia by the applicant's origin, each year.
Work out each origin's share.
Compare Australians' applications at every office with those at home.
assumptions: WIPO's origin is the first applicant's residence.
limits: Before 1995 most origins are unknown ({U64}).

observations.headline: The United States is Australia's main partner in cross-border invention
observations.statement: Of inventions made in Australia (international applications, 2020), 7.0% were owned by US residents, 3.7% by Chinese and 1.6% by Swiss; 7.1% had a US co-inventor and 3.5% a Chinese one. Of Australian-owned inventions, 4.0% were made in the United States.

points: In the OECD's tables, "World" as a partner is the country's own total: 2,117 inventions made in Australia in 2015, 1,762 owned in Australia; 1,720 and 1,489 in 2022.
China's share of foreign ownership was 0.0% (2000), 3.7% (2020) and 0.5% (2022).

questions.how: Inventions made here but owned abroad may send their returns overseas.

prep.what: The OECD's three cross-border tables are read with "World" as each country's total.
prep.why: A partner's count only means something as a share of that total.

steps: Take the totals for inventions made in, and owned in, Australia.
Take each partner's share in 2020.
assumptions: Ownership is the applicant's residence; invention is the inventor's.
limits: International applications only; inventions filed only in Australia are not counted.

observations.headline: Measuring What Matters mostly repeats labour statistics held elsewhere; Closing the Gap mixes observations with projections
observations.statement: 3,767 of Measuring What Matters' 5,159 values are monthly copies of ABS labour and price series, which stay the main measures. Closing the Gap's 11,349 values include 353 projections (trajectories to each target, to 2031) and 443 model estimates; 809 are not available or not published.

points: So a projected value is never read as an observation; its status says which it is.

questions.how: Wellbeing and First Nations outcomes are part of public value; this says how to read them safely.

prep.what: Each value keeps the publisher's status, so projections and model estimates are marked.
prep.why: A projection is not an observation (ADR 0019).

steps: Count each framework's values by kind of period and status.
Compare Measuring What Matters' monthly series with the ABS series already in the corpus.
assumptions: The publishers' own labels say which values are projected or modelled.
limits: Australia only; no comparison with other countries.

observations.original:
**U72 (descriptive). Measuring What Matters is mostly monthly labour statistics held elsewhere; Closing the Gap mixes
observations with projections.**
- **Measuring What Matters:** 3,767 of its 5,159 values are monthly (28 series: employment, unemployment and wages,
  copies of the ABS series in `abs_labour` and `abs_prices`, which stay the main measures), 972 are for years, 273 for
  financial years and 35 for groups with no period. Its two stacked tables now carry their blocks (30 and 24 values).

observations.headline: WIPO counts more Australian patent families than reach IP Australia; Google Patents holds older families' filings abroad incompletely
observations.statement: WIPO counts 16,726 patent families with an Australian applicant first filed in 2015 to 2019. The Google Patents families of IP RAPID's patents with a founding applicant in Australia number 14,174, equal to 84.74% of WIPO's count. WIPO's share filed in more than one office holds steady (64.73%), while Google Patents shows 15.15% filed abroad for 2000 to 2004 families and 46.14% for 2015 to 2019.

figures.label: Google Patents' Australian families reaching IP Australia, as a share of WIPO's count (2015 to 2019)
WIPO's share filed in more than one office
Australian PCT patents shown "Australia only", FY2000 to FY2004 against after FY2010

points: 2000 to 2004: 21,047 WIPO families against 13,834 Google Patents families (65.73%); 66.37% of WIPO's were filed in more than one office.
So about one Australian family in six in recent years never reaches IP Australia. That is an upper bound: WIPO counts filings at every office, and the two count families differently.

**A break in the links.** Australian applicants' PCT patents appear "Australia only" 73.63% of the time (FY2000 to FY2004) and 59.44% (FY2005 to FY2009), against 13.69% and 11.76% after FY2010, and their US grants double at the same break (19.32% and 22.35% to 45.13% and 53.69%). Before FY2010 the links from Australian patents to their filings abroad are incomplete.
**Decision:** for Australian applicants, family measures are read from FY2010 on (OQ21 asks whether to repair the older links).

questions.how: Shows how fully the family measures of value can be trusted for Australian applicants, and from when.

prep.what: WIPO's patent families by origin (all, and foreign-oriented) joined to the national lens.
prep.why: An independent count of Australians' families, to check Google Patents' coverage.

steps: Compare WIPO's and Google Patents' counts of Australian families, and their shares filed abroad.
Check standard patents that must have a filing abroad (a priority outside Australia and the US).
assumptions: A family with a priority from another office must have a published filing abroad.
limits: WIPO and Google count families differently, so the shares are bounds.
observations.next: Stage 2 tests whether {B11}'s fall is practice or records ({B55}).

observations.original:
**U115 (descriptive). WIPO counts more Australian patent families than reach IP Australia, with a steady share filed
abroad; Google Patents holds older Australian families' filings abroad incompletely.**
- WIPO's families with an Australian applicant, at any office: 21,047 first filed in 2000 to 2004 and 16,726 in 2015
  to 2019; 66.37% and 64.73% of them filed in more than one office (61.73% to 66.37% in every five years since 2000).
- The Google Patents families of IP RAPID's patents with a founding applicant in Australia (standard and
  second-tier; ADR 0037): 13,834 and 14,174, which is 65.73% and 84.74% of WIPO's count. So about one Australian family in six in recent years never
  reaches IP Australia (an upper bound: WIPO counts filings at every office, and the two count families differently).
- Of those families, Google Patents shows 15.15% filed abroad (2000 to 2004) and 46.14% (2015 to 2019), while WIPO's
  share stayed flat.
- **The coverage check.** Standard patents claiming a priority from an office other than Australia's or the United
  States' (which must have a published filing abroad) appear "Australia only" 1.96% to 5.45% of the time to FY2004,
  0.81% to 0.86% since FY2005; 10.5% of FY2000 to FY2004 patents have no Google Patents family at all (0.46% to 1.65%
  in the other years). Australian applicants' patents that entered through the PCT, an international application,
  appear "Australia only" 73.63% of the time (FY2000 to FY2004) and 59.44% (FY2005 to FY2009), against 13.69% and
  11.76% after FY2010; their US grants double at the same break (19.32% and 22.35% to 45.13% and 53.69%).
- **Decision:** for Australian applicants, family measures (offices, US grant, citations) are read from FY2010 on.
  Before then the links from Australian patents to their filings abroad are incomplete, in Google Patents' families
  or in the corpus's match of older Australian numbers to them; which, is not settled here (flagged for the owner).
- **Restated (2 November 2026, ADR 0037):** first selected by the current holder's origin (13,518 and 14,057 families;
  "Australia only" 74.92% and 59.21%); the filer's moves these by under 1.3 points.

observations.headline: Four of the GII's six blanks for Australia can be filled approximately; Australia's researchers sit outside business more than almost any member's
observations.statement: Supplementary values, kept apart from the GII's rows, fill four indicators. Australia's research talent in business is 33.91% of researchers, against an OECD median of 52.99%; only 16.7% of members are lower. GERD financed by business is 51.78%, against a median of 49.5%.

figures.label: researchers working in business (median 52.99%)
GERD financed by business (median 49.5%)
researchers per million people (median 5,320)

points: Pupil-teacher ratio, secondary: 11.7 students per teacher (2025), against a median of 11.02.
Microfinance loans and utility models by origin stay blank: no Australian series, and the GII's utility model counts could not be reproduced (ADR 0033).
Read beside the GII, never used to recalculate a score or rank.

questions.how: Completes Australia's place on the GII's research measures.
Where researchers work is a candidate condition for how much research becomes invention ({B61}).

prep.what: Each value computed from the ABS's schools and R&D surveys, with its period and how it differs from the GII's definition.
prep.why: The GII leaves these blank for Australia.

steps: Compute each value as close to the GII's definition as the ABS's tables allow.
Compare with the GII's values for OECD members.
assumptions: Combining the ABS's sector surveys (business 2023-24, higher education 2024, government 2024-25) approximates one year.
limits: Approximate; never part of the GII's own rows.
observations.next: Stage 2 relates them to patenting across members ({B61}).

observations.original:
**U120 (descriptive). Four of the six GII indicators blank for Australia can be filled from Australia's own statistics,
approximately; Australia's researchers sit outside business more than almost any OECD member's.** Supplementary values
(never part of the GII's rows; ADR 0033), beside the GII's values for OECD members:
- **Pupil-teacher ratio, secondary:** 11.7 full-time equivalent students per teacher (2025; 11.8 in 2023), against an
  OECD median of 11.02 (55.6% of members have fewer pupils per teacher).
- **GERD financed by business:** 51.78% (business 2023-24, higher education 2024, government and private non-profit
  2024-25), against a median of 49.5% (56.8% of members lower).
- **Researchers per million people:** 4,870, against a median of 5,320 (38.9% of members lower).
- **Research talent in business:** 33.91% of researchers, against a median of 52.99%; only 16.7% of members lower.
- Microfinance loans (4.1.3) and utility models by origin (6.1.3) stay blank: no Australian series, and the GII's
  utility model counts could not be reproduced (ADR 0033).
- **Decision:** the values sit in `national_indicators` as `gii_supplementary`, each with its period and how it
  differs. They are read beside the GII, never used to recalculate a score or rank (B61).

observations.headline: The timeline has one row per month since 1904, with each series starting only where it can be trusted
observations.statement: The timeline holds 1,473 months, January 1904 to September 2026, in 79 columns: 28 monthly series of applications and events, the price index and the policy changes, and, added after Stage 2, fees, the Reserve Bank's rates, the national accounts and the PBS. After the repairs, series begin between January 1904 and December 2003, and none has a gap inside its span.

figures.label: months
Australian standard patent applications in April 2013, the busiest month

points: The busiest month of standard patent applications, from Australian and overseas applicants alike, is April 2013 (1,044 and 5,381), when Raising the Bar took effect; of second-tier applications, August 2021 (2,789), when innovation patents closed; of provisional applications, March 2026 (1,274).
Origin is the filer's: a founding applicant in Australia, IP Australia's definition of a resident application.
The last months are empty only where the register is still recording: six months for trade mark and design cessations, three for designs by origin.

questions.how: Month-by-month series are what before-and-after comparisons of policy changes need.
Long-run series show how use of the system has changed over a century.

prep.what: Each series starts at the first month from which its records are continuous and complete; earlier months are empty, not zero.
prep.why: Before that, the register holds survivors, partial records or batch dates, so a month's count is not what happened that month (ADR 0010, 0014).

prep.what: Each event is counted once, even where the register records it twice.
prep.why: Duplicate records would inflate the counts.

steps: For each series, find its first and last month with a value.
Check for gaps inside each series' span.
Find each series' busiest month.
assumptions: A month with no record inside a series' span really had none.
limits: A long series is not complete back to 1904: each starts where its records do.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares months around events, within each series' span.

observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U22 (descriptive). One row per month, with each series where it can be read.**
- The lens holds 1,473 months (January 1904 to September 2026) in 79 columns (the overview above): five calendar columns, 28 monthly
  series, the CPI and the policy changes (the 35 profiled here), and, added after Stage 2, 26 fee columns (5.7), four
  of the Reserve Bank's (5.8), ten from the national accounts (5.9) and four from the PBS (5.10). First given as 35
  columns, then 61. The calendar columns are complete; months have 28 to 31 days.
- After the repairs, the series begin between January 1904 (standard patents of unknown origin) and December 2003
  (patent oppositions), as the table above shows. None has a gap inside its span. The last months are empty only
  where the register is still recording: six months for trade mark and design cessations, three for designs by
  origin.
- The series by origin count the filer's origin, a founding applicant in Australia (IP Australia's definition of a
  resident application; ADR 0024, 0037). The busiest month of standard patent applications from Australian and
  overseas applicants alike is April 2013 (1,044 and 5,381), when Raising the Bar took effect; of second-tier applications, August 2021 (2,789), when
  innovation patents closed; of provisional applications, March 2026 (1,274).

observations.headline: Eighteen series started too early, on records that hold only survivors or batches, and one policy change was missing
observations.statement: Before records were computerised, the register holds only rights still alive then. Only 2.0% of trade marks filed in early 1981 were never registered, against 52.0% from the first quarter of 1983. So those years count survivors, not filings, and eighteen series now start later. The rise of the patent term from 16 to 20 years (1 July 1995) was missing from the policy list and has been added.

figures.label: trade marks never registered, early 1981 against early 1983
series given a later start
the patent term from 1 July 1995, the policy change added

points: **Designs:** 0.4% and 0.7% never registered in the second half of 1985, then 26.3% in the first quarter of 1986.
The survivor months had counted 44,231 trade marks from Australian applicants and 75,470 from overseas ones (3.1% and 8.5% of each series).
**Batches.** Patent cessations were dated in batches to April 1995: 29.8% of the 104 months from September 1986 hold none.
**Partial records.** Grants are recorded only for patents filed from 1979: 1.0% to 1.9% of standard patents filed in 1976 to 1978 have a grant date, against 68.5% of those filed in 1979.
**Real, not an artefact:** patent expiries all but stop from July 1995 and resume in July 1999, because every patent then in force gained four more years.

questions.how: A false rise or fall in a series could be mistaken for a policy's effect; these repairs prevent that.
Long-run comparisons are honest only from where the records are complete.

prep.what: Eighteen series start by hand where their records become complete, each with its reason in the build code.
prep.why: The general rule (the first month from which 9 of the next 12 have a record) started them too early (ADR 0014).

prep.what: The 1995 term change is checked against the Act itself and added to the policy register.
prep.why: The patent expiry series shows it plainly, and the register's note on the 1990 Act was wrong.

steps: For trade marks, designs and provisionals, work out by quarter of filing the share never registered, or the count.
Find the quarter where the share jumps from near zero to a normal level: before it, only survivors are held.
For event series, find months with no events followed by backlogs: signs of batch dating.
Set each series' start after these, and check the patent expiry series against the 1995 Act.
assumptions: A sudden jump in the share never registered marks the start of complete records, not a real change in filing.
limits: Before each new start, the register cannot say how many applications were really made.
observations.next: Every count by year in the rights lens carries this note ({U5}, {U10}).
observations.section: 5.0 Data overview and sanity checks
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U23 (descriptive). Eighteen series started too early (the table), and one policy change was missing (ADR 0014).**
(First given as fifteen, which the table's 18 rows do not match.)
- **Survivors.** By quarter of filing, 2.0% of trade marks filed in early 1981 were never registered, 22.6% in the
  third quarter of 1982 and 52.0% from the first quarter of 1983 (51.0% at the end of 1988). Of designs, 0.4% and 0.7%
  in the second half of 1985, then 26.3% in the first quarter of 1986. Provisional applications run at 251 to 355 a
  quarter in the quarters shown before mid-1985, and 1,372 in the last quarter of 1985. A register that keeps only what survived records almost no
  failures, so the earlier months count survivors, not filings: 44,231 trade marks from Australian applicants and
  75,470 from overseas ones over the 921 months from April 1906 (3.1% and 8.5% of each series).
- **Batches.** Patent cessations were dated in batches to April 1995: 29.8% of the 104 months from September 1986 hold
  none, and others hold several months' worth (46,671 cessations, 11% of the series). Expiries to December 1994 hold
  29.4% of their series. Both are dated weekly or daily since (the chart).
- **Partial records.** IP RAPID records grants only for patents filed from 1979: 1.0% to 1.9% of standard patents
  filed in 1976 to 1978 have a grant date, against 68.5% of those filed in 1979. So the 16,557 grants before 1985 are
  some of the grants made (2.5% of the series).
- **What remains real.** Patent expiries all but stop from July 1995 and resume in July 1999 (the chart; measured in
  5.4). Australia raised the standard patent term from 16 to 20 years on 1 July 1995, for every patent still
  in force, so patents filed from July 1979 expired four years later than they would have. The policy register now
  holds this change, checked against the Act (the Patents (World Trade Organization Amendments) Act 1994), and its
  note on the Patents Act 1990, which said the 1990 Act brought in 20-year patents, is corrected: the 1990 Act's term
  was 16 years.
- The rights lens keeps every right; only counts by year of filing are affected. Section 1's note is corrected (U5).

observations.headline: Large monthly series are steady; small ones are noisy and need longer periods
observations.statement: Over FY2017 to FY2026 the steadiest series is standard patent applications from overseas (a median 2,306 a month, varying by only 0.08 of its average). The most variable are second-tier patents (1.82, from the rush before their closure and the near-silence after) and small series such as extensions of term.

figures.label: relative variation of overseas standard patents, the steadiest series
relative variation of second-tier patents, the most uneven

points: Small series: patent oppositions (median 5 a month), extensions of term (5) and plant breeder's rights granted (13.5).
Outliers: 12 months each for provisional applications (the rise of 2025 and 2026) and second-tier patents (2021).
The "origin unknown" series are mostly zero for standard patents (95% of months), as they should be once origins are recorded; for trade marks only 16.67% of months are zero.
**Decision.** Series with a median under 10 a month are compared by quarter or year, not by month.

questions.how: Tells later stages which series can show a policy effect month by month and which need longer periods.

prep.what: Each series is described over the ten latest complete financial years.
prep.why: A recent decade shows how each behaves now.

steps: For each series, work out its median, mean and standard deviation over FY2017 to FY2026.
Divide the standard deviation by the mean to compare series of different sizes.
Count outlying months by the box-plot rule.
assumptions: Ten years is long enough to describe each series' usual behaviour.
limits: Variation includes real events (rushes) as well as noise.
observations.next: Small series are grouped into quarters or years in Stage 2.
