observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U24 (descriptive). The shape of the monthly counts, FY2017 to FY2026.**
- **Steadiest:** standard patent applications from overseas (median 2,306 a month; a standard deviation 0.08 of the
  mean), trade mark cessations (0.12), design cessations (0.14) and trade mark applications (0.15 from Australian and
  overseas applicants alike).
- **Most variable:** second-tier patents (1.82, from the rush to file before their closure and the near-silence
  after), plant breeder's rights granted (0.79), extensions of term (0.72) and design lapses (0.69).
- **Outliers** (the box-plot rule): 12 months each for provisional applications (the rise of 2025 and 2026) and
  second-tier patents (2021), 7 for patent cessations (a pause in February 2020, 5.5) and 7 for plant breeder's
  rights granted.
- **Small series:** patent oppositions (median 5 a month; 2.5% of months none), extensions of term (5; 7.5% none) and
  plant breeder's rights granted (13.5; 0.83% none). The "origin unknown" series are mostly zero for standard patents (95% of months), as they should
  be once origins are recorded; for trade marks only 16.67% of months are zero, a median 5 a month whose founding
  applicant has no country though a current one may (by the holder's origin, 45.83% of months were zero).
- **Decision:** in Stage 2, series with a median under 10 a month are compared by quarter or year, not by month.

observations.headline: Growth in standard patents has slowed to 0.4% a year; trade marks and designs are growing faster
observations.statement: Standard patent applications grew 3.9% a year in the 1990s, 1.3% from 2000 to 2010, 2.0% from 2010 to 2019 and 0.4% from 2019 to 2025, with overseas applicants setting the pace. Trade marks grew 4.3% a year and designs 5.5% a year from 2019 to 2025.

figures.label: a year, standard patents' growth, 2019 to 2025
a year, designs' growth, 2019 to 2025
standard patent applications in 2021, the highest year

points: Australians' standard patents grew 1.1%, 2.5%, 0.9% and 0.9% a year in the four periods (by the filer's origin); overseas applicants' 4.2%, 1.1%, 2.1% and 0.3%.
Trade marks grew 6.9%, 3.3%, 2.7% and 4.3% a year in the four periods, so their growth since 2019 is faster than in the 2010s but slower than in the 1990s.
Designs grew almost entirely from overseas; Australians' ran at 1,903 (2022) to 2,678 (2013) a year from 1990.

**Falls.** In 2009, standard patents fell 10.9% (26,598 to 23,707), designs 15.2% and trade marks 4.5%, the year after the global financial crisis began; trade marks fell 11.2% in 2022 from the 2021 peak.

questions.how: The long-run path of each kind of right is context for any claim about the system's contribution.

prep.what: Calendar-year totals are used only for complete years, and growth is the steady yearly rate between two years.
prep.why: Part years would look like falls; a yearly rate compares periods of different lengths.

steps: Add up each series by calendar year, from each series' start.
Work out the average yearly growth between chosen years.
Note the years with falls.
assumptions: Growth between two years summarises the path between them; the years in between may differ.
limits: Counts grow with the economy and with overseas demand; growth alone is not a measure of value.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares changes, not levels, so that series that both grow over decades are not mistaken for related.
observations.section: 5.1 Long-run trends in applications, by type and origin
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U25 (descriptive). Growth has slowed for standard patents, and quickened since 2019 for trade marks and designs.**
- **Standard patents:** 2,926 applications in 1930, 3,748 in 1950, 13,160 in 1970 and 14,990 in 1990, then 21,995
  (2000), 32,399 (2021, the highest) and 30,448 (2025). Average growth per year: 3.9% in the 1990s, 1.3% from 2000 to
  2010, 2.0% from 2010 to 2019 and 0.4% from 2019 to 2025. Overseas applicants set the pace (4.2%, 1.1%, 2.1% and
  0.3%); Australian applications grew 1.1%, 2.5%, 0.9% and 0.9% a year (by the filer's origin, ADR 0037).
- **Trade marks:** 22,028 (1990) to 97,343 (2025), growing 6.9%, 3.3%, 2.7% and 4.3% a year. In the chart, applications
  from Australians stay above those from overseas throughout.
- **Designs:** 4,190 (1990) to 10,303 (2025): 0.2%, 3.2%, 2.7% and 5.5% a year. In the chart, the growth is almost all
  from overseas applicants; Australians' applications run at 1,903 (2022) to 2,678 (2013) a year from 1990.
- **Provisional applications:** 7,434 in 2000, falling 2.6% and 1.5% a year to 4,036 in 2022, then 6,874 in 2025
  (U8 has the rise of FY2026).
- **Second-tier patents:** 276 (1990), 7,833 (2021) and 52 (2025): the closure (5.4).
- **Plant breeder's rights:** 134 (1990) and 350 (2000), then 264 to 374 a year (10.1% a year in the 1990s, about
  −1% since).
- **Falls:** in 2009, standard patents fell 10.9% (26,598 to 23,707), designs 15.2% (6,060 to 5,136) and trade marks
  4.5% (59,271 to 56,612), the year after the global financial crisis began; in 2022, trade marks fell 11.2% from the
  2021 peak (88,751 to 78,844).
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** the heading said growth had "quickened" for trade marks, which grew faster in the 1990s (6.9%)
  than since 2019 (4.3%); Australians' designs ("near 2,000 to 2,700") were read from the chart.

observations.headline: Australians file a quarter less in January; overseas applicants barely pause
observations.statement: From 2010 to 2019, Australians' January filings were 75% of an ordinary month for standard patents and trade marks and 67% for designs, while overseas applicants' were 90% to 96%. Provisional applications, about 95% Australian, were at 70%. For Australian standard patents, January was at 80% in the 1990s, 82% in the 2000s, 75% in the 2010s and 74% in 2020 to 2025.

figures.label: of an ordinary month, Australian standard patents in January
overseas standard patents in January

points: Australian trade marks also dip in December (82) and peak in August (115).
The office's output follows its own calendar: trade mark registrations run at 133% of an ordinary month in January and 68% in December, following working days and processing, not demand.
**Decision.** Months are compared with the same month a year earlier, or as 12-month totals.

questions.how: Seasons in demand and in the office's output matter for service planning and for reading monthly figures.

prep.what: Each month is compared with the 12 months centred on it, and the median of each calendar month is taken over 2010 to 2019.
prep.why: Comparing with the months around it removes the trend; a decade before COVID-19 and after the financial crisis gives a typical pattern.

steps: For each series and month, divide the count by the centred 12-month average around it.
Take the median for each calendar month over 2010 to 2019 (100 = an ordinary month).
Repeat January's figure by decade to see whether the lull has changed.
assumptions: A decade's median month is the series' typical seasonal pattern.
limits: The reasons (holidays, business cycles) are not in the data.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares months with the same month a year earlier.
observations.section: 5.2 Seasonal patterns
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U26 (descriptive). Australians file less in January; the office has rhythms of its own.**
- **January is the quiet month for Australian filers** (2010 to 2019; a month's count against the average of the
  months around it, so 75% is 25% below that average): standard patents 75%, trade marks 75% and designs 67%, by the
  filer's origin (ADR 0037). Two series not split by origin dip too: provisional applications 70% (about 95% of them
  Australian, U7) and plant breeder's rights 71% (about 44% Australian). Overseas applicants barely pause: 95% for
  standard patents, 90% for trade marks and 96% for designs.
- **The lull is deepening for patents:** January's share for Australian standard patents was 80 (1990s), 82, 75 and
  74 (2020 to 2025); for provisional applications 73, 72, 70 and 63. For Australian trade marks it is steady (77, 79,
  75, 77).
- Australian trade marks also dip in December (82) and peak in August (115).
- **The office's output has its own calendar:** trade mark registrations run at 133% of an ordinary month in January
  and 68% in December; patent grants at 56% in April and 80% in December. These follow the office's working days and
  processing, not demand.
- **Plant breeder's rights granted** cluster in some months (September 170, March 91 against January 47, February 45
  and July 51): quarters, not months, are the unit (U24).
- **Decision:** in Stage 2, months are compared with the same month a year earlier, or as 12-month totals, never with
  the month before.

observations.headline: Patent grants peaked in 2016; trade mark cessations reached their highest in 2025
observations.statement: Patent grants peaked at 25,687 in 2016, three years after the rush to file before Raising the Bar, and were 19,612 in 2025. Trade mark registrations reached 70,634 in 2021. Trade mark cessations (registered marks let go) rose from 7,240 in 1996 to 35,484 in 2025, the peak, though not steadily: 29,802 in 2019 and 28,319 in 2023.

figures.label: patent grants in 2016, the peak
trade mark cessations in 2025, the peak

points: Patent expiries rose from 30 (1996) to 4,019 (2025), as patents filed under the 20-year term reach it.
Ownership transfers: trade mark assignments peaked at 18,370 (2019), patent assignments at 6,015 (2015).
Trade mark oppositions rose from 824 (1996) to 2,309 (2025, the peak).
Trade mark cessations fell to 3,773 in 2002 while lapses rose: accounted for by the gap between two Acts' first terms and the large filing year of 2000 ({U38}).

questions.how: What happens to rights (granted, kept, let go, sold, challenged) is the flow behind any measure of their value.

prep.what: Events are counted once per right and day, by calendar year, from each series' start.
prep.why: The register sometimes records the same event twice (ADR 0010).

steps: Add up each event series by calendar year.
Find each series' peak year.
assumptions: The date recorded for an event is when it happened (after each series' start, where batch dating ends).
limits: Event counts mix rights of every age; lifetimes per right are in {U36}.
observations.next: Stage 2 relates events to policy changes and to the applications behind them.
observations.section: 5.3 What happens to rights, over time
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U27 (descriptive). Outcomes over time.**
- **Patent grants** peaked in 2016 (25,687), three years after the rush to file before Raising the Bar (5.4), and
  were 15,739 in 2023 and 19,612 in 2025.
- **Trade mark registrations** rose from 19,578 (1996) to 70,634 (2021, the peak) and 70,616 (2025).
- **Lapses** (applications that ended): patents peaked in 2010 (13,945) and were 12,294 in 2025; trade marks peaked
  in 2017 (19,767).
- **Cessations** (registered rights let go) rose for trade marks from 7,240 (1996) to 35,484 (2025, the peak), and for
  patents from 8,202 to 18,919 (2021, the peak) and 15,244 (2025). Design cessations were 6,218 to 6,612 in each year
  shown since 2016.
- **Expiries** of patents rose from 30 (1996) and 861 (2000) to 4,019 (2025), as patents filed under the 20-year term
  reach it (U23).
- **Ownership transfers:** trade mark assignments rose from 9,389 (1996) to 18,370 (2019, the peak); patent
  assignments from 1,802 to 6,015 (2015, the peak), and 3,910 in 2025.
- **Oppositions:** trade marks 824 (1996) to 2,309 (2025, the peak); patents 50 to 112 in the years shown since 2005,
  and 154 at their peak (2015).
- **Extensions of term** for pharmaceutical patents peaked at 114 in 2000, the first full year of the 1999 regime,
  and have run at 14 to 76 a year since.
- **Trade marks in 2002:** cessations fell from 7,847 (2000) to 3,773 (2002), while lapses rose from 8,026 to 16,718 and
  registrations from 18,310 to 29,902. First left as a lead for the events attachment; U38 has since shown it, by age
  at cessation and year of filing: the gap between the 1955 Act's seven-year first term and the 1995 Act's ten-year
  one, and the filing peak of 2000. What U38 does not show is anything beyond the register's terms (for example,
  whether owners behaved differently under the new Act).
- Cessations of trade marks are not a steady rise: 29,802 (2019), 28,283 (2021), 28,319 (2023) and 35,484 (2025).

observations.headline: Around some policy changes filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses; around others nothing stands out
observations.statement: In April 2013, the month Raising the Bar took effect, Australians filed 1,044 standard patent applications, 4.41 times their average month in the year before. In August 2021, when the innovation patent closed to new applications, 2,789 second-tier applications came in (4.31 times), then 95.9% fewer a month in the year after. Patent expiries fell 98.4% when the term rose to 20 years.

figures.label: Australians' usual monthly patent filing, in April 2013
second-tier applications a month after the innovation patent closed
patent expiries after the term rose to 20 years

points: **Rushes before a change:** Raising the Bar (Australians 4.41 times their usual month, overseas applicants 2.65 times; in the year after, 34.0% and 7.7% fewer a month) and the innovation patent's closure. Filing also rose after each change was enacted and before it took effect: second-tier applications by 176.4%, Australian standard patents by 45.3%.

**Steps:** patent expiries (the 20-year term), extensions of term (the 1999 scheme, from 0.08 to 11.17 a month), second-tier applications when the innovation patent replaced the petty patent (+71.5%), and designs under the Designs Act 2003 (overseas applications +40.4%, Australians' +3.4%).
**Pauses when an Act began:** no trade mark registrations in January 1996 (Trade Marks Act 1995; 4,021 in March) and 113 patent grants in June 1991 (Patents Act 1990), against about 1,025 a month.

**Nothing stands out:** joining the PCT (entries through it come about 30 months after filing abroad), the plain packaging of tobacco, and the 2018 and 2019 Productivity Commission responses. Overseas trade marks fell 17.2% in the year after Australia joined the Madrid Protocol (July 2001), but they had been falling since early 2000.

**Against the direction expected:** after the designs grace period (March 2022), Australians' design applications fell 16.5% and overseas applicants' rose 0.2%. A grace period would not be expected to lower filing, so the fall has some other cause, which this comparison cannot name.
All compare the 12 months after with the 12 before; trends and seasons are not allowed for here ({B37} does).

questions.how: These dated changes are the raw material for natural experiments, the designs that can estimate what a policy actually changed.
Shows which levers have moved behaviour visibly in the past, and which have not.

prep.what: Each of the 17 policy changes is placed in the month it took effect (or, for two, was enacted), checked against the Federal Register of Legislation.
prep.why: A wrong date would put the change in the wrong place (ADR 0011, 0014).

prep.what: Each change is paired with the series it targets.
prep.why: A change to trade mark law should show in trade mark series, not patents.

steps: For each change, take its target series for 24 months either side.
Compare the change's month and the 12 months after with the average month of the 12 before.
Class each response as a rush, a step, a pause or nothing visible.
assumptions: The month a change took effect (or was enacted) is the right month to compare around. Stage 1 does not assume the change caused what is seen, since trends, seasons and other events could also be at work.
limits: A before-and-after comparison of one series cannot separate a change's effect from anything else that happened at the same time.
Fee changes, IP Australia's most direct lever, were added after Stage 2 ({U108} to {U111}) and compared in {B47} to {B49}.
observations.next: Stage 2 measures each candidate against trends and seasons, with placebo dates ({B37}).
observations.section: 5.4 The 17 policy changes, one at a time
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U28 (descriptive). Four kinds of response, and changes with none visible.** All compare the average month in the
12 months after a change's month with the 12 months before; trends and seasons are not allowed for.
- **Rushes to file before a change.** Raising the Bar (April 2013): 1,044 standard patent applications from
  Australians (4.41 times their average month in the year before) and 5,381 from overseas (2.65 times); in the year
  after, 34.0% and 7.7% fewer a month. The innovation patent's closure (August 2021): 2,789 applications (4.31 times),
  then 95.9% fewer (26.25 a month). Anticipation shows after each enactment: second-tier applications rose 176.4% in
  the year after the phase-out was enacted, and Australian standard patents 45.3% in the year after Raising the Bar
  was.
- **Steps.** Patent expiries fell 98.4% (289.5 to 4.67 a month) when the term rose to 20 years. Extensions of term
  went from 0.08 a month to 11.17 under the 1999 regime (60 in December 1999, the chart). Second-tier applications
  rose 71.5% (50.58 to 86.75 a month) when the innovation patent replaced the petty patent. Under the Designs Act
  2003, design applications from overseas rose 40.4% and registrations 24.5%; Australians' applications 3.4%.
- **Pauses at commencement.** The Trade Marks Act 1995: no trade mark registrations in January 1996, 4,021 in March
  (5.5), and Australians' applications at 0.5 times their usual month in January 1996; assignments published rose
  79.3%. The Patents Act 1990: 113 patent grants in June 1991, against about 1,025 a month (5.5).
- **None visible:** Australia joining the PCT (March 1980; entries through it come about 30 months after filing
  abroad); the plain packaging of tobacco (Australian trade marks −4.0%, overseas +5.6%, and no series counts tobacco
  marks); the Productivity Commission responses of 2018 and 2019 (trade mark oppositions +3.1%). Overseas trade marks fell 17.2% in the year after Australia
  joined the Madrid Protocol (July 2001), but the chart shows them falling from early 2000. Plant breeder's rights
  applications rose 22% after the 1994 Act, on 21 to 25 a month: too few to read.
- **Not the way the change would push:** the designs grace period (March 2022): Australians' design applications fell
  16.5% in the year after, overseas applicants' rose 0.2%. A grace period would not lower filing, so the fall has some
  other cause, which this comparison cannot name. (Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043): listed under "None visible".)
- **Decision:** Stage 2's candidates are the two rushes, the four steps and the two pauses, each with placebo dates.
  Fee changes, the other lever IP Australia holds, were missing here (R3); they were added after Stage 2 (5.7, U108
  to U111, in `fee_changes`) and tested in B47 to B49. `policy_events` keeps the 17 changes of 5.4.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, ADR 0037):** the series by origin now count the filer's origin, not the current
  holder's; the largest change is the Designs Act 2003 (overseas designs +34.1% and Australians' +6.5% by the holder).

later.what: Of the rushes Stage 1 saw, Raising the Bar's holds with each series' trend and season held, and is followed by a lower level (about 28% fewer a month) that recovers.

observations.headline: Forty-two months still stand out after the repairs; each is explained and kept
observations.statement: After the repairs, 42 months in 12 series are at least three times, or under a third of, the months around them. They are rushes, the register's start-up in 1904, pauses and backlogs when new Acts began, and one transfer of many patents at once (1,603 patent assignments in July 2015).

figures.label: unusual months, all explained
patent assignments in July 2015, one large transfer

points: **Pauses and backlogs:** patent grants in June 1991 (113); trade mark registrations in January and March 1996 (0, then 4,021); patent cessations in February 2020 (7).
**The register's first months:** applications could be lodged from February 1904, before the Patents Act 1903 took effect on 1 June 1904.
**Design lapses** fall to 0 to 16 in April in six of the seven years from 1996 to 2002 ({U39}).
**The July 2015 transfer:** the patents assigned on 2 July 2015 are now held mostly in Finland (198) and the United States (170).
**Decision.** No more months are removed; pauses are pooled with their backlogs, rushes are studied.

questions.how: Unusual months must be explained before any month can be read as a policy effect.

prep.what: Each month is compared with the median of the two years around it, in series running at 50 or more a month.
prep.why: A two-year median is not pulled about by one odd month.

steps: For each series, work out the median of the 25 months centred on each month.
Flag months at least three times or under a third of it.
Look up what happened in each flagged month.
assumptions: A month three times its neighbours is unusual enough to need explaining.
limits: Smaller oddities are not flagged.
observations.next: Stage 2 pools pauses with their backlogs, or uses 12-month totals.
observations.section: 5.5 Artefacts
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U29 (descriptive). What still stands out, and what it is.** The table lists 42 months in 12 series.
- **Rushes, kept:** April 2013 (Australian standard patents, 5.52 times the median of the two years around it) and
  August 2021 (second-tier patents, 6 times). They are the policy responses of U28.
- **The register's first months:** standard patents of unknown origin run at 0 to 35 a month from January to May 1904
  and 394 in June 1904. Applications could be lodged from February 1904, before the Patents Act 1903 took effect on
  1 June 1904, so the months before June are a start-up, best left out of any comparison.
- **Pauses and their backlogs, kept:** patent grants in June 1991 (113, after the Patents Act 1990 commenced) and in
  October and November 1998 (248, then 3,373); trade mark registrations in January and March 1996 (0, then 4,021, the
  Trade Marks Act 1995); patent cessations in December 2006 (82) and February 2020 (7). February 2020 is also the
  month the innovation patent's phase-out was enacted, but the pause is in cessations of every kind of patent, so
  nothing in the data links the two.
- **Single low months in steady series:** trade mark registrations in January 1987 (151) and September 1991 (339),
  design registrations in January 1992 (77), trade mark lapses in October 1986, August 1987 and April 1996 (122, 94
  and 243), and patent assignments in February 1992, August 1998, January 2000 and March 2026 (42 to 75); patent
  assignments were also high in June 1994 (347).
- **A recurring low:** design lapses fall to 0 to 16 in April in six of the seven years from 1996 to 2002, and to 0 in
  October 2002, in a series of 59 to 76 a month. U39 shows it is how lapses were dated (April's lapses dated in other
  months), not fewer lapses, and pools those years' months in Stage 2.
- **The origin field, not the count:** trade marks of unknown origin fall to 14 to 40 a month from November 1983 to
  May 1984 (and 87 in July 1985), against about 240. Australian and overseas trade marks are not flagged in those
  months, so what changed is the origin recorded.
- **An effect of the method:** patent expiries in February 1995 (240, 3.22 times) stand out only because the two years
  around them include the near-empty months after July 1995 (U23).
- **A transfer of many patents at once:** patent assignments in July 2015 (1,603, 4.2 times the median), published
  over the month's five weekly issues (395, 646, 325, 163 and 73); the patents assigned on 2 July 2015 are now held
  mostly in Finland (198) and the United States (170). One transfer of a portfolio fits this; the data do not name it.
- **Decision:** no further months are removed. Stage 2 pools each pause with its backlog (for example, patent
  cessations in February and March 2020) or uses 12-month totals; rushes are studied, not removed; the months before
  June 1904 are left out.

observations.headline: The consumer price index is complete each quarter from 1948, so money can be compared across years
observations.statement: The price index has 312 quarters, from the September quarter 1948 to the June quarter 2026, with none missing. Prices rose about 40-fold, from 2.59 to 102.31. Price rises have run at a median 2.3% a year from 1990 to 2019 and 3.6% from 2020 to 2026.

figures.label: quarters, none missing
rise in prices since 1948

points: The median yearly rise was 3.0% from 1949 to 1969 and 8.7% from 1970 to 1989 (highest 17.5%, March quarter 1975).
Prices fell in 13 quarters.
**Decision.** Money is adjusted with this quarterly index, and shown as recorded beside it, with the base stated (September 2025 = 100).

questions.how: Costs and benefits from different years can be compared only once inflation is taken out.

prep.what: The quarterly index is attached to the timeline; the monthly index (from April 2024 only) is not.
prep.why: One series must cover the whole span.

steps: Check the index for missing quarters.
Work out the change over four quarters, and its median in each era.
assumptions: The all-groups index for the eight capital cities stands for prices everywhere in Australia.
limits: A general price index may not suit every kind of spending (R&D costs rise differently).
observations.next: Every money series is adjusted in Stage 2.
observations.section: 5.6 The Consumer Price Index, quarterly
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U30 (descriptive). The CPI is complete, quarterly, from 1948.**
- 312 quarters, from the September quarter 1948 to the June quarter 2026, with none missing.
- Its base is the month of September 2025 (= 100), as the ABS labels it. A quarter is the average of its three months
  (July to September 2025: 99.63, 99.55 and 100.0), so the September quarter 2025 is 99.73.
- Prices rose about 40-fold: from 2.59 (September quarter 1948) to 102.31 (June quarter 2026).
- The median change over four quarters was 3.0% from 1949 to 1969 (highest 25.6%, to the December quarter 1951), 8.7%
  from 1970 to 1989 (17.5%, March quarter 1975), 2.3% from 1990 to 2019 and 3.6% from 2020 to 2026 (7.9%, December
  quarter 2022). Prices fell in 13 quarters.
- **Decision:** money series are deflated with this quarterly index, and shown as recorded beside it, with the base
  stated. `abs_prices` also holds the monthly CPI from April 2024 (29 months); it is not attached, as one series
  must serve the whole span.

observations.headline: The official fees are read from every version of the fee regulations, and today's agree with IP Australia's website
observations.statement: Six sets of regulations have 281 versions on the Federal Register of Legislation; 160 are read (8,612 rows of fee schedules), and the gaps come from the amending instruments. The fees run from 1982 for designs, 1989 for trade marks, 1991 for patents and 1994 for plant breeder's rights, in 49 series of 23 fees.

figures.label: versions of the fee regulations
fee series (23 fees)
fees compared that agree with IP Australia's pages today

points: Today's fees: $400 to file a standard patent, $550 to examine it, $250 for a trade mark class from the pick list, $2,000 to examine a plant variety.
Where the Register holds no text (most designs and patents versions before 1999), the fees come from the amending instruments: 94 of the 285 spells at one amount.
The fee columns join the timeline, and each change joins the policy register (lever "fees"), kept apart from Stage 1's 17 policy changes.

questions.how: Fees are IP Australia's most direct lever; this is their full history.
Each fee change is a candidate natural experiment ({B47} to {B49}).

prep.what: Every compilation's fee schedule read from the Register's EPUB files, with the 1980s and 1990s filled from the amending instruments by hand (ADR 0031).
prep.why: The Register holds the text of only 163 of the versions.

steps: Read every version's fee schedule into one row per fee and date.
Fill the versions without text from the instruments that amended them.
Check the latest amounts against IP Australia's fee pages.
assumptions: A fee applies from the date its regulation commenced.
limits: Official fees only; attorneys' fees, often larger, are not recorded.
observations.next: Stage 2 tests filing and lapsing around each change ({B47} to {B49}).
observations.section: 5.7 IP Australia's official fees (added after Stage 2; ADR 0031)
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U108 (descriptive). The official fees are read from every version of the fee regulations: designs from 1982, trade
marks from 1989, patents from 1991 and plant breeder's rights from 1994; today's agree with IP Australia's website.**
- Six sets of regulations have 281 versions on the Federal Register (102 for the Patents Regulations 1991). The
  Register holds the text of 163; 160 are read (8,612 rows of fee schedules), one patent compilation being left out
  because it already shows fees that began later (ADR 0031).
- Where the Register holds no text (the 1955 Act's trade mark regulations after 1958; most designs and patents
  versions before 1999), the fees come from the amending instruments, read by hand or, where one replaces a whole
  schedule, by the same rules (`gaps.yaml`): 94 of the 285 spells at one amount.
- 49 series of 23 fees (patent renewals by anniversary). The latest version gives the same amount as IP Australia's
  fee pages for all eight fees compared (for example $400 to file a standard patent, $550 to examine it, $250 for a
  trade mark class from the pick list, $2,000 to examine a plant variety).
- **Decision:** the fee columns join the timeline lens (`fee_*`, 26 columns) and each change joins `policy_events`
  (lever "fees"); the timeline's `policy_events` column keeps the other changes, so section 5.4 is unchanged.

observations.headline: In real terms a trade mark costs about a quarter of what it did in 1990, and keeping a patent for its full term costs what it did in 1995
observations.statement: In dollars of June 2026, a trade mark (one class, filing and registration) cost 944 in January 1990 and 250 now. A standard patent's filing, examination and grant fell from 2,261 (January 1995) to 1,250. Its renewals for the full term cost 16,140 in January 1995, 11,992 in January 2010 and 16,550 now.

figures.label: a trade mark, June 2026 dollars
a standard patent's filing, examination and grant
a patent's renewals for the full term

points: A trade mark's renewal: 1,141 to 400.
A plant breeder's right: 4,615 (January 1995) to 2,900. A design's filing: 210 (January 1990), 309 (January 2010), 200 now.
In dollars of the day, a patent's full-term renewals rose from 6,995 to 16,550.

questions.how: Getting a right has become much cheaper in real terms; keeping a patent has not.
Lower costs to obtain a right bear on who can afford to file.

prep.what: Each fee deflated by the quarterly Consumer Price Index to June 2026 dollars.
prep.why: Prices in dollars of the day are not comparable over 36 years.

steps: Sum the fees that make up each cost (for example filing, examination and grant).
Deflate by the CPI.
assumptions: The CPI is the right measure of what a dollar buys for filers.
limits: Official fees only.
observations.next: Stage 2 tests whether changes in cost moved filing or lapsing ({B47}, {B49}).

observations.headline: A standard patent's renewal fees have moved towards its last years
observations.statement: The renewal fee at a patent's 19th anniversary was 4.69 times the 5th's in January 1992 and 8.94 times in June 2026. The share of the full term's renewals paid from the 15th anniversary rose from 48.7% to 62.1%.

of full-term renewals paid from the 15th anniversary

points: 5.56 in January 2003 and 3.6 in January 2010.

Find the share of the full term's renewals paid from the 15th anniversary.

observations.headline: The industries table covers 19 divisions over 37 years; IP and value added run through all of them, business and R&D counts only through recent years
observations.statement: IP columns and gross value added are filled for every division and year, FY1990 to FY2026. Business counts cover FY2023 to FY2026, business R&D only FY2024, wages FY1998 to FY2026 (18 divisions; the index leaves out agriculture) and creative value added FY2016 to FY2025 for 10 divisions.

the only year of business R&D by division

points: So Stage 2 can relate IP to businesses over four years and to R&D in one, across 19 divisions: few points, so comparisons are of patterns, not models.

Gross value added (from the national accounts, added after Stage 2) grows from $829,808 million (FY1990) to $2,358,315 million (FY2026) across the divisions. Manufacturing was the largest division in FY1990 (14.2%) and is 6.0% by FY2026, when mining is largest (12.5%).
Value added gives 37 years for every division, enough to follow change within a division; Stage 2 used it in one year only ({B57}), so the longer comparison is open for Stage 3.

questions.how: Industry is one of the dimensions Q2 asks about; this says how much can be compared, and when.
R&D by industry is a complementary capability; there is only one year of it.

**U73 (descriptive). The lens covers 19 divisions over 37 years; IP and gross value added run through all of them,
while the ABS's business and R&D series cover one to four recent years.**
- IP columns are filled for every division and year, FY1990 to FY2026, and so is gross value added (`gva_cvm`, chain
  volume, AUD million a year, from the national accounts; added after Stage 2, U116). Its divisions' sum grows from
  $829,808 million (FY1990) to $2,358,315 million (FY2026); manufacturing was the largest division in FY1990 (14.2%)
  and FY2000 (11.7%) and is 6.0% by FY2026, when mining is largest (12.5%); arts and recreation is smallest
  throughout (0.79% to 0.89%). Shares are of the divisions' sum, since chain volume values are not strictly additive. Businesses, entries and exits cover FY2023 to

observations.headline: The crosswalks carry nearly every right to an industry; a patent's division is usually clear, its subdivision often is not
observations.statement: The published crosswalks carry 98.42% to 99.73% of standard patents (FY1990 to FY2024) and 99.82% to 99.93% of trade marks to an industry. A standard patent's largest division share has a median of 0.996, but its largest subdivision share only 0.727. A trade mark's division is less clear (median 0.792).

So division counts for patents are close to certain; subdivision counts and all trade mark counts are spread estimates.

questions.how: Says how precisely IP can be placed in industries, which limits every industry comparison.

prep.what: Each right is split equally over its classes, and each class over industries by the crosswalk's probabilities.

**U74 (descriptive). The crosswalks carry nearly every right, and a patent's division is usually clear, but its

- **Carried:** 98.42% to 99.73% of standard patents (FY1990 to FY2024; 92.71% in FY2026, whose filings are not all
  classified yet), 99.82% to 99.93% of trade marks, and second-tier patents from 52.69% (FY1990, many petty patents
  unclassified) to 100% (FY2024).
- **B6:** subclass marks unknown to the crosswalk fall from 12,143 to 71 (of 2,518,546), and patents with no known

  mark's division is less clear (median 0.792; 39.28% with 90% or more in one division).
- **So** division counts for patents are close to certain, subdivision counts are spread estimates, and trade mark
  counts are spread at both levels.

observations.headline: Nine in ten patents fall in manufacturing, partly because the patent crosswalk leaves out services
observations.statement: Of standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026, manufacturing is allocated 90.78%, utilities 4.76% and agriculture 2.04%; no service industry gets more than 0.23%, because the crosswalk used here leaves services out. A patent's industry says what kind of product its technology is, not who files or uses it. Trade marks spread more widely: manufacturing 55.65%, professional services 11.05%.

figures.label: of standard patents fall in manufacturing
of trade marks fall in manufacturing

points: Within manufacturing: machinery and equipment 31.18% of all standard patents, chemicals (including pharmaceuticals) 30.17%.
Manufacturing's share of trade marks fell from 73.94% (FY1990) to 56.51% (FY2000) and has stayed near 55%.
**With services in the crosswalk** (added after Stage 2, {U114}), manufacturing's share over FY2016 to FY2025 is 79.67% rather than 90.63%.

**The 2002 break:** accommodation and food services have no trade marks to FY2001 and 1.67% from FY2003. That matches the Nice classification's 8th edition, which split class 42 into classes 42 to 45 in January 2002, so trade mark shares are compared from FY2003 on, or across the break with that caveat.

questions.how: Which industries IP serves is part of who benefits; the crosswalk's limit must be stated with any answer.
Industry is one condition that may decide whether protection produces value.

prep.what: Rights are counted as expected counts through the crosswalks, FY2017 to FY2026.
prep.why: A right can belong partly to several industries ({U74}).

steps: Add up each division's expected count of standard patents and trade marks.
Work out each division's share.
Follow each division's share over time, and look for breaks.
assumptions: A patent's division says what kind of product its technology is.
limits: Industry counts are allocations by technology, not counts of what each industry's businesses file.
The crosswalk without services gives service industries almost no patents; the one with services is compared in {U114}.

observations.original:
**U75 (descriptive). Nine in ten patents fall in manufacturing, because the patent crosswalk leaves out services;
trade marks spread across industries, with a break in 2002.**
- **Standard patents, FY2017 to FY2026:** manufacturing 90.78%, utilities 4.76%, agriculture 2.04%, mining 1.15%,
  construction 0.94%; no service division above 0.23%. The lens's main measure uses ALP's recommended crosswalk *excluding
  services*, which assigns patents only to goods-producing industries, so a patent's division says what kind of
  product its technology is, not who uses it. The crosswalk with services, added after Stage 2, is compared in U114:
  over FY2016 to FY2025 manufacturing takes 90.63% without services and 79.67% with them (U114's window is a year
  earlier than this bullet's, hence 90.63% against 90.78%). The shares hardly move: manufacturing 90.93% (FY1990), 89.97% (FY2010), 90.82% (FY2026).
- **Within manufacturing:** machinery and equipment 31.18% of all standard patents and basic chemicals and chemical
  products (including pharmaceuticals) 30.17%, then food products 5.07% and polymer products 4.81%.
- **Trade marks:** manufacturing 55.65%, professional, scientific and technical services 11.05%, information media
  4.55%, administrative services 4.22%, finance 2.94%. Manufacturing's share fell from 73.94% (FY1990) to 56.51%
  (FY2000) and has stayed near 55%.
- **The 2002 break:** accommodation and food services have no trade marks to FY2001 and 1.67% from FY2003, health
  care 0.46% (FY2001) to 1.59%, while professional services fall from 12.95% to 8.43%: the Nice classification's 8th
  edition split class 42 into 42 to 45 in January 2002. Trade mark shares are compared within FY2003 on, or across
  the break with that caveat.

observations.headline: Universities file patents through their commercialisation companies to very different degrees
observations.statement: UNSW files 96.5% of its patent applications through NewSouth Innovations, the University of Newcastle 72.8% through Newcastle Innovation and Adelaide 43.9%, while Queensland files 2.1% through UniQuest and Sydney, Monash and QUT under 1%. observations.headline: US patents often cite the institutions' research; few of the citing patents have an Australian applicant or inventor
observations.statement: Per 1,000 works published 2010 to 2014, US patents cite 107.7 of medical research institutes' works, 64.56 of public research agencies' and 43.26 of universities'. 93.6% of these citations come from US patents with no Australian applicant or inventor; most US patents have no Australian party, whatever they cite.

figures.label: medical research institutes' works cited by a US patent, per 1,000
of the citations come from US patents with no Australian party

points: Peter MacCallum 161.5, QIMR Berghofer 140.9, the Florey 119.3, Data61 115.1; Melbourne leads the universities (64.25).
Works published in 2010 drew 26,933 US patent citations; 2024's 268, because citations accumulate for years, so recent years are not comparable.

**What this does not show.** The citing patents are US patents only, and a citation (often added by an examiner or an attorney) is not use. So this is not a measure of where Australian research is used.
The counts are lower bounds: about 5.6% more patent-cited Australian works are missing from the harvest ({U121}).
97.0% of the institutions' standard applications filed 2000 to 2024 are found in Google Patents, but only 4.3% of their provisionals, which are rarely published.

questions.how: Where public research reaches invention bears on public value. This measure shows how often US patents cite the research, and is clear about what a citation cannot show.
Sets out what citation counts can and cannot measure, before they are used to look for gaps between research and invention.

prep.what: Citations from US patents to the institutions' works come from the Reliance on Science dataset, by the work's publication year.
prep.why: It links patents to the research they cite.

steps: Count works cited by a US patent, by kind of institution, for works published 2010 to 2014.
Divide by works published.
Work out the share of citations from patents with an Australian applicant or inventor.
assumptions: A citation shows a link between a patent and a paper; it may have been added by an examiner or an attorney, so it is not evidence that the invention used the research.
limits: US patents only; recent works have had little time to be cited.
The share from patents with no Australian party mostly reflects that most US patents have none.
observations.next: Stage 2 related citations to the institutions' own patenting ({B45}, {B46}). Stage 3 is to compare citations in fixed-age windows.

3.5% to 8.3%), so the counts are lower bounds, and whether the loss falls evenly enough to leave the rankings below

- **Citations:** works published in 2010 drew 26,933 US patent citations, 2015's 27,269, 2020's 7,819 and 2024's 268:
  citations accumulate for years, so recent years are not comparable. 6.40% of the citations come from patents with
  an Australian applicant or inventor.
- **Per 1,000 works (2010 to 2014):** medical research institutes 107.7 are cited by a US patent, other research
  institutes 74.39, public research agencies 64.56, health services 60.65, universities 43.26. Peter MacCallum 161.5,
  QIMR Berghofer 140.9, the Florey 119.3, Data61 115.1; Melbourne leads the universities (64.25).
- **Families:** 97.0% of the institutions' standard applications filed 2000 to 2024 are found in Google Patents, but
  only 4.3% of their provisionals, which are rarely published. Of families first filed 2005 to 2019, 55.95% of the
  public research agencies' were granted in the US, 51.37% of universities' and 44.70% of medical research
  institutes'; the agencies' are cited most (7.25 families citing them within five years, universities 5.62).
- **So** 93.6% of the US-patent citations to the institutions' works come from patents with no Australian applicant
  or inventor. The citing patents are US patents only, most of which have no Australian party whatever they cite,
  and a citation (often an examiner's or an attorney's) is not use: this is not a measure of where Australian
  research is used, a question for Q1 (B46).
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** this read "the research-to-invention link runs mostly through foreign patents", and the
  heading "rarely from Australian inventions".

observations.headline: The harvest's "cited at least once" filter drops few patent-cited Australian works
observations.statement: A sample of 20,000 of the 5,002,883 patent-cited works outside the harvest found 23 Australian ones. Scaled up, about 5,753 patent-cited Australian works are missing (5.6% of those found; interval 3.5% to 8.3%), 2,501 of them for want of a scholarly citation (2.4%) and most of the rest under merged OpenAlex ids.

figures.label: patent-cited Australian works missing (3.5% to 8.3%)
lost to the filter itself
Australian works in the harvest

points: 10 of the 23 were never cited by another paper; 12 are held under another id (a merged record).

**Decision:** no re-harvest. An undercount of a few per cent, if spread evenly over the institutions, would not change their order or {B45} and {B46}. That is an assumption: the sample's 23 works are too few to test it by institution. Stage 3 reads the counts as a [[lower-bound]].

questions.how: Shows that the count of the institutions' works cited by US patents is close to complete, a few per cent short.

prep.what: A random sample of patent-cited works not in the harvest, looked up in OpenAlex (about 200 calls, free).
prep.why: Measures what the harvest's filter leaves out without fetching everything.

steps: Sample works cited by US patents that the harvest does not hold.
Look each up, and count the Australian ones and why each was missed.
Scale up with an interval.
assumptions: The sample is random, so its share of Australian works represents the rest.
limits: A small count (23) gives a wide interval.
observations.next: Stage 3 reads institutions' patent-cited works as lower bounds.

observations.original:
**U121 (descriptive). The "cited at least once" filter drops few patent-cited Australian works: about 2.4% more would be
found without it; merged OpenAlex ids lose about as many again.** Of 5,106,527 works US patents cite (Reliance on
Science), the harvest holds 103,644 Australian ones, with 614,148 patent citations. A sample of 20,000 of the other
5,002,883 found 23 Australian works: 10 never cited by another paper (the filter's loss) and 12 that OpenAlex now holds
under another id (a merged record; Reliance on Science cites the old one). Scaled up, about 5,753 patent-cited
Australian works are missing (5.6% of those found; 95% interval 3.5% to 8.3%), 2,501 of them for want of a scholarly
citation (2.4%; 1.2% to 4.4%). The Australian works found in the sample carry 24 of its 154,131 patent citations.
- **Decision:** no re-harvest. An undercount of a few per cent, if spread evenly over the institutions, would not change
  their order or B45 and B46 (an assumption: the sample's 23 works are too few to test it by institution); Stage 3 notes it as a lower bound. Dropping the filter would recover only the
  uncited half; the merged ids would need every cited work's id resolved (about 50,000 calls, several days of the
  free allowance), if a question ever needs it.

observations.headline: Every pair of measures for each type of right was checked; 221 pairs passed every test, in two separate decades
observations.statement: Each type of right was checked on rights filed FY2010 to FY2019 and again on different rights, filed FY2000 to FY2009. 221 distinct pairs of measures passed all four tests for a [[lead]]. The two decades agree closely on which pairs are strong (a rank [[correlation]] of 0.867 across 5,006 pairs), though a lead's size often differs between them.

figures.label: distinct leads across six types of right
agreement between the two decades on how strong each pair is
leads whose strength differs by more than 0.1 between the decades

points: Leads as pairs of variables: 484 for standard patents, 296 for trade marks, 252 for designs, 41 for provisionals, 414 for second-tier patents and 99 for plant breeder's rights. As distinct pairs of measures (one measure counted once, however many versions of it there are): 59, 45, 32, 9, 62 and 14.
81, 20, 62, 7, 155 and 29 pairs passed in the first decade but did not hold in the second, so they are not leads.
Years in force is not part of this check: for a right still in force it is only how long it has lasted so far. Lifetimes are compared with survival curves instead ({U36}, {B4}).

No pair failed on the correction for the number of pairs alone. With samples this large, almost everything is "statistically significant"; the size threshold (0.1) and the second decade did the sorting.

questions.how: Sorts which measures of the rights (lifetimes, reach, citations) move with which features of the filer, so that the value measures are read with what they depend on.
Shows which pairs involving who files (origin, applicant type, representation) are strong enough to follow up.

prep.what: Each type of right is screened on its own, on up to 200,000 rights in each decade, chosen by a fixed rule (a hash of the right's number) so the same rights come back on every run.
prep.why: Pooling the types mostly shows that patents differ from trade marks; a fixed sample makes the screen repeatable.

prep.what: Every column of the lens is named as a number, a category or left out (with the reason) in one file, and measures that are versions of one another are grouped, so that a pair "related by construction" is never counted as a lead.
prep.why: A status and the flags made from it, or a total and its parts, always go together; that is arithmetic, not a finding.

steps: Measure every pair of variables on one scale from 0 (unrelated) to 1 (perfectly related), whatever their kinds.
Keep a pair only if it is at least small (0.1) and survives the [[multiple-testing|correction for many tests]] in FY2010 to FY2019.
Measure it again in FY2000 to FY2009, and keep it only if it is at least 0.1 there too, in the same direction.
Drop pairs that are two versions of one measure, and count the rest once per pair of measures.
assumptions: A strength of 0.1 is the smallest association worth following up, as is conventional for rank correlations.
A pair that holds across two decades of changing practice and records is more than an accident of one period.
limits: A lead says two measures go together. It says nothing about why, and either could depend on a third (see B4).
The screen finds associations that are monotone (one rises as the other rises or falls); a relationship that rises then falls could be missed.
observations.next: The leads are sorted by judgement into mechanics of the IP system ({B2}), record quirks ({B3}) and substantive signals ({B4}), which the planned pairs then measure properly.
observations.section: 1.0 The screen: every pair, within each type of right
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**B1 (descriptive). The screen of the rights lens: 221 distinct leads, all of them past the correction for the
number of pairs, most of them holding in a second decade.**
- Six types of right were screened, each on up to 200,000 rights filed FY2010 to FY2019 and again on those filed
  FY2000 to FY2009; 23 (provisionals) to 52 (standard patents) variables had at least one measured pair.
- **Leads:** 484 pairs for standard patents, 296 for trade marks, 252 for designs, 41 for provisionals, 414 for
  second-tier patents and 99 for plant breeder's rights; as distinct pairs of measures, 59, 45, 32, 9, 62 and 14
  (221 in all, as printed). 81, 20, 62, 7, 155 and 29 pairs passed in the first decade but did not hold in the second.
- **No pair failed on the correction alone** ("not significant": 0 for every type): with samples this large the
  conventional threshold of 0.1 and the second decade did all the sorting, as expected.
- **The two decades agree closely:** across the 5,006 pairs measured in both, the strengths' order agrees with a
  Spearman rho of 0.867. Of 1,586 leads, 245 differ between the decades by more than 0.1, so a lead's size is often
  period-specific even when its existence is not.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, audit S2 L1 R32; ADR 0041):** years in force is no longer screened. For a right still
  in force it is only how long the right has lasted so far, so the screen mixed finished and unfinished lifetimes, and
  the more recent decade's far more. It was 223 distinct leads, 5,207 pairs and 0.859; lifetimes are read from
  survival curves by cohort (section 1.2 and B4).

observations.headline: The strongest pairs are how the IP system works, not findings, and are recorded but not carried forward
observations.statement: The strongest leads are what the filing rules and the way records are made would produce anyway. Australian filers file their international (PCT) applications at IP Australia (strength 0.945), and the inventions they file are made here (0.892). A patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination (0.83).

figures.label: filer in Australia with IP Australia as the PCT receiving office
time to grant with the time taken to request examination
how much more often than chance an Australian filer uses IP Australia for a PCT application

points: Each held in the earlier decade too: 0.938, 0.851 and 0.817.
**The applicant sets part of the pace.** A standard patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination; the office is not the only source of delay.

**A record effect.** Wider families have fewer inventors of unknown country (0.526; 0.582), because Google Patents takes inventors' countries from foreign publications, which narrow families lack ({U95}).
**Trade marks:** expedited examination goes with a priority claim (0.78; 0.763), the recording {U103} explained.
**Provisionals:** individuals have no ABN (0.757; 0.738). **Trade marks:** a founding applicant's country goes with its priority office (0.731; 0.774).

questions.how: Clears away pairs that only restate the rules, so that the measures carried forward are about value, not procedure.

prep.what: The screen's leads, each with a 95% [[interval|interval]] for its strength from repeated resampling.
prep.why: Shows how precisely each strength is known.

steps: Read the strongest leads for each type of right.
Ask of each whether the filing rules or the way records are made would produce it anyway.
Record those that would as mechanics, and do not carry them to Stage 3 as signals.
assumptions: The judgement of what counts as "mechanics" is the analyst's, set out here so a reader can disagree.
limits: A mechanical pair can still matter for a later question (time to grant depends on the applicant's choices, which an intervention could change); it is simply not evidence about value.
observations.next: Not carried to Stage 3 as signals; later analyses allow for them (for example, time to grant is read from the examination request).

observations.original:
**B2 (descriptive). The strongest leads are mechanics of the IP system, recorded and not carried forward.** Each is
expected from how rights are filed and recorded:
- Australian filers file their PCT applications at IP Australia (filer origin × PCT receiving office 0.945, interval
  0.942 to 0.949; 0.938 in FY2000 to FY2009; the filer in Australia with `au` 17.9 times chance), and the inventions
  they file are made here (filer origin × an inventor in Australia 0.892, interval 0.888 to 0.895; 0.851).
- A standard patent's time to grant rises with the time its owner waits before asking for examination (rho 0.83,
  interval 0.829 to 0.832; 0.817): the applicant, not only the office, sets the pace.
- Wider families have fewer inventors of unknown country (rho 0.526; 0.582): Google Patents takes inventors' countries
  from foreign publications, which narrow families lack (U95).
- Trade marks: expedited examination goes with a priority claim (0.78; 0.763), the recording U103 explained, and a
  founding applicant's country with its priority office (0.731; 0.774).
- Provisionals: individuals have no ABN (0.757; 0.738).

observations.headline: IP RAPID gives no applicant country for designs that were never registered
observations.statement: The strongest design pair is status against unknown origin (0.98). Every lapsed and every withdrawn design is of unknown origin in IP RAPID (100%), against 0.22% of ceased and 0.01% of registered ones filed FY2010 to FY2019. So "origin unknown" designs are, in recent decades, the applications that never reached registration.

registered designs with no origin (FY2010 to FY2019)
lapsed and withdrawn designs still unknown after the register's fill

points: The same in the earlier decade (0.996).

So a comparison of origins on IP RAPID alone quietly drops the designs that failed, and must use the filled origin instead.

questions.how: Prevents a false reading of who files designs: failed applications would otherwise vanish from the comparison.

prep.what: Each design's origin as IP RAPID gives it, beside the origin filled from IP Australia's register.
prep.why: The register holds countries that IP RAPID leaves out.

Compare with the filled origin.
assumptions: The register's country for a design is the same kind of fact as IP RAPID's.
limits: Explains the earlier observations {U7} and {U13} for recent decades; older unknowns may have other causes.

observations.original:
**B3 (descriptive). A record quirk: IP RAPID gives no applicant country for designs that were never registered.** The
screen's strongest design pair is status against applicants of unknown country (0.98, interval 0.976 to 0.982; 0.996
in FY2000 to FY2009). In the table above, every lapsed and every withdrawn design in both decades is of unknown
origin in IP RAPID (100%), against 0.22% of ceased and 0.01% of registered ones filed FY2010 to FY2019. The register's
countries fill nearly all of them (after the fill, 1.12% of lapsed and 3.81% of withdrawn designs filed FY2010 to
FY2019 remain unknown). So IP RAPID's "origin unknown" designs (U7, U13) are, in recent decades, the applications that
never reached registration: an origin comparison on IP RAPID alone drops failed applications, and must use the
filled origin (ADR 0029).

observations.headline: The substantive leads, each held in both decades and followed up below
observations.statement: Beyond the mechanics, the screen points to pairs that bear on the questions: patents filed without an attorney are more often withdrawn; how many countries a patent family reaches varies with the route, the applicant's country and the technology; women's share among inventors varies with the technology; and attorney markets are local.

figures.label: how much more often than chance a standard patent with no agent is withdrawn
median offices in a family, Australian against Italian applicants
how much more often than chance South Australian filers use one attorney firm (Collison & Co)

points: **Representation and outcome:** standard patents (0.243; 0.217), trade marks (0.317; 0.274), second-tier patents (0.491; 0.474); designs filed through an agent who is not an attorney (0.323; 0.281). Followed up in {B5} to {B7}.

**Origin and reach:** the offices a standard patent's family is filed in vary with its route (0.431; 0.481), the applicant's country (0.386; 0.489) and the technology (0.328; 0.31: organic fine chemistry a median of 11). Followed up in {B11} and {B12}.

**Technology and inventors' gender:** women's estimated share varies with the technology (0.268; 0.297), highest in biotechnology. The apparent links with China are a quirk of the name dictionary ({U97}), not a finding. Followed up in {B17} and {B18}.

**Trade marks:** individuals go with clothing (class 25, 2.1 times chance); overseas applicants with medical apparatus (class 10, 1.9 times); attorneys file more classes per mark (a mean 1.958 against 1.466 filing alone).

**Lifetimes**, read from survival curves rather than the screen: designs still in force after the renewal at 5 years range from 20.1% for clothing (class 02) to 75.9% for medical and laboratory equipment (class 24), filed FY2010 to FY2019 (20.8% and 74.6% for FY2005 to FY2009). Innovation patents still in force after 5 years: 56.7% with an applicant that has an ABN against 38.6% without (54.7% and 34.5% in the earlier period); 78.2% for applicants in the United States, 40.8% in Australia and 21.4% in China (China's 46.1% in the earlier period, on 72 patents, does not replicate).
**Plant breeder's rights:** the genus goes with overseas applicants (grapes highest) and with the time to grant (citrus a median 2,692 days).

questions.how: Lifetimes, reach and citations, the value signals, are tied to who files and in what field, so they must be compared within those groups.
Representation and origin go with outcomes, a first sign of who is served well and who is not.
Filing without an attorney goes with withdrawal, which is where help to file could matter.

prep.what: Each lead with its candidate [[third-factor|third factors]]: the variables tied to both members by at least 0.1 in the screen.
prep.why: Names what could explain a pair before it is measured properly.

steps: Set aside the mechanics ({B2}) and record quirks ({B3}).
Group what remains by theme, and note each lead's strength in both decades.
Plan a proper measurement for each theme, in units that mean something (grant rates in [[percentage-point|points]], years in force).
assumptions: The strength scale treats a yes/no, a category and a number alike, so strengths of different kinds of pair can be compared.
limits: A strength is a summary; the planned pairs below say how big a difference is in plain units.
Every lead has candidate third factors; none is a cause.
observations.next: Each theme is measured in the sections that follow, then carried to Stage 3 where it survives.

  replicated). **Restated (2 November 2026, audit S2 L1 R32; ADR 0041):** this bullet gave the screen's medians of
  years in force ("9.41 years for class 04, 5 for class 02"; "China lowest, a median 2.54 years"; "6.54 years against
  3.54"), which mixed finished and unfinished lifetimes, so were not survival medians.
- **Plant breeder's rights:** the genus goes with overseas applicants (0.513; 0.544; grapes, `vitis`, highest) and with
  the time to grant (0.336; 0.357; citrus a median 2,692 days).

observations.original:
**B5 (observational). Australian individuals file alone far more than anyone else; organisations and overseas filers
almost never do, for patents.** Share filed with no attorney or agent, FY2010 to FY2019 (FY2000 to FY2009):
- **Standard patents:** Australian individuals 26.11% (19.79%), Australian organisations 3.54% (6.97%), overseas
  individuals 1.14% (1.35%), overseas organisations 0.28% (0.14%).
- **Trade marks:** Australian individuals 68.28% (58.82%), Australian organisations 40.23% (42.67%), overseas
  organisations 5.37% (10.47%).
- **Designs do not replicate:** Australian individuals filed 22.76% of their designs alone in FY2010 to FY2019 but
  2.15% in FY2000 to FY2009, when 5,499 of their 8,142 designs went through an agent who is not an attorney.
  How agents were recorded for designs seems to have changed between the decades; design representation is compared
  within one decade only.

observations.headline: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
observations.statement: Of the standard patents Australian individuals filed alone in FY2010 to FY2019, 4.8% were granted, against 40.6% of those filed with an attorney: a gap of 35.8 [[percentage-point|points]] (interval 33.9 to 37.5). In FY2000 to FY2009 the gap was 36.8 points. It stays among applications whose examination was requested (34.4 points).

figures.label: Australian individuals' standard patents granted, filed alone against with an attorney
the gap, FY2010 to FY2019 (36.8 in FY2000 to FY2009)
the gap among applications that were examined

points: **Filing alone goes with not asking for examination:** 25.2% of individuals' lone applications were examined, against 75.9% with an attorney.

**Australian organisations do not show it in both decades:** a gap of 40.0 points in FY2010 to FY2019 but -6.0 in FY2000 to FY2009, when the 1,149 applications organisations filed alone were granted 62.1% of the time. Those earlier lone filers may have been firms with their own patent staff; the data do not say.
**Trade marks show it in both decades, for both:** with an attorney, Australian individuals' marks are registered 24.3 points more often, organisations' 23.6 points.

**Designs cannot be read here:** the comparison keeps only designs with a known filer, and IP RAPID gives no origin for nearly every design that lapsed or was withdrawn ({B3}), so its 99.4% to 100% registered reflects that selection, not designs' registration rate.

**Not a cause.** Representation counts an agent recorded at any time, so an application dropped early may never appoint one (the arrow can run backwards); and those who file alone differ in resources and experience.

questions.how: Individuals who file without help end with far fewer granted patents. Whether that reflects the system serving them less well, or weaker or abandoned applications, is not shown here.
The lead for whether help to file would add value, the kind of intervention Q4 asks about; testing it needs a design that comes after Stage 3.
Representation is a condition that goes with whether a filing becomes a right at all.

prep.what: Grant rates among standard patents whose outcome is known (pending applications left out), by the filer's origin and type and by representation, with Wilson intervals for each rate and Newcombe intervals for the gaps.
prep.why: An [[interval|interval]] shows how precisely each rate and gap is known.

prep.what: Representation is from the repaired attorney columns ({U20}); "filed alone" means no agent other than the applicant was ever recorded.
prep.why: The register's own flag counted applicants as their own agents ({U2}).

steps: For Australian individuals, find the share of standard patents granted, filed alone and with an attorney.
Take the difference, with its interval, in each decade.
Repeat among applications whose examination was requested, to set aside those never pursued.
Repeat for Australian organisations and for trade marks.
assumptions: Patents filed long enough ago have had time to reach an outcome (the decades end in FY2019).
limits: The arrow can run backwards (an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney), and resources and experience differ.
Candidate [[third-factor|third factors]]: applicant type and origin, whether examination is requested, the route of filing.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3, which tests the gap with these third factors held steady. Any claim that help to file would raise grants needs a design that comes after Stage 3.

observations.original:
**B6 (observational). Standard patents filed alone are rarely granted; the gap is about 36 points for Australian
individuals in both decades, and holds among applications that were examined.**
- **Australian individuals:** 4.8% of standard patents filed alone were granted (interval 3.9% to 6.0%) against 40.6%
  with an attorney (39.2% to 42.1%), FY2010 to FY2019: a gap of 35.8 points (33.9 to 37.5). FY2000 to FY2009: 8.3%
  against 45.1%, a gap of 36.8 points (34.9 to 38.7).
- **Among those whose examination was requested,** the gap stays: 34.4 points (30.0 to 38.3) and 33.7 (29.5 to 37.6).
  Filing alone also goes with not asking for examination: 25.2% of individuals' lone applications against 75.9% with
  an attorney (FY2010 to FY2019).
- **Australian organisations do not replicate:** a gap of 40.0 points (37.4 to 42.1) in FY2010 to FY2019, but -6.0
  (-8.9 to -3.1) in FY2000 to FY2009, when the 1,149 applications organisations filed alone were granted 62.1% of
  the time. The earlier decade's lone filers may have been firms with their own patent staff; the data do not say.
  (Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043): this called the 1,149 applications "organisations", and the patent-staff reading a fact.)
- **Trade marks** replicate for both: with an attorney, Australian individuals' marks are registered 24.3 points more
  often (23.6 to 24.9; FY2000 to FY2009: 23.2, 22.3 to 24.0), organisations' 23.6 points (23.3 to 23.9; 21.3).
  **Designs** cannot be read from this table: it keeps designs with a known filer in IP RAPID, which gives no
  origin for nearly every design that lapsed or was withdrawn (B3: 2,680 and 446 filed FY2010 to FY2019), so its
  99.4% to 100% registered is that selection, not designs' registration rate (Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043); audit S2 L1 R09).
- **Not a cause.** Representation counts an agent on the record at any time, so an application dropped early may
  never appoint one (the arrow can run backwards), and those who file alone differ in resources and experience.
  Candidate third factors: applicant type and origin (the screen's applicant type × representation, 0.272; 0.277),
  whether examination is requested, the route of filing. Q4 asks whether help to file would add value; this is the
  lead.

later.what: Australian individuals' patents filed alone: -31.2 points with the route, year, state and co-filers held together, against -35.8 raw (FY2010 to FY2019); -31.7 against -36.8 in FY2000 to FY2009. Trade marks hold for individuals and organisations. Australian organisations' patents hold in FY2010 to FY2019 only.

observations.headline: Australian organisations' patents took longer to grant than overseas ones in one decade but not the other, so this is not a lead
observations.statement: Granted standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019 took a median 3.12 years from application for Australian organisations, against 2.65 for overseas organisations (a difference of 0.476 years). In FY2000 to FY2009 it was 3.41 against 3.32 (0.082). The gap does not hold in both decades.

figures.label: the gap in median time to grant, FY2010 to FY2019
the gap, FY2000 to FY2009

points: Counted from the examination request instead, the gap is 0.17 years in the later decade and -0.079 in the earlier.

**The route is the likely third factor:** an international (PCT) application's clock in Australia starts at national phase entry, about 30 months after its priority ({U6}), and overseas filers use the PCT most ({B15}).

questions.how: Checks whether Australian applicants wait longer for their rights; on this evidence, not consistently.

prep.what: Medians with bootstrap intervals that resample whole patents, from application and from the examination request.
prep.why: Medians are not pulled by the few very slow cases.

steps: Find the median years to grant for each group of filer, in each decade.
Take the difference with its interval.
Repeat from the examination request.
assumptions: Only granted patents have a time to grant; those never granted are not in the comparison.
limits: Recorded, not carried: a difference in one decade only is not a lead.
observations.next: Not carried to Stage 3.

observations.original:
**B7 (observational). Australian organisations' standard patents took longer to grant than overseas organisations' in
FY2010 to FY2019, but not in FY2000 to FY2009: not a lead.** Granted standard patents, median years from application:
Australian organisations 3.12 against 2.65 for overseas organisations (a difference of 0.476 years, interval 0.435 to
0.52; rank-biserial 0.179), but 3.41 against 3.32 in FY2000 to FY2009 (0.082, 0.044 to 0.123; 0.016). From the
examination request the difference is 0.17 years (0.153 to 0.181) in the later decade and -0.079 (-0.099 to -0.057) in
the earlier. The route is the candidate third factor: a PCT application's clock starts at national phase entry,
about 30 months after its priority (U6), and overseas filers use the PCT most (section 1.5); the screen ties time to
grant to the route (0.304; 0.237: claiming an Australian application, a median 1,617 days).

observations.headline: For patents filed in the same number of countries, Australian organisations' more often stay in force for 10 years than overseas organisations', except those filed only in Australia
observations.statement: Among standard patents with a date of patent in FY2010 to FY2016, filed in two to four offices, 71.8% of Australian organisations' were still in force after 10 years, against 65.1% of overseas organisations'; in five or more offices, 75.6% against 66.5%. For patents filed in Australia alone there is no difference (73.3% against 74.6%). Australian organisations' patents also reach fewer offices and are cited less ({B11}, {B12}), so the signals of value do not agree.

figures.label: still in force after 10 years, filed in five or more offices, Australian against overseas organisations
the same, filed in Australia alone (no difference)

points: **In the earlier cohort** (date of patent FY2005 to FY2009, where reach is less reliable, {B55}): 77.5% against 68.4% in two to four offices and 77.0% against 69.2% in five or more; in Australia alone 72.7% against 78.0%.

**So the gap is not about narrow patents paying fewer fees:** it is absent among Australia-only patents (and reversed in the earlier cohort), and largest among the widest. 22.9% of Australian organisations' patents are filed in Australia alone, against 4.5% of overseas organisations', so a pooled comparison mixes the groups.

**Pooled, after 10 years:** Australian organisations 75.1% and 73.8% (date of patent FY2005 to FY2009 and FY2000 to FY2004), overseas organisations 69.7% and 64.2%, Australian individuals 60.3% and 55.2%, overseas individuals 64.3% and 57.3%.

**Within technology fields** (31 with enough patents), Australian organisations' share in force at 10 years is below overseas organisations' in 11 fields in FY2005 to FY2009 and in 3 in FY2000 to FY2004.
**Between cohorts,** the later one is more often in force in every group. The cohorts met different renewal fees ({B49}), so this is a difference between cohorts, its cause open.

questions.how: Years in force is the working measure of private value the owner adopted. Within the same reach Australian organisations' patents more often stay in force, but they reach fewer offices and are cited less, so which signal, if any, measures value is for Stage 3 to test.
Comparing within reach and within fields separates the filer from what it files.

prep.what: [[survival-curve|Survival curves]] of granted standard patents by filer, counted from the date of patent, with Greenwood intervals for the share in force at 10 and 15 years (ADR 0041).
prep.why: A survival curve keeps patents still alive, rather than dropping them ({U36}).

prep.what: The comparison is made within groups of family reach (Australia only, two to four offices, five or more), for dates of patent FY2010 to FY2016, when Google Patents' reach is reliable for Australian filers ({B55}).
prep.why: A patent filed only in Australia pays one set of renewal fees, so reach could explain a gap in years in force; comparing within reach sets that aside.

steps: Draw each group's survival curve from the date of patent, for each cohort and reach group.
Read the share in force at 10 and 15 years, with intervals.
Repeat within each technology field with enough patents, and compare the groups field by field.
Set the result beside reach ({B11}) and citations ({B12}) for the same filers.
assumptions: Keeping a patent in force (paying renewals) is a sign the holder values it, as adopted for Stage 2.
limits: Private value, not public value.
Selection at grant differs by filer, and before FY2003 the founding applicant may be a later holder ({U35}).
The [[third-factor|third factors]] (selection at grant, the kind of applicant, firm size) are not held steady here.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 with its third factors, beside reach and citations. A sharper test is each patent's renewal when a fee changed ({B49}).
