observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**B8 (observational). Within the same family reach, Australian organisations' standard patents are more often still
in force at 10 years than overseas organisations', except those filed in Australia alone; beside B11 and B12, the
signals do not agree.** Share of granted standard patents still in force (95% interval):
- **Within reach (A22; date of patent FY2010 to FY2016, when Google Patents' reach is reliable, B55):** filed in two
  to four offices, Australian organisations 71.8% (69.3% to 74.1%) against overseas organisations 65.1% (64.5% to
  65.8%); in five or more, 75.6% (73.7% to 77.4%) against 66.5% (66.1% to 66.8%); in Australia alone, 73.3% (70.7% to
  75.8%) against 74.6% (73.2% to 76.0%), no difference. FY2005 to FY2009 (provisional, B55): 77.5% against 68.4%,
  77.0% against 69.2%, and in Australia alone 72.7% against 78.0%.
- **So the gap is not the narrow patent's single set of fees:** there is none among Australia-only patents (in the
  earlier cohort it reverses), and it is largest among the widest. The pooled comparison mixes in composition: 22.9%
  of Australian organisations' FY2010 to FY2016 patents are filed in Australia alone, against 4.5% of overseas
  organisations'.
- **Pooled, after 10 years:** Australian organisations 75.1% (73.7% to 76.5%) for date of patent FY2005 to FY2009 and
  73.8% (72.5% to 75.0%) for FY2000 to FY2004; overseas organisations 69.7% (69.3% to 70.1%) and 64.2% (63.8% to
  64.5%); Australian individuals 60.3% and 55.2%; overseas individuals 64.3% and 57.3%. After 15 years: Australian
  organisations 53.0% and 42.0%; overseas organisations 43.2% and 38.5%.
- **Within technology:** in 31 fields with enough patents in each period, Australian organisations' share in force at
  10 years is below overseas organisations' in 11 (FY2005 to FY2009; median gap 4.3 points, from -18.9 to 22.6) and in
  3 (FY2000 to FY2004; median 5.3, from -3.7 to 34.6).
- **Beside B11 and B12 (A1's condition):** the same organisations' patents reach fewer offices (B11) and are cited
  less, mostly because of that reach (B12). A longer time on the register is not, on its own, a sign of more private
  value: the three signals disagree, and which, if any, measures value is for Stage 3 to test.
- **Between cohorts:** the later cohort is more often in force at 10 years in every group (overseas organisations
  69.7% against 64.2%). The cohorts met different renewal fees (September 2002's rise, B49), and before FY2003 the
  founding applicant may be a later holder (U35); this is a difference between cohorts, its cause open.
- **Third factors:** selection at grant (which applications reach grant differs by filer and representation, section
  1.1), the kind of applicant within each group, and firm size.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, audits S2 L1 R11 to R13, R33, R36; ADR 0041):** the heading said Australian
  organisations "keep their standard patents longer", carried alone, against A1's condition; with cohorts by year of
  application and every patent counted from its date of patent the figures were 78.7% against 72.3% after 10 years;
  the within-field check covered one period ("all but 9" of 32 fields); B6 and B10 were cited for Australians' grant
  rate and for reach (reach is B11); and "every cohort lengthened its patents' lives" read a difference between
  cohorts as a change in behaviour.

later.what: Within the same reach, hazard ratios of 0.648 to 0.811 with field, route, cohort, co-filers and classes held together: Australian organisations' patents are less likely to end. Among Australia-only patents the halves disagree (0.959, then 0.730), so B8's "no difference" there is neither confirmed nor overturned.

observations.headline: Technology fields differ in how many of their patents stay in force for 10 years, but the order of fields is unstable
observations.statement: The share of standard patents still in force 10 years after their date of patent (FY2005 to FY2009) runs from 51.9% to 84.9% across 35 technology fields. The fields' order agrees with the earlier period's (FY2000 to FY2004) with a rank [[correlation]] of only 0.311.

figures.label: in force after 10 years, across 35 fields
agreement of the fields' order between two periods (weak)

points: A weak [[replication]], so field differences in years in force are not carried on their own, only as something to hold steady when comparing filers ({B8}).

questions.how: Whether the field a patent is in is a condition for how long it is valued; only weakly, on this evidence.

prep.what: The same survival curves as {B8}, by technology field (WIPO's 35 fields).
prep.why: Fields are the natural unit for comparing technologies.

steps: Read each field's share in force after 10 years, in each period.
Rank the fields in each period and compare the two orders.
assumptions: WIPO's 35 fields group patents in a way that means the same in both periods.
limits: A weak agreement means a field's position often changes between periods.
observations.next: Field is a [[third-factor]] in Stage 3, not a signal on its own.

observations.original:
**B9 (descriptive). Technology areas differ in the share of their patents still in force at 10 years, but the order
is unstable.** Date of patent FY2005 to FY2009: from 51.9% to 84.9% across the 35 fields (chart above). The fields'
order agrees between the two periods with a Spearman rho of 0.311: weak, so field differences are not carried on
their own, only as a control for B8. Restated (2 November 2026, ADR 0041): with the earlier specification the range
was 59.4% to 81.2% and the rho 0.459.

observations.headline: Overseas organisations' trade marks and designs most often stay in force past the first renewal, Australian individuals' least
observations.statement: Of trade marks filed FY2010 to FY2015, 56.2% of overseas organisations' were still in force after 10 years, 45.9% of Australian organisations' and 26.0% of Australian individuals'. Among Australian filers, marks with an attorney on the record before the renewal stayed in force 50.8% of the time, against 31.7% with no agent then: a gap of 19.1 [[percentage-point|points]].

figures.label: trade marks in force after 10 years, overseas organisations against Australian individuals
Australians' marks in force after 10 years, with an attorney against no agent before the renewal
designs in force after 5 years, overseas organisations against Australian individuals

points: The earlier period (FY2003 to FY2009) gives much the same: 56.3%, 44.6% and 27.7%; with an attorney before the renewal 49.7%, no agent 34.4%.

**Why "before the renewal" matters.** An agent recorded at any time includes one added for the renewal itself: Australian marks whose agent first appears more than 9.5 years after filing are 89.5% in force at 10 years. Counting agents at any time had made the attorney gap look larger (23.4 points, not 19.1).

Designs in force after 5 years (FY2010 to FY2019): overseas organisations 69.9%, Australian organisations 44.4%, Australian individuals 28.2%; Australians with an attorney before the renewal 46.7%, no agent 31.1%.
Intervals are within about a point for the large groups and wider for small ones, and the differences hold in both periods.
**Not a cause.** Individuals file alone most ({B5}), and whether the business behind a mark survived is not in these data.

questions.how: Staying in force past a renewal is a sign of private value for trade marks and designs, as years in force is for patents.
Australian individuals' and lone filers' rights stay in force least; why is not shown here.
Adds renewal to grant ({B6}) as an outcome that goes with representation.

prep.what: Survival curves of trade marks and designs from registration, by filer and by representation, read at the first renewal (10 years for trade marks, 5 for designs).
prep.why: Those are the first points at which a holder must pay to keep the right.

prep.what: Representation is read as it stood before the renewal, from the date an agent who is not an applicant first appears (ADR 0041).
prep.why: An agent recorded at any time includes one appointed for the renewal itself, which would make represented marks look more often renewed. IP RAPID dates most trade marks' agents from registration, so "before the renewal" means on the record by then, not necessarily at filing.

steps: Read the share in force at 10 years (trade marks) and 5 years (designs) for each group, in two periods.
Repeat for Australian filers by representation.
assumptions: Keeping a mark or design in force is a sign its holder values it.
limits: The survival of the business behind a mark is not in these data, and individuals file alone most ({B5}).
The date an agent first appears cannot be used for patents ({U40}), so this check is for trade marks and designs only.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3, with applicant type as the main [[third-factor]].

observations.original:
**B10 (observational). Trade marks and designs: overseas organisations' are most often in force after the first
renewal, Australian individuals' least; Australians with no agent before the renewal less often than those with an
attorney, by less than representation "at any time" suggested.**
- **Trade marks in force after 10 years** (earliest filing FY2010 to FY2015; FY2003 to FY2009): overseas
  organisations 56.2% (56.3%), Australian organisations 45.9% (44.6%), overseas individuals 37.9% (40.5%), Australian
  individuals 26.0% (27.7%). Among Australian filers, by an agent on the record at any time: an attorney 52.0% (52.1%),
  another agent 34.6% (30.3%), alone 28.6% (30.2%).
- **Representation before the first renewal (S2 L1 R34):** "at any time" includes an agent added for the renewal
  itself. Australian marks whose agent first appears more than 9.5 years after filing are 89.5% (99.0%) in force at 10
  years (3,143 and 4,298 at risk): renewed through the agent who joined for it. Read before the renewal: an attorney
  50.8% (49.7%), another agent 30.8% (27.9%), no agent (alone, or an agent only later) 31.7% (34.4%). The attorney gap
  is 19.1 points (15.3), not 23.4 (21.9). IP RAPID dates most trade marks' agents from registration, so "before the
  renewal" means on the record by then, not necessarily at filing.
- **Designs in force after 5 years** (FY2010 to FY2019; FY2005 to FY2009): overseas organisations 69.9% (62.1%),
  Australian organisations 44.4% (46.4%), Australian individuals 28.2% (27.0%); Australians with an attorney 47.2%
  (50.8%), alone 28.9% (28.8%). Before the renewal: an attorney 46.7% (50.7%), no agent 31.1% (29.3%); few designs'
  agents first appear after the renewal fell due (208 at risk, 88.1%).
- Intervals are within about a point for the large groups, and wider for small ones (overseas individuals' designs
  33.8% to 40.0% in FY2005 to FY2009). The differences hold in both periods. **Third factors:** applicant type
  (individuals file alone most, B5), the survival of the business behind a mark, which these data do not hold, and
  the reverse path above, removed only as far as an agent's arrival is dated.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, audits S2 L1 R12, R30, R34; ADR 0041):** the heading said "renew" and "Australians who
  file alone renew far less", with representation at any time only, and "every interval is within about 1 point".

later.what: Trade marks in force after 10 years: -14.4 points held together against -19.1 raw (FY2010 to FY2015), and -11.0 against -15.3 (FY2003 to FY2009); designs after 5 years -16.3 and -14.1, almost all of the raw gap.

observations.headline: Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries than overseas filers'; the apparent narrowing since the 2000s is mostly a gap in older records
observations.statement: Of standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019, 40.68% of Australian organisations' were filed only in Australia, against 8.23% of overseas organisations'. 22.63% reached five or more offices, against 69.58%; 32.82% were granted in the United States, against 67.13%.

figures.label: Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia (FY2010 to FY2019)
overseas organisations'
granted in the United States

points: Australian individuals: 60.12% only in Australia.

In FY2000 to FY2009 the records show Australian organisations 73.0% only in Australia, 13.09% in five or more offices and 15.81% granted in the US. That apparent change is mostly a gap in the older records: Australian organisations' patents that came through the PCT, which must have an international filing, appear in Australia alone 63.22% of the time in those years ({B55}). So the earlier figures for Australian filers are provisional, not a replication.

questions.how: How far a patent family reaches is a common sign of the value its owner expects. Australian organisations' patents reach fewer offices, whether because their owners expect less from them or for reasons of cost and market; these data do not say which.
Reach is the main condition behind citation differences ({B12}).

prep.what: Each standard patent's [[patent-family]] from Google Patents: the offices it was filed in, and whether it was granted in the United States ({U92}).
prep.why: A family shows where else the same invention was protected.

Compare the two decades.
assumptions: Google Patents holds each family's filings abroad completely; this fails for older Australian families ({B55}).
limits: Reach is chosen and paid for by owners, so it measures expected private value.
For Australian applicants, read from FY2010 only.

observations.original:
**B11 (observational). Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries than overseas filers'; the apparent
narrowing since FY2000 to FY2009 is mostly a gap in the older records (B55).** Standard patents, FY2010 to FY2019 (FY2000 to FY2009):
- **Filed only in Australia:** Australian organisations 40.68% (73.0%), Australian individuals 60.12% (87.37%),
  overseas organisations 8.23% (7.34%), each within about a point.
- **Five or more offices:** Australian organisations 22.63% (13.09%), overseas organisations 69.58% (72.35%).
- **Granted in the United States:** Australian organisations 32.82% (15.81%), overseas organisations 67.13% (61.93%).
- The gap holds in both decades, but Australian organisations' share filed only here fell from 73.0% to 40.68%. First left as a
  lead (practice, or how fully Google Patents holds older families); B55 has since shown it is mostly the older
  records: Australian organisations' PCT-route patents appear in Australia alone 63.22% of the time in FY2000 to
  FY2009. So the FY2010 to FY2019 figures stand, and the FY2000 to FY2009 ones for Australian applicants are
  provisional, not a replication.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, audit S2 L1 R29):** the heading said the gap had narrowed.

later.what: Five or more offices holds (-31.9 points held together, against -47.5 raw); filed only in Australia weakens (+9.3 against +32.7, 28.4% left). Fewer offices remains at the same field, route and year.

observations.headline: Australians' patents are cited less within their field and year, and most of the gap goes with how far they reach
observations.statement: On a scale where 50 is a typical patent of the same field and year, overseas organisations' patents score 52.3 for citations within five years, Australian organisations' 32.3 and Australian individuals' 24.0 (FY2010 to FY2019). Among patents filed in the same number of offices, the gap shrinks or reverses.

figures.label: citation percentile, overseas against Australian organisations
among patents filed in one office, Australian organisations ahead
among patents filed in five or more offices

points: In FY2000 to FY2009: 53.6, 25.0 and 20.2; among one-office patents 16.0 against 12.5; five or more offices 57.6 against 58.2. These earlier figures for Australian filers rest partly on incomplete family records ({B55}).
Among patents filed in 2 to 4 offices: 39.9 against 50.7 (42.0 against 52.1).

**So reach is the main [[third-factor]]:** a narrow family is seldom cited wherever it comes from. Citations and reach are therefore not independent evidence of value: a wider family has more documents to cite, and owners choose and pay for reach.

questions.how: Citations are a sign that an invention is built on by others, one route to public value; for Australians it mostly follows reach.
Reach looks like a condition for being cited.

prep.what: Each patent's citing families within five years ({U94}), turned into a [[percentile]] among patents of the same technology field and filing year.
prep.why: Fields and years are cited at very different rates, so a raw count would compare unlike with unlike.

steps: Rank every patent's five-year citations among others of its field and year.
Average the ranks for each group of filer.
Repeat within bands of family reach.
assumptions: Citations within five years are comparable across fields once ranked within them.
limits: Older Australian families' reach is incomplete in the records ({B55}), so the earlier decade is less reliable.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 with reach as the third factor.

observations.original:
**B12 (observational). Australians' patents are cited less within their field and year, and most of the gap goes
with family reach.** Mean percentile of citations within five years, within field and year (50 = typical):
- **All reach:** overseas organisations 52.3 (FY2010 to FY2019) and 53.6 (FY2000 to FY2009); Australian organisations
  32.3 and 25.0; Australian individuals 24.0 and 20.2.
- **Within the same reach** the gap shrinks or reverses: among patents filed in one office, Australian organisations
  15.2 against overseas organisations' 11.6 (16.0 against 12.5); in five or more offices, 50.6 against 57.7 (57.6
  against 58.2). Among those filed in 2 to 4 offices, 39.9 against 50.7 (42.0 against 52.1).
- So reach is the main third factor: a narrow family is seldom cited wherever it comes from. Citations and reach
  are therefore not independent evidence of value: a wider family has more documents to cite, and owners choose and
  pay for reach.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** the earlier decade's overseas single-office figure was given as 12.6 (the table's 12.5), and
  citations and reach were called "two readings of the same expected value".
- The FY2000 to FY2009 figures for Australian applicants, overall and within reach, rest partly on incomplete family
  records (B55), so they are provisional; the FY2010 to FY2019 ones stand.

later.what: Citations within five years of priority: rate ratio 0.312 raw, 0.729 with every factor held (0.700 in the second half). Reach accounts for about three fifths of the gap, but about 27% to 30% fewer citations remain.

observations.headline: Expedited patents are slightly more often still in force at 10 years, but the link differs by filer, and "expedited" mixes kinds of request
observations.statement: Pooled, 72.6% of expedited standard patents with a date of patent in FY2003 to FY2009 were still in force after 10 years, against 68.9% of others; for FY2010 to FY2016, 67.6% against 66.6%, a difference within overlapping intervals. The link is not explained by who asks for [[expedited|expedited]] examination, but it differs by filer: higher for overseas organisations, lower for Australian individuals in both periods.

figures.label: expedited against other patents in force after 10 years (FY2003 to FY2009)
the same, FY2010 to FY2016 (intervals overlap)
overseas organisations, expedited against not (FY2003 to FY2009)

points: **By filer:** overseas organisations 79.7% against 68.7%, then 67.9% against 66.4%; Australian organisations 71.6% against 76.1%, then 73.7% against 74.1%; Australian individuals 55.1% against 65.0%, then 59.7% against 68.5% (expedited lower in both periods).

**Not who asks:** weighting each filer group's own gap by the expedited patents' mix of filers gives 5.88 and 0.68 points, against 3.79 and 1.03 pooled, so the mix of filers does not account for the pooled gap.

**Who asks, and for what.** 0.84% of overseas organisations' examined patents were expedited in FY2003 to FY2009 and 8.0% from FY2010; Australian individuals' 19.71% and 19.95%. From 2014, overseas organisations' patents with a Japanese priority were expedited more often (1.53% in 2013 to 7.98%), as were those with a US priority (3.07% to 6.77%). That coincides with the Global Patent Prosecution Highway (6 January 2014), under which an applicant whose claims another office has allowed asks for faster examination, and IP RAPID records the request as expedited examination. So "expedited" mixes urgency with work-sharing that follows examination abroad.
**Expedited applications are granted more often** in every group of standard patents: Australian organisations 69.72% against 57.04%, overseas organisations 82.53% against 76.18% (FY2010 on).
IP Australia's commissioned study found expedited patents kept longer (ADR 0024); here the pooled link is small, holds in both periods and differs by filer.

questions.how: Expedited examination is a service IP Australia offers; whether it goes with longer-lived rights is a question about its value, and the answer depends on who asks and why.
Tests a value signal (years in force) against a choice the filer makes.

prep.what: Survival curves of granted standard patents, expedited or not, pooled and by filer, counted from the date of patent, for two cohorts (ADR 0041).
prep.why: Counting from the start of the term would give later-granted patents years in which they could not end, and flatter the expedited, which are granted sooner.

prep.what: A check for a composition effect ([[simpsons-paradox|Simpson's paradox]]) that weights each filer group's own gap by the expedited patents' mix of filers, and by the others' mix.
prep.why: If the expedited were simply a different mix of filers, the weighted gaps would vanish.

steps: Compare expedited and other patents pooled, in each period.
Repeat within each group of filer, and weight the groups' gaps by each mix.
Measure how the share of patents expedited changed, by filer and by the office of first filing, year by year.
assumptions: The expedite request is recorded as made ({U34} found trade mark records changed; patents' did not).
limits: The urgency behind a request (a product on the market, a dispute) is not recorded, and could explain both a request and a longer life.
Requests that follow examination abroad would be expected to go with grant and a longer life, so the pooled link mixes two kinds of request.
observations.next: Read in Stage 3 by filer and by kind of request, not as one pooled signal.

observations.original:
**B13 (observational). Expedited standard patents are slightly more often in force at 10 years, pooled, in both
periods; the link is not a composition effect, it differs by filer, and "expedited" mixes kinds of request.**
- **Pooled:** expedited 72.6% (71.3% to 74.0%) against not 68.9% (68.5% to 69.2%) for date of patent FY2003 to
  FY2009, and 67.6% (66.6% to 68.6%) against 66.6% (66.3% to 66.9%) for FY2010 to FY2016: higher in both, by 3.7 and
  1.0 points, the second within overlapping intervals.
- **Not composition:** with each filer group's own gap weighted by the expedited patents' mix of filers the gap would
  be 5.88 and 0.68 points (8.61 and 1.16 at the other group's mix), against 3.79 and 1.03 pooled. Overseas
  organisations are 71.71% and 80.09% of the expedited, 87.66% and 90.23% of the rest; the mix does not explain the
  pooled gap.
- **By filer:** overseas organisations 79.7% against 68.7% (FY2003 to FY2009) and 67.9% against 66.4% (FY2010 to
  FY2016, intervals overlapping); Australian organisations 71.6% against 76.1%, then 73.7% against 74.1%; Australian
  individuals 55.1% against 65.0%, then 59.7% against 68.5% (expedited lower in both).
- **Who asks, and for what (S2 L1 R35):** 0.84% of overseas organisations' examined patents were expedited in FY2003
  to FY2009 and 8.0% from FY2010; Australian individuals 19.71% and 19.95%. By year of request, the share rose in 2011
  and 2012 for every kind of filer (Australian organisations 24.85% and 41.26%; overseas organisations with neither a
  US nor a Japanese priority 23.98% and 32.64%), then fell back. From 2014 overseas organisations' patents with a
  Japanese priority rose from 1.53% (2013) to 7.98%, and with a US priority from 3.07% to 6.77%, and stayed there. The
  2014 rise coincides with the Global Patent Prosecution Highway (6 January 2014), under which an applicant whose
  claims another office has allowed asks for accelerated examination; IP RAPID records such a request as expedited
  examination. So "expedited" mixes urgency with work-sharing, which follows examination abroad and would be expected
  to go with grant and a longer life. The 2011 and 2012 rise came before Raising the Bar (15 April 2013); its cause is
  not shown.
- **Expedited applications are granted more often** in every group of standard patents (not for overseas filers'
  trade marks, in the same table; scoped 2 November 2026, pass 8): for example Australian organisations 69.72%
  against 57.04%, overseas organisations 82.53% against 76.18% (FY2010 on, by year of application).
- IP Australia's commissioned study found expedited patents kept longer (ADR 0024); here the pooled link is small,
  holds in both periods and differs by filer. Third factors: the filer, the kind of request, and the urgency behind a
  request (a product on the market, a dispute), which the data do not record.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, audits S2 L1 R12, R14, R35; ADR 0041):** with cohorts by year of application and every
  patent counted from its date of patent, the earlier text had 76.8% against 68.7% (FY2010 to FY2016) and 68.7%
  against 71.3% (FY2003 to FY2009), called the pooled link "a composition effect" and "Simpson's paradox" with no
  decomposition, and named urgency as the third factor. That specification is the first table above: its five-year
  figures (expedited 99.3%, not expedited 100%) are the immortal time that a later grant gives.

later.what: Pooled, not detected once held in FY2010 to FY2016 (1.021) and reversed in FY2003 to FY2009 (1.124): the earlier period's raw advantage goes once the field, route and cohort are held with the filer. Australian individuals' expedited patents are more likely to end, in both periods (1.264 and 1.249).

On IP Australia's commissioned study's wider measure, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents), the link with a longer life is not found either: those patents are more likely to end, held together (1.276 and 1.383).

observations.headline: Expedited trade marks are a few points more often in force after 10 years for Australians, and slightly less for overseas organisations, so this is not a lead
observations.statement: Among trade marks with no priority claim recorded, filed FY2010 to FY2015, 49.8% of Australian organisations' expedited marks were still in force after 10 years, against 45.5% of the rest; Australian individuals 28.7% against 25.8%; overseas organisations 59.0% against 60.2%. For Australians the differences are 1.1 to 4.3 points, small beside the gaps between filers in {B10} (15 to 30 points).

figures.label: the difference for Australians, expedited against not
overseas organisations, expedited against not

points: FY2003 to FY2009: Australian organisations 45.6% against 44.5%, Australian individuals 30.1% against 27.5%, overseas organisations 57.5% against 60.6%.
Marks with a priority claim are left out because their expedite event was recorded differently over time ({U34}).

questions.how: Expedited trade mark examination does not, on this evidence, go with marks being kept longer.

prep.what: Trade marks with no priority claim recorded only.
prep.why: Priority-claiming marks carried the expedite event almost always until FY2018 ({U103}).

steps: Read the share in force after 10 years for expedited and other marks, by filer, in two periods.
assumptions: Without a priority claim, the expedite event is recorded consistently.
limits: Not a lead; recorded so that it is not tested again by accident.

**B14 (descriptive). Trade marks: expedited marks are a few points more often in force after 10 years for Australians,
and less for overseas organisations: not a lead.** Marks with no priority claim recorded, in force after 10 years
(earliest filing FY2010 to FY2015; FY2003 to FY2009), expedited against not: Australian organisations 49.8% against
45.5% (45.6% against 44.5%), Australian individuals 28.7% against 25.8% (30.1% against 27.5%), overseas organisations

this stage looks for"); the figures moved with the cohorts (by earliest filing).

observations.statement: Overseas organisations' standard patents (FY2010 to FY2019) came mostly through the PCT (74.7%). Australian organisations' came through the PCT 45.4% of the time and by claiming an earlier Australian application 21.0%; Australian individuals' by claiming an Australian application 31.2%, the PCT 28.9% and directly 27.9%.

**B15 (descriptive). Each kind of filer has its own route into Australia, and divisionals doubled.** Standard patents,
FY2010 to FY2019 (FY2000 to FY2009):
- **Overseas organisations:** the PCT 74.7% (78.2%), a priority abroad 8.9% (13.4%), divisionals 15.6% (7.1%).

observations.original:
**B17 (observational). Women among inventors in Australia: the field matters more than the filer, and the order of
fields holds.** Standard patents, inventors in Australia (44,251 inventor places on 22,335 patents, 93.38% with an
estimate):
- **By field,** FY2010 to FY2019 (FY2000 to FY2009): from 4.2% in civil engineering (4.3%) and 5.2% in transport
  (4.1%) to 24.4% in pharmaceuticals (20.4%) and 26.9% in biotechnology (27.2%). The order of the 12 fields with
  enough inventors agrees between the decades with a Spearman rho of 0.86.
- **By filer** (origin and type from one party, ADR 0037): Australian organisations 12.18% (11.79% to 12.6%) and
  15.9% (15.09% to 16.72%); Australian individuals 11.13% (9.8% to 12.4%) and 11.22% (9.5% to 12.8%); overseas
  organisations 10.57% and 9.83%.
  Organisations' and individuals' intervals overlap in FY2010 to FY2019, so the filer gap does not replicate for
  standard patents.
- Expected counts from names, read for inventors in Australia only (U97). Third factor: the field, which the
  filer groups may weight differently (not shown here; Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043): this said which fields each files more, which
  no output above shows).

later.what: The filer gap is not detected with the filer clustered (+1.05 points, FY2010 to FY2019), and with the field held it turns negative (-2.82): B17's reading that the field matters more than the filer is confirmed.

These estimates use the applicant's country, not the inventor's, so they are not set beside {B17}'s.

**B18 (observational). Provisional applications: Australian organisations' inventors include more women than
Australian individuals', in both decades, and the states' order holds.** (Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043): the heading said
"organisations'" and "individuals'"; overseas filers go the other way, individuals 16.6% and organisations 6.66% in
FY2013 to FY2022.)
- **By filer,** FY2013 to FY2022 (FY2003 to FY2012): Australian organisations 21.19% (20.89% to 21.49%) and 25.51%;
  Australian individuals 16.12% (15.68% to 16.51%) and 18.9% (18.49% to 19.23%). Overseas
  organisations 6.66% and 6.05%.
- **By state:** the ACT highest in the later decade (25.59%; 27.03% before), Western Australia and New South Wales
  lowest (17.83% and 17.92%; 18.49% and 19.56%); South Australia fell from 32.23% to 21.92%. The seven states with 500
  or more estimated inventors keep their order with a Spearman rho of 0.821.

  Australian organisations' only 70.15% (FY2024), 63.91% (FY2025) and 71.03% (FY2026), against 93.48% to 95.86% for

observations.headline: Australian-filed patents now held only overseas are more common among the wider and the granted ones, and among organisations'
observations.statement: Of standard patents with an Australian founding applicant filed FY2003 to FY2011, 14.52% of those whose family reaches five or more offices now have only overseas holders, against 3.75% of those filed in one office; 9.96% of granted patents against 1.15% of those never granted; and 6.91% of organisations' against 1.57% of individuals'. These compare two moments, filing and today; the path in between is not seen.

figures.label: now held only overseas, five or more offices against one
granted against never granted
agreement of the fields' order between periods

points: **Later filings** (FY2012 to FY2021), which have had less time to change hands: 6.25% and 1.16% by reach, 4.81% and 0.87% granted or not, organisations 2.84% and individuals 1.81%.

**A higher rate is not most of the patents:** of those now held only overseas, 44.22% are single-office patents in the earlier period (34.54% in five or more offices), and 18.9% in the later one (47.47% in five or more).
**By field:** highest in materials and metallurgy (9.33% in the later period), organic fine chemistry (8.21%) and biotechnology (7.96%); lowest in handling (0.83%).

**What this does not show.** Reach and grant are seen today, not necessarily before the holder changed (a new holder can extend a family or see a patent through to grant), and neither measures what an owner valued. Before FY2010 Australian filers' family records are incomplete ({B55}), so the earlier period's reach bands are provisional.

questions.how: Whether value created in Australia is realised abroad is a Q1 question. This shows which Australian-filed patents now have only overseas holders, not where value goes.
Shows which kinds of Australian-filed patents more often end up held only overseas.

prep.what: Two endpoints for each patent, from the holder history ({U18}, ADR 0040) - an Australian founding applicant at filing, and only overseas holders now (at least one with a known country).
prep.why: The register records who filed and who holds now, not each transfer in between.

prep.what: The filer's type is that of the first founding applicant in Australia (ADR 0037).
prep.why: It is the party whose origin makes the patent Australian-filed.

steps: Take standard patents with an Australian founding applicant, in two periods of filing.
Find the share now held only by overseas holders, by reach, grant, filer and field.
Compare the order of fields between the periods.
assumptions: The holder history is recorded from FY2003 ({U17}); a change of holder can be a sale, a merger or a change of name.
limits: Reach and grant are tied to each other and to the field; Stage 3 separates them.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3, with the filing firm's age ({B26}).
observations.section: 1.7 Australian-founded rights now held only overseas, by technology, applicant type and reach
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**B19 (observational). Australian-founded patents now held only overseas are more common among the wider and the
granted ones and among organisations', and the order of fields holds.** Standard patents with an Australian founding
applicant whose current holders are all overseas, FY2003 to FY2011 (FY2012 to FY2021, which have had less time to
change hands). Two endpoints, not a transfer history:
- **By reach:** five or more offices 14.52% (6.25%), two to four 5.5% (2.56%), one office 3.75% (1.16%). The earlier
  period is mostly before FY2010, when Australian filers' family records are incomplete (B55), so some of its
  "one office" patents are wider; its reach bands are provisional, the later period's stand.
- **A higher rate is not most of the patents:** of those now held only overseas, 44.22% are single-office patents in
  the earlier period (34.54% in five or more offices) and 18.9% in the later one (47.47% in five or more). Reach is
  unknown for 1,626 and 966 patents (21 and 2 of them held overseas), shown apart.
- **Granted or not:** granted 9.96% (4.81%), never granted 1.15% (0.87%).
- **By filer** (the type of the first founding applicant in Australia, ADR 0037): organisations 6.91% (2.84%),
  individuals 1.57% (1.81%); the organisations' gap holds, smaller, in the later period.
- **By field:** highest in materials and metallurgy (9.33% in the later period; 9.51% earlier), organic fine chemistry
  (8.21%; 6.51%) and biotechnology (7.96%; 5.07%); lowest in handling (0.83%; 2.38%), thermal processes (1.02%; 3.71%)
  and furniture and games (1.05%; 1.3%). The 27 fields' order agrees with a Spearman rho of 0.805.
- **So** the overseas-held rate is higher among wide and granted patents. Reach and grant are seen today, not
  necessarily before the holder changed (a new holder can extend a family or see a patent through to grant), and
  neither measures what an owner valued. Whether value created in Australia is realised abroad is a question for Q1,
  not something this shows. Third factors: reach and grant are tied to each other and to the field; the filing
  firm's age is in section 2.5.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, audit S2 L1 R25, R26):** first headed "Patents that move overseas are the wider and
  the granted ones", read as "the rights that leave are the ones their owners valued most".

later.what: Granted patents hold (+5.6 and +2.8 points held together); wide patents weaken (40.1% and 43.7% of the raw gap left); organisations weaken, then are not detected in FY2012 to FY2021.

observations.headline: Most of the fall in Australian organisations' "Australia only" patents is a gap in older records, not a change in practice
observations.statement: Of Australian organisations' standard patents that entered through the PCT, Google Patents shows 63.22% in Australia alone for FY2000 to FY2009 and 11.42% for FY2010 to FY2019, a fall of 51.8 points. An international application seen in Australia alone two times in three is not a believable practice, and WIPO's share of Australian families filed in more than one office stayed flat (64.6% in 2006, 63.65% in 2022).

figures.label: PCT patents shown in Australia alone, FY2000 to FY2009 against FY2010 to FY2019
WIPO's share of Australian families filed in more than one office, 2006 and 2022
the same share through Google Patents

points: Patents filed directly: 83.14% and 65.65%, a fall of 17.5 points, part of which may be real practice.
WIPO's and Google Patents' year-on-year changes barely move together (-0.354 over 1991 to 2005, 0.24 over 2006 to 2022).

**So** {B11}'s fall from 73.0% to 40.68%, and the earlier decade's results on reach and citations for Australian applicants (including {B19}'s reach bands), rest partly on incomplete records; the FY2010 to FY2019 results stand. {B8}'s years in force come from IP RAPID and are not affected.
**Limits of this check:** the two decades' samples differ in route and in Google Patents' coverage, so this explains the gap rather than measuring the true older shares.

questions.how: Protects the value measures (reach, citations) from a records gap that would make Australians look more inward than they were.

prep.what: WIPO's patent families by origin ({U115}) set beside Google Patents' families of the same applicants.
prep.why: WIPO counts families at every office, independently of Google's links.

steps: For Australian organisations' PCT patents, compare the share shown in Australia alone between decades.
Compare WIPO's and Google Patents' shares of Australian families filed abroad over time.
assumptions: A PCT application, made to seek protection abroad, is rarely kept only in Australia.
limits: Whether the gap is Google Patents' or the corpus's match of older numbers is not settled (OQ21).
observations.next: Family measures for Australian applicants are read from FY2010 only, unless the owner has the older links repaired (OQ21).

observations.original:
**B55 (observational). Most of B11's fall in Australian organisations' "Australia only" patents is a gap in older
records, not a change in practice.**
- Australian organisations' standard patents that Google Patents shows in Australia alone: of those that entered
  through the PCT, 63.22% (FY2000 to FY2009) and 11.42% (FY2010 to FY2019), a fall of 51.8 points (95% interval 50.5
  to 53.0); of those filed directly, 83.14% and 65.65%, a fall of 17.5 points (16.2 to 18.7). (The filer's origin and
  type, ADR 0037.) An international
  application seen in Australia alone two times in three is not a believable practice.
- WIPO's share of Australian-origin families filed in more than one office was 64.6% in 2006 and 63.65% in 2022;
  through Google Patents it rose from 33.92% to 57.45%. Their year-on-year changes barely move together (rho -0.354

  applicants (B11, B12, and B19's reach bands), rest partly on incomplete records; B8's years in force come from IP
  RAPID and are not affected, though reach is one of its candidate third factors; the FY2010 to FY2019 results stand. Part of the
  fall among direct filings may be practice.

  shares.

  (U115; flagged for the owner).

observations.headline: Most firm leads describe who is in the lens or how the registers work; a few are substantive
observations.statement: Several leads reflect how the lens was built: a government supplier has fewer trade marks (a median 0 against 1), because a firm without a contract is in the lens only if it has IP or another link. The substantive ones: larger firms claim more R&D and report more income, public companies claim far more R&D than private ones, and firms that hold patents also hold designs.

figures.label: median R&D claimed, public against proprietary companies
how much more often than chance patent holders also hold designs
R&D spend with total income, among large taxpayers who claim R&D

points: **How the lens was built:** entity type goes with rights held (0.365; 0.366) and with whether an older firm's age may be cut short (0.452; 0.451; local government 14.8 times chance), which is how ABNs began in 1999 and 2000.
R&D spend rises with contract value (0.176; 0.184), and government suppliers cluster in the ACT (a median of 1 contract against 0 in NSW).
The R&D and income pair is 0.346 in the second half: it holds, smaller, among the few firms that are both large taxpayers and R&D claimants.

questions.how: Separates who is in the lens from what goes with filing, so later firm findings are not artefacts of how firms were found.
Firm size and form appear as conditions tied to R&D and IP together.

observations.original:
**B21 (observational). Most firm leads describe who is in the lens, or the registers' mechanics; a few are
substantive.**
Strengths below are the first half, then the second (for example "0.365; 0.366").
- **How the lens was built:** a government supplier has fewer trade marks (a median 0 against 1; 0.316 in both halves),
  because a firm without a contract is in the lens only if it has IP or another link; entity type goes with rights
  held (0.365; 0.366) and with whether an older business's age is truncated (0.452; 0.451: local government 14.8 times
  chance), which is how ABNs began in 1999 and 2000. (0.441, 0.438 and 15.9 times before 2 November 2026, when undated
  firms were counted as not truncated; their flag is now empty, ADR 0039.)
- **Substantive, and followed up below:** larger firms both claim more R&D and report more income (average R&D spend ×
  total income, rho 0.485, interval 0.406 to 0.552, among the few firms that are both large taxpayers and claimants; 0.346
  in the second half); public
  companies claim far more R&D than proprietary ones (a median $1.381m against $0.297m; 0.225; 0.232); firms that hold
  patents also hold designs (5.5 times chance; 0.247; 0.248); R&D spend rises with contract value (0.176; 0.184); and

observations.headline: Among firms that came in another way, filing IP goes with being a company and older; for government suppliers, also with a city address and an advantaged postcode
observations.statement: Of active R&D Tax Incentive claimants, 51.41% have filed IP; of government suppliers, 25.02%; of large taxpayers, 40.45%. Among suppliers, public companies have filed in 65.1% of cases and sole traders in 1.2%; firms in major cities 27.8% against 8.4% in very remote areas.

figures.label: R&D claimants that have filed IP
government suppliers that have filed, public companies against sole traders
suppliers that have filed, most disadvantaged to most advantaged tenth of postcodes

points: Trade marks dominate: 45.26%, 23.75% and 39.35% have filed one; standard patents 12.26%, 3.12% and 7.54%.

**Age:** claimants under 3 years old 26.9%, 20 years or more 67.4%. Age is partly time: an older firm has had longer to file, and age is on the record at 22 October 2026, not when the firm claimed or contracted.

**Advantage:** for suppliers the share rises with the postcode's advantage, with a dip in the third and fourth tenths (a rank correlation of 0.806 over the tenths; 0.782 in the second half). For R&D claimants no gradient was detected (48.47% to 50.92% across the tenths).
**City and country, R&D claimants:** major cities 51.9%, inner regional 49.8%, outer regional 39.3%; the gap is in outer regional areas only.
Each figure held in the second half (for example 51.89%, 25.09% and 41.2% overall).

Small, young and regional firms that do business with government but have no filing linked are a group IP Australia could reach; whether they need IP is not shown.

prep.what: Active ABNs that entered the lens through an R&D claim, a government contract or a large taxpayer's report, with whether each has filed IP as a founding applicant.
prep.why: These firms are known to exist and be active, whether or not they have filed.

steps: For each way in, find the share of firms that have filed any IP, and each kind.
Split by entity group, age, remoteness and the advantage of the postcode.
Check every figure in the second half.
assumptions: A firm's registered postcode stands for where it is ({U47}).

observations.section: 2.1 Who files IP, among firms that came in through another door
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**B22 (observational). Among firms that came in through another door, filing IP goes with being a company and
older; for government suppliers, also with a city address and an advantaged postcode.** Active ABNs, first half (second half in brackets):
- **Overall:** 51.41% of R&D Tax Incentive claimants have filed IP (51.89%), 25.02% of government suppliers (25.09%),
  and 40.45% of the large taxpayers (41.2%). Trade marks dominate: 45.26%, 23.75% and 39.35% have filed one; standard
  patents 12.26%, 3.12% and 7.54%.
- **Entity group (government suppliers):** public companies 65.1% (63.7%), private companies 31.4% (31.2%), trusts
  7.2% (8.0%), partnerships 6.5% (6.1%), sole traders 1.2% (1.3%). Claimants: public companies 63.8% (64.7%), private
  50.7% (51.1%).
- **Age:** claimants under 3 years old 26.9% (30.3%), 20 years or more 67.4% (66.6%); suppliers 3.2% (2.9%) and
  35.7% (35.6%). Age is partly time: an older firm has had longer to file. Age is on the record at 22 October 2026,
  not when the firm claimed or contracted, so a firm "under 3 years" now was younger still when it claimed in
  2021-22 to 2023-24. The undated firms (32,348 with cancelled ABNs, 252 not in the ABR extract) are outside these active-ABN tables.
- **Remoteness (suppliers):** major cities 27.8% (28.0%), inner regional 17.1% (16.4%), very remote 8.4% (8.3%).
  For R&D claimants the city gap is small beside outer regional areas only: major cities 51.9% (52.1%), inner regional
  49.8% (51.4%), outer regional 39.3% (46.7%).
- **Advantage of postcode:** for suppliers the share rises, with a dip at deciles 3 and 4, from 20.2% in the most disadvantaged tenth of
  postcodes to 27.14% in the most advantaged (Spearman rho over the deciles 0.806; 0.782 in the second half). For R&D
  claimants there is no gradient (rho 0.236 in the first half and -0.055 in the second; 48.47% to 50.92% in the first, 55.38% to 52.74% in the
  second): once a firm does
  R&D, where it is registered does not go with filing.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** the heading put "in a city" for both doors (claimants differ little except in outer regional
  areas), and the suppliers' gradient was "steady".
- **Third factors:** firm size (companies, older firms and city firms are larger), industry (not in the ABR), and
  where a business is registered rather than where it works (U47).

later.what: Among claimants, age holds (+23.1 and +22.4 points for any filing) and public form holds for a standard patent (+8.0 and +9.4); a city address does not replicate (+5.6, then +0.5).
Among suppliers, form, age and a city address hold with the others held (+31.2, +14.6 and +12.3 points); the advantaged postcode is not detected once held (+4.6 raw, -0.0 held).

observations.headline: More R&D spend goes with patenting, but only weakly; about half of R&D claimants have no IP filing linked to their business number, at any level of spend
observations.statement: Among 17,514 active R&D claimants, 9.5% of the lowest-spending tenth have filed a standard patent, rising to 24.1% of the highest-spending tenth. The rank [[correlation]] between spend and patent applications is only 0.120. 52% of the lowest spenders and 43.1% of the highest have no IP filing linked to their business number.

figures.label: claimants that have filed a standard patent, lowest to highest tenth of R&D spend
spend with patent applications (small)
claimants with no filing linked, 95.7% of them private companies

points: The lowest tenth spends a median $44,790 a year; the highest $3.79m.

**No filing linked** is most common among claimants under 3 years old on the record (72.9%) and least among those 20 years or more (32.6%); more common in private companies (49.2%) than public ones (36.2%), and in outer regional areas (60.3%) than major cities (48%). It does not rise or fall in step with the postcode's advantage.
**Who they are, together:** 55.3% of the 8,444 are private companies 3 to 10 years old on the record; only 2.4% are under 3.

**Another link to IP explains little of it:** of the claimants with no filing linked, 10.9% of those 20 years or more, and 4.1% of those under 3, are linked to IP another way (holding a right, another IP record, or an older IP Australia dataset).

**Not proven non-filers.** A firm can file without its business number being recorded, or through a related company. The second half of the claimants agrees: 9.8% and 24.3%; spend with patents 0.128; no filing linked 52.3% and 43%.

questions.how: Claimants with no filing linked, mostly private companies of 3 to 10 years, are a group for Q4 to examine. Whether they have output worth protecting, or file through another entity, is not measured here.
R&D is only loosely tied to patenting, so R&D alone is a weak condition for IP.

prep.what: Claimants ranked into tenths by recorded R&D spend, in one random half of the firms and checked in the other.

prep.what: "No filing linked" means no application is linked to the claimant's ABN by IP RAPID's filer's ABN or IP Australia's register (ADR 0036); "no link to IP" also means no right held, no other IP record and no IPLORD link.
prep.why: A count of linked filings can only show what the records link, so neither is called "never filed".

steps: For each tenth of spend, find the share that has filed a standard patent and the share with no filing linked.
Find the share with no filing linked by age, entity group, remoteness and advantage, and who they are together.
Check how many of them are linked to IP another way.
assumptions: A claimant's own ABN is the one its filings would carry.

observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**B23 (observational). More R&D spend goes with patenting, but only weakly; about half of claimants have no filing
linked to their ABN at any spend.** 17,514 active claimants with a recorded spend; first half, with the second half in brackets or after a
semicolon:
- **Standard patents:** 9.5% of the lowest-spending tenth of claimants (median $44,790 a year) have filed one, rising
  to 24.1% of the highest-spending tenth (median $3.79m); 9.8% and 24.3% in the second half. Spearman's rho between
  spend and patent applications is 0.120 (0.128): small.
- **No filing linked** (`ip_record` not filed, ADR 0036): 52% of the lowest-spending tenth and 43.1% of the highest
  (52.3% and 43%). With no link to IP of any kind: 49.6% and 39.3% (49.2% and 38.8%).
- **By group,** no filing linked is most common among claimants under 3 years old on the record (72.9%; 69.3%) and
  least among those 20 years or more (32.6%; 33.4%), more common among private companies (49.2%; 48.7%) than public
  ones (36.2%; 35.3%), and more common in outer regional areas (60.3%; 53.3%) than in major cities (48%; 47.7%). It
  does not vary in order with the advantage of the postcode (43.3% to 51.5% across the deciles).
- **Another link to IP explains little of it.** Of the claimants with no filing linked, those linked to IP another
  way (holding a right, on another IP record, or through IPLORD) are 10.9% (13.4%) of those 20 years or more, 6.1%
  (5.5%) of those 3 to 10 years old and 4.1% (3.8%) of those under 3; numerators and denominators are in the table.
- **Who they are, jointly:** of the 8,444 claimants with no filing linked, 95.7% are private companies, and 55.3% are
  private companies 3 to 10 years old on the record (2.4% are under 3 years old).
- **So** the claimants who do R&D with no filing linked to their ABN are mostly private companies of 3 to 10 years:
  a group for Q4 to examine, not a proven set of non-filers. Whether they have output worth protecting, or file
  through another entity, is not measured here; industry, which the ABR does not give, is the main missing third
  factor.
- **Restated (1 November 2026, ADR 0036):** this observation first counted only IP RAPID's own panel (`ip_filed_total`
  = 0) and called the group "missing filers" who had "never filed IP" (54% of the lowest-spending tenth; 74.4% of
  claimants under 3). It also gave IPLORD's links as a share of all claimants in a group, not of those with no filing
  linked (54.3% of the oldest), and called the young claimants' count "close to exact"; neither held.

later.what: Spending above the median goes with a standard patent at the same form, age and place (+4.3 and +4.7 points held together), weakly, as B23 read it; with any filing it weakens (+2.4 and +2.8).

observations.headline: Government suppliers that have filed IP have more contracts and more contract value, within each kind of entity shown except trusts
observations.statement: Suppliers that have filed IP have a median 3 contracts against 2, and a median total contract value per supplier of $273,400 against $113,800 (a difference of $159,700). median contracts

observations.original:
**B24 (observational). Government suppliers that have filed IP have more contracts and more contract value, within
each kind of entity shown but trusts; large taxpayers with IP do not report clearly more income.**
The rank-biserial correlation is the size of each gap (0 none, 1 complete; 0.1 small), in each half of the lens.
- **Suppliers:** a median 3 contracts against 2, in both halves. Each supplier's total contract value: a median of
  $273,400 with IP against $113,800 without in the first half (a difference of $159,700, interval $135,700 to
  $185,000; rank-biserial 0.205), and $277,300 against $110,000 in the second (0.212).
- **Within entity groups** the gap holds in both halves (rank-biserial, first half then second): private companies
  0.114 and 0.126, public companies 0.2 and 0.214, government bodies 0.387 and 0.317, other entities 0.27 and 0.265;
  for trusts it is negligible (0.044 and 0.065).
- **Large taxpayers:** median income $214.6m with IP against $186.8m without in the first half (rank-biserial 0.079),
  and $204.0m against $200.2m in the second (0.04; interval -$8.3m to $19.5m, which includes no difference): not a
  lead.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** the heading said "within every kind of entity", though for trusts the gap is negligible and
  sole traders and partnerships are not shown; "a median contract value" is each supplier's total.

  for the 7,126 firms with a WGEA report (headcount; added after Stage 2, 2.6), and this comparison was not redone
  among them, so size remains the main candidate third factor. Turnover is not in the lens.

observations.headline: Within firms, the first trade mark usually comes before the first patent or design; one first filing in five is dated before the firm's first public registration
observations.statement: Of 4,550 firms with a first trade mark and a first standard patent both filed FY2010 to FY2026, 72.86% filed the trade mark first; of 3,851 with a first trade mark and a first design, 65.62%. Measured from the firm's first public registration, first trade marks came a median 2.61 years after it and first standard patents 5.22 years. But 18.02% of first trade marks and 19.57% of first standard patents are dated before that registration.

figures.label: of firms filed their first trade mark before their first standard patent
median age at first trade mark and first standard patent
of first standard patents dated before the firm's first public registration

points: **Trade marks:** 32.25% of first trade marks came within the firm's first year, and 17.99% after 10 years or more. **Standard patents:** 7.11% within the first year, 29.65% after 10 years or more. **Designs:** a median 5.24 years.
**Firms first seen from 2001 only:** 2.24 years for trade marks, 3.97 for standard patents and 3.96 for designs; shorter, since such a firm can be at most about 25 years old here.
**One in five before registration.** For those firms the registration date is not the business's start, so a recorded age is not a lower bound on age at filing for about one firm in five.

**Who is counted in the within-firm order:** only firms whose two first filings both fall in FY2010 to FY2026; a firm whose first of either came earlier, or whose second has not come yet, is left out, so pairs filed close together weigh more. 5.09% of firms filed their first trade mark and design on the same day.
The second half of the firms agrees: medians of 2.66 and 5.39 years, and 32% within the first year for trade marks.

questions.how: Shows when firms first come to IP, and that a trade mark usually comes first, the moment an intervention aimed at new filers would meet them.

prep.what: Filings dated before the firm's first registration are counted apart, not dropped.

observations.headline: By firm, the youngest filers are not clearly more often those whose patents are now held only overseas; patents filed before a firm's first registration are the most often held overseas
observations.statement: Of the 346 youngest firms (under 2 years old when they filed) in FY2003 to FY2011, 4.34% have an Australian-filed standard patent now held only overseas, against 3.63% of 1,186 firms 10 years or more; in FY2012 to FY2021, 2.96% of 709 against 3.33% of 2,135. Patents filed before the firm's first public registration are the most often held only overseas in both periods (7.01% and 7.77%).

figures.label: firms with a patent now held only overseas, youngest against 10 years or more (FY2003 to FY2011)
the same, FY2012 to FY2021
patents filed before the firm's first registration, now held only overseas

points: **Counted by patent**, the youngest firms' share is 5.79% (26 of 449) in the earlier period and 2.89% (24 of 831) in the later one, against 3.24% and 2.33% for firms 10 years or more. But patents of one firm are not independent, so the firm counts above are the safer reading: one firm holds 23.08% of the youngest band's overseas-held patents in the earlier period.
**Reach is not ruled out:** the youngest firms' patents are less often filed in five or more offices in the earlier period (12.03%, against 15.61% to 19.43%) and in the middle in the later one.

**Whose business number:** a patent joins a firm by its first founding applicant with an ABN, which for a jointly filed patent need not be the Australian party (1,194 of the 26,204 patents joined are jointly filed).
**Not shown:** whether a young firm was sold, its founders moved, or its patents' returns went abroad. Those are hypotheses, not observations.

questions.how: Whether young firms' inventions end up held abroad bears on where value made here is realised; by firm, the youngest are not clearly different from older firms.

observations.original:
**B26 (observational). By firm, the youngest filers are not clearly more often those whose Australian-founded
patents are now held only overseas (4.34% against 3.63% in FY2003 to FY2011, 2.96% against 3.33% in FY2012 to
FY2021); patents filed before the firm's first registration are the most often held overseas in both periods.**
(Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043); audit S2 L2 R30: the heading led with the patent-level rate, "a little more common among the youngest
firms'", where the firm counts are the safer reading.) Standard patents filed FY2003 to FY2021 with an Australian founding applicant, joined to the
firm by its ABN (firms not truncated, 2.5), whose current holders are all overseas. Two endpoints, not a transfer
history; the unit is the patent application unless the firm is named:
- **Firms under 2 years old when they filed:** 5.79% of patents (26 of 449; interval 3.98% to 8.35%) for FY2003 to
  FY2011 filings, 2.89% (24 of 831; 1.95% to 4.26%) for FY2012 to FY2021. **2 to 5 years:** 2.34% and 2.16%; **5 to
  10 years:** 4.69% and 1.39%; **10 years or more:** 3.24% (2.75% to 3.81%) and 2.33% (2.03% to 2.67%). In the later
  period the youngest firms' interval overlaps every other band's.
- **By firm:** 4.34% of the 346 youngest firms of the earlier period have a patent now held only overseas, against
  3.63% of 1,186 firms 10 years or more; in the later period 2.96% of 709 against 3.33% of 2,135. The patent-level
  intervals above treat each patent as independent, which they are not within a firm, so the firm counts are the
  safer reading. One firm holds 23.08% of the youngest band's overseas-held patents in the earlier period, and 44.26%
  of the 5-to-10-year band's: a single firm can move a band.
- **Filed before the firm's first registration:** 7.01% (258 of 3,683) and 7.77% (138 of 1,776) of patents; 6.23% and
  5.77% of firms. Who these filers were when they filed (a founder, or a business before its ABN) is not in the data.
- **Firms first seen from 2001 only:** the youngest 5.82% and 2.89%; the earlier period's ten-plus band holds 2
  patents, so the first version's 4,341 there were companies registered before 2001.
- **Reach is not ruled out.** The youngest firms' patents are less often filed in five or more offices in the earlier
  period (12.03%, against 15.61% to 19.43%) and in the middle in the later one (21.18%, against 20.32% to 26.05%);
  shares across bands do not test reach within them, and the earlier period's family records are incomplete (B55).
  Reach is unknown for 24 to 272 patents a band, counted in the denominators.
- **Whose ABN:** the patent joins the firm by the first founding applicant with an ABN (`filer_abn`), which for a
  jointly founded patent need not be the Australian party: 1,194 of the 26,204 patents joined (4.56%) are jointly
  founded, and in 171 the first founding applicant is not Australian.
- **Not shown:** whether a young firm was sold, its founders moved, or its patents' returns went abroad; those are
  hypotheses for Q1, not observations.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, audit S2 L2 R15, R16, R18 to R20):** first headed "Patents filed by the youngest firms
  move overseas more often, in both periods", with 5.72% (33 of 577) and 3.93% (37 of 941) for the youngest, from a
  sample said to be firms first seen from 2001 that kept every untruncated firm, ages from calendar years, patents
  counted as independent, and reach said not to explain the gap.

later.what: Patents filed before the firm's first registration are more often now held only overseas with grant, reach, field, route and year held (+5.40 and +6.21 points); firms under 2 years old are not detected either way, as B26 read it.

observations.statement: Counting every WGEA employer (9,742), with those the firms table does not hold counted as having no filing linked: 2,533 of the 5,208 employers with fewer than 250 staff have a filing linked (about half), against 113 of the 155 with 5,000 or more (nearly three in four). The gap is 24.3 [[percentage-point|points]] (interval 16.7 to 30.8). For a standard patent it is 21.5 points (14.9 to 29.1), rising band by band.

Of the four SEIFA indexes, education and occupation goes with filing most (0.675 with firms with a filing linked per business, 0.455 with standard patents per person); median personal income goes with standard patents at 0.287.

observations.original:
**B27 (observational). The places lens: 128 distinct leads, 79 of them about IP or R&D; the IP measures move together,
and with education and occupation more than income.** Postal areas in two halves (1,377 in the first, 1,264 in the second; figures are the first half,
then the second); 274 pairs are
leads, 11 hold in one half only, and the halves agree with a Spearman rho of 0.962.
- **The kinds of IP go together across places:** standard patents and provisionals per person (rho 0.765 in the first
  half, 0.779 in the second), standard patents and trade marks (0.693; 0.718), trade marks and designs (0.688; 0.706). Firms
  with a filing linked and R&D claimants, per business, are the strongest pair (0.879; 0.894).
- **Of the four SEIFA indexes, education and occupation (IEO) goes with filing most:** with firms with a filing linked per
  business 0.675 (0.67), trade marks per person 0.64 (0.679), R&D claimants 0.568 (0.599), provisionals 0.534
  (0.579), standard patents 0.455 (0.476) and designs 0.409 (0.415). Median personal income, by comparison, goes
  with standard patents at 0.287 (0.364).
- **Business density:** areas with more GST-registered businesses per person file more standard patents (0.513;
  0.626).
- **Claimants with no filing linked are rarer where filing is common:** the share of R&D claimants with no filing
  linked to their ABN falls with designs (rho -0.253; strength 0.202 in the second half, in the same direction),
  firms with a filing linked (-0.241; 0.158), standard patents (-0.215; 0.204), R&D claimants (-0.2; 0.167) and trade
  marks (-0.178; 0.196) per business, and with government suppliers per business (-0.263; 0.158).
- **Restated (1 November 2026, ADR 0036):** the firm counts now include every linked filing (`ip_record`); counted
  from IP RAPID's own panel, the screen had 124 distinct leads (75 on IP or R&D), and the share (then called "never
  filed IP") fell with designs (-0.259) and standard patents (-0.229) per business.
- Every rate is shown only where 10 or more applications are expected (U53), so these pairs cover the larger areas
  (431 areas for standard patents per person in the discovery half), and they are between places, not firms.

later.what: The advantage measures repeat each other (variance inflation 11.4 to 86.0), and one component carries 49.5% of the areas' variation: B27's single measures are mostly one measure.
Areas form no distinct kinds (silhouette 0.269 at best); the clearest structure is 288 advantaged, educated city areas holding 56% of placed standard patents.

observations.headline: Most attached indicators go with filing along one broad gradient of advantage, education and business density
observations.statement: 6,406 area indicators from five sources were set against six filing rates: 24,947 pairs are leads in both halves. Standard patents per person go most with financial and professional businesses per resident, and are lowest where more single mothers receive Parenting Payment; trade marks go most with professional businesses and Year 12 completion.

figures.label: indicators screened against filing
leads in both halves
professional, scientific and technical businesses per resident with trade marks per person

points: Standard patents per person (3,882 leads): financial and insurance businesses with a turnover of $200k to less than $2m per resident (0.595), professional businesses with $2m to less than $5m (0.593); most negative, single mothers receiving Parenting Payment (-0.482) and children whose mothers have low educational attainment (-0.477).
Trade marks per person: Year 12 completion (0.697), bachelor degrees (0.685), house prices (0.689); most negative, Year 9 as the highest year of school (-0.598) and land area (-0.594).

**So** the attachments describe one dimension of places (urban, educated, professional, business-dense, healthier) more than many separate signals. The Clean Energy Regulator's installations are the exception: 0 of its 11 indicators are leads with trade marks.

questions.how: Filing follows one broad gradient of place advantage, so who benefits from IP is tied to where people live.
Warns against reading any one area indicator as a driver of filing.
