observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B48 (observational). Across the larger changes, bigger rises go with smaller steps in filing, but the interval
includes none.** Spearman's rho between the change in the fees to obtain a right and the step that follows: -0.307
over 34 pairs of 18 changes (95% bootstrap interval resampling changes, -0.638 to 0.049; resampling pairs, as before,
-0.639 to 0.070). The direction is a price's; the size cannot be told from no association with 18 changes, several of
them confounded with Acts. Restated (2 November 2026, audit S2 L5 R07; ADR 0042): the interval resampled pairs,
though a change's two pairs share its cost.

observations.headline: After three changes in renewal fees, cessations rose more than in any comparison month; only one, trade marks after July 1993, survives every check
observations.statement: Cessations (registered rights let go) were compared before and after each change in the fees to keep a right, and at [[placebo|placebo]] months. After three changes they rose more than at any placebo month: patents after September 2002 and trade marks after July 1992 and July 1993. Checked against each series' own trend, and in the window that fits how each series is dated, only trade marks after July 1993 (a 2.041% rise) still stand out, and why so small a rise would move cessations is not shown.

figures.label: renewal fee changes followed by more cessations than any placebo month
still beyond every placebo month after both checks (trade marks, July 1993)
of placebo months as large as the September 2002 patent rise, once the trend is allowed for

points: **Patents, September 2002** (15 anniversaries' renewals up or newly charged, a median rise of 15.3%): cessations in months 7 to 18 rose more than at any of 72 placebo months, but they were already rising; against the trend, 38.89% of placebo months moved as much.
**Other patent changes:** October 2020 (a median rise of 29.5%) 31.25% of placebo months as large, 12.5% against the trend; July 2012 66.67%; August 2010 came before a fall (6.944%).

**Trade marks**, whose cessations are dated at the anniversary: July 1993 none of 66 placebo months as large, with or without the trend; July 1992 5.556%, and 38.89% against the trend. The 40% cut of November 1998 and the 33.33% rise of November 2016 show nothing beyond the ordinary.
**Designs:** no change beyond the ordinary, including July 2004 ($55 to $275, when the 2003 Act's renewal replaced the first extension).
**The trend check is itself noisy:** against the trend, two other patent changes also stand out, in opposite directions (March 2007 up, August 2010 down), so passing it is a weak test.

**What this can and cannot show.** A month's cessations mix rights at many anniversaries, so an effect smaller than the series' ordinary movement could not show here. Whether fees move renewal is for a test at each right's own anniversary, in Stage 3.

questions.how: In national counts, most changes in renewal fees show no response beyond ordinary variation, but this design could miss an effect smaller than the series' usual movement.
The renewal fee changes are candidates for a sharper test at each right's anniversary, in Stage 3.

prep.what: For each change in the fees to keep a right, the anniversaries whose fee changed and the median change ({U109}), and monthly cessations of granted rights.
prep.why: Holders decide at each renewal whether to keep paying, and IP RAPID records cessations apart from lapses.

prep.what: Two checks - the window fitted to how each series is dated (patents' months 7 to 18, trade marks' 1 to 12), and a baseline that carries the two years before forward by their own trend (ADR 0041).
prep.why: A series that was already rising would look as if it rose after a change.

steps: Take each change in renewal fees.
Measure the change in cessations in the window after it, against the year before and against the trend.
Compare each with the same measure at placebo months.
assumptions: Holders respond within a year and a half, when renewals at the new fee fall due.
limits: National counts mix rights of every age; the right-level test is sharper.
A placebo share is a rank among overlapping windows, not a probability.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 as the right-level test of renewal at each anniversary a fee changed.
observations.section: 5.4 Official fee changes against placebo dates (added after Stage 2; ADR 0031)
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B49 (observational). Cessations rose beyond every placebo month after three changes in the fees to keep a right;
only one, trade marks after July 1993, survives every check.** Months after each change against the year before, in
logs, beside the same measure at the placebo months; then two checks (the second table): the window by how each
series is dated, and a baseline that carries the two years before forward by their own trend.
- **Patents:** September 2002 (15 anniversaries' renewals up or newly charged, the 5th to the 20th, a median rise of
  15.3%; the full term's renewals up 16.17%): cessations in months 7 to 18 up 0.353 (0% of 72 placebos as large). Cessations were already
  rising: against the trend the step is 0.189 (38.89% of placebos as large), within the ordinary. October 2020 (19
  anniversaries up or newly charged and the 10th cut, a median rise of 29.5%; 42.82% over the term) 0.114 (31.25%), 0.6 against the trend (12.5%); July 2012
  (17 up or newly charged, a median 11.1%) 0.069 (66.67%); August 2010 (the 10th to the 19th, a median 12.9%) came before a fall
  (-0.236, 6.944%).
- **Trade marks**, whose cessations are dated at the anniversary, so months 1 to 12 hold the first renewals a change
  affected: July 1993 (a rise of 2.041%) 0.232 (0% of 66), and 0.235 against the trend (0%); July 1992 (4.255%) 0.059
  (5.556%), 0.093 against the trend (38.89%). In patents' window (months 7 to 18) both were beyond every placebo
  month (0.148 and 0.283). The series starts in 1987 and climbs in its first years; why a 2% rise would move
  cessations is not shown. The 40% cut of November 1998 and the 33.33% rise of November 2016 show nothing beyond the
  ordinary in either window.
- **Designs:** no change beyond the ordinary in either window (13.85% to 93.22% of placebos as large), including July
  2004, when the 2003 Act's renewal replaced the first extension (a different step: $55 to $275).
- **The trend check moves on its own:** against the trend, two other patent changes are also beyond all but 1.389%
  of placebos, in opposite directions (March 2007 +0.696, August 2010 -0.761), though neither is beyond the ordinary
  on the flat baseline; the trend baseline is itself noisy, so passing it is a weak test (added 2 November 2026,
  pass 8).
- **For Q4 and Q5:** the national series show no response beyond placebo variation for most changes, at this
  design's power: a month's cessations mix cohorts at many anniversaries, so an effect smaller than the series'
  ordinary movement could not show. Whether fees move renewal is for the test at each right's anniversary (the rights
  lens), in Stage 3. These are cessations of granted rights, which IP RAPID records apart from lapses.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, audits S2 L5 R04 to R06; ADR 0041):** the heading said that "no other change in the
  fees to keep a right, up or down, moved cessations beyond the ordinary", though the trade mark bullet showed July
  1992 and July 1993 beyond every placebo month; trade marks' and designs' window was patents'; September 2002 was
  not checked against the trend; the fee was the full term's total, not the anniversaries changed; and the reading
  for Q4 and Q5 was "fee changes have been a weak lever".

later.what: At each right's own anniversary no response is seen after any of nine fee changes; for patents within about 1.4 points either way. B49's cessations beyond every placebo month are not seen at the anniversary ({M34} reads the national series again).

The steps hold in the national series (patents 0.476, trade marks 0.219, controls quiet), but at each patent's own anniversary nothing changes ({M28}): more patents reached those anniversaries, not more were let go.

observations.headline: The dollar's value does not go consistently with filing from overseas; Australian interest rates and overseas applicants' filing move together
observations.statement: As changes from one year to the next, by quarter, the dollar against overseas applicants' standard patents is -0.215 in 1991 to 2008 and 0.261 after: the sign flips. The [[cash-rate|cash rate]] moves with overseas applicants' trade marks (0.46 and 0.198) and designs (0.293 and 0.348). Australians' filing barely moves with either (-0.172 to 0.242 over six pairs).

figures.label: the dollar with overseas standard patents, before and after mid-2008
the cash rate with overseas applicants' trade marks

points: A dearer dollar goes with more overseas designs, not fewer (0.198 and 0.169). A shared business cycle would explain that and a price would not, but that is a hypothesis.
**Weak readings.** These are rank correlations of changes that depend on the quarters before, with no interval or correction for many tests, so each is a weak reading.

**For Stage 3:** the business cycle, here in the cash rate, is a [[third-factor]] for any before-and-after comparison ({B37}, {B47}); the exchange rate is not a usable price signal at this resolution.

questions.how: Points to a cycle that before-and-after comparisons of policy must allow for.

prep.what: The Reserve Bank's cash rate and exchange rates ({U113}) as year-on-year changes by quarter, 68 quarters (1991 to mid-2008) and 72 (mid-2008 on).
prep.why: Matches the timeline screen's form ({B36}).

prep.what: Filing by origin counts the filer's origin (ADR 0037).
prep.why: IP Australia's definition of a resident application.

steps: Relate each Reserve Bank series to each filing series, before and after mid-2008.
assumptions: Monthly averages (cash rate) and month-end values (dollar) stand for the quarter.
limits: Two periods of 68 and 72 quarters; the cycle may differ again, and the readings carry no interval.
observations.next: The cycle is a third factor in Stage 3, which also uses block resampling for intervals on changes like these.
observations.section: 5.5 The dollar and the cash rate against filing (RBA; added after Stage 2, gap B1)
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B52 (observational). The dollar's value does not go consistently with filing from overseas; Australian interest
rates and overseas applicants' filing move together.** Year-on-year changes by quarter, 68 quarters (1991Q3 to 2008Q2)
and 72 (2008Q3 on):
- The dollar in US dollars against overseas applicants' standard patents: -0.215, then 0.261: the sign flips between
  periods. Against overseas designs it is positive in both (0.198 and 0.169): a dearer dollar goes with more, not
  fewer, which a shared cycle would explain and a price would not (a hypothesis).
- The cash rate against overseas applicants' trade marks: 0.46 and 0.198; against their designs 0.293 and 0.348.
- Australians' filing barely moves with either (-0.172 to 0.242 over six pairs in two periods). (Origin is the filer's, ADR
  0037.)
- **For Stage 3:** the business cycle, here in the cash rate, is a third factor for any before-and-after comparison
  (B37, B47); the exchange rate is not a usable price signal at this resolution. These are correlations of serially
  dependent quarterly changes, with no interval or correction, so each is a weak reading.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** the heading said rates and overseas filing "rise together in booms", a mechanism the
  correlations do not show; "a shared cycle, not a price" was a conclusion; "the ten pairs" were six (audit S2 L5
  R11).

later.what: With blocks, the cash rate goes with overseas applicants' trade marks before 2008 (0.460) but not after (0.198); the dollar's pairs are not clear of zero.

observations.headline: Real GDP goes with overseas applicants' patenting, more strongly since 2008; the states' demand was not seen to track Australians' filing
observations.statement: As changes from one year to the next, by quarter, real [[gdp|GDP]] goes with overseas applicants' standard patents at 0.158 to mid-2008 and 0.38 after; with Australians' standard patents at -0.056 and 0.191. Of 16 pairs of a state's final demand with Australians' filing, two keep their sign at 0.1 or more in both periods, a number chance could give (not computed here).

figures.label: real GDP with overseas applicants' standard patents, before and after mid-2008
pairs of a state's demand with Australians' filing that keep their sign

points: Overseas applicants' trade marks and designs: 0.051 to 0.205. Australians' trade marks 0.207 and -0.201.
The two that keep their sign are the Northern Territory's (patents 0.143 and 0.14, trade marks -0.178 and -0.29).

**So** the business cycle ({B52}) and real growth go with filing from overseas more than with Australians' filing, though Australians' standard patents reach 0.191 with GDP since 2008. These are changes that depend on the quarters before, with no interval, so each is a weak reading.

questions.how: Overseas applicants' filing in Australia moves with the Australian economy, which fits filing for the market here, though these data do not show why.
Growth is another third factor for before-and-after comparisons.

prep.what: GDP and each state's final demand from the national accounts ({U116}), quarterly, as year-on-year changes.
prep.why: The timeline holds them in each quarter's last month, and changes match the screen's form ({B36}).

prep.what: Filing by origin counts the filer's origin (ADR 0037).
prep.why: IP Australia's definition of a resident application.

steps: Relate year-on-year changes in GDP and in states' demand to filing, in two periods.
assumptions: Chain volume GDP measures real growth.
limits: Two periods, small links, and no correction for the 16 state pairs.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 as a third factor, with block resampling for intervals.
observations.section: 5.6 GDP and the states' demand against filing (ABS; added after Stage 2, gap B2)
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B56 (observational). Real GDP goes with overseas applicants' patenting, more strongly since 2008; the states' demand
does not track Australians' filing.** Year-on-year changes by quarter, as B52:
- Real GDP against overseas applicants' standard patents: 0.158 (1991Q3 to 2008Q2) and 0.38 (2008Q3 on); against
  their trade marks and designs 0.051 to 0.205. Against Australians' standard patents (by the filer's origin, ADR
  0037) -0.056 and 0.191; their trade marks 0.207 and -0.201.
- Each state's final demand against Australians' standard patents and trade marks: of 16 pairs, two keep their sign at
  0.1 or more in both periods (the Northern Territory: patents 0.143 and 0.14, trade marks -0.178 and -0.29), a
  number chance could give (not computed here).
- **For Stage 3:** the cycle (B52) and real growth go with filing from overseas more than with Australians' (whose
  standard patents reach 0.191 with GDP since 2008); these are serially dependent changes with no interval.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** this said the states' two pairs were "about what chance gives", which the page does not
  compute, and that growth goes with filing "not from here" (audit S2 L5 R11).

later.what: Real GDP against overseas applicants' standard patents, 0.158 and 0.380 (0.181 and 0.313 with the cash rate held): not clear of zero once the quarters' dependence is allowed for.

B56 compared changes in the same quarter. With a lead, trade marks' growth goes with GDP's growth the next quarter (0.038 over 1983 to 2023, GDP's own growth held), clear before 2008 (0.019) and not detected after (0.048, p 0.316).

observations.headline: The labour market moves with overseas applicants' trade marks; IP judgments were not seen to move with oppositions
observations.statement: As year-on-year changes by quarter, more work in Australia goes with more trade mark filing from overseas: the unemployment rate against overseas applicants' trade marks is -0.561 before 2008 and -0.224 after. Australians' trade marks move against employment and participation in both periods, but their sign with unemployment flips. IP judgments were not seen to move with oppositions. Individuals' trade marks rose from 2.01 to 7.8 a year per 1,000 owner-managers between FY1992 and FY2026.

figures.label: unemployment against overseas applicants' trade marks (1991 to 2008, then from 2008)
Australian individuals' trade marks a year per 1,000 owner-managers, FY1992 to FY2026
owner-managers' level against individuals' trade marks across the years (a shared trend, not a link)

points: 68 quarters (1991Q3 to 2008Q2), then 72; no intervals here, because the changes are serially dependent; Stage 3 resamples them in blocks ({M36}).

**Overseas applicants:** employed persons against their trade marks 0.466 and 0.282; participation 0.228 and 0.292. Against their standard patents: unemployment -0.278 and -0.317. As the cash rate did ({B52}).

**Australians:** employment against their trade marks -0.182 and -0.332, participation -0.3 and -0.236; unemployment -0.256, then 0.382 (the sign flips). Against their standard patents every pair is 0.238 or less.
**IP judgments:** on trade marks against trade mark oppositions -0.274 (50 quarters), then 0.134 (66); on patents against patent oppositions 0.021 from 2008.

**Owner-managers as a denominator:** individuals' standard patents fell from 0.49 to 0.24 a year per 1,000 owner-managers (FY2021), 0.33 in FY2026; provisionals from 2.71 (FY1992) to 0.6 (FY2024), then 2.47 in FY2026, after U8's surge.

observations.original:
**B40 (observational). Across divisions, trade marks allocated per business go with business R&D per business;
patents' pairs do not pass, held back by the crosswalk's zeros.** Counts by division are applications allocated by what they protect (a patent's technology, a trade mark's goods and services), mostly overseas applicants', per 1,000 of the division's businesses: not what the division's businesses file (U75). 19
divisions, FY2024 then FY2025 (business R&D fixed at FY2024): 8 leads (4 distinct), 27 pairs below the correction.
- **Trade marks per 1,000 businesses** rise with business R&D per business (rho 0.709; 0.682) and fall with the
  number of businesses in the division (-0.675; -0.674). The second sets a ratio against its own denominator, so it is
  partly arithmetic: a ratio falls as its denominator grows unless the count grows as fast. That divisions of many
  small traders (construction, agriculture, property) receive few marks per business may be so, but the screen cannot
  show it.
- **Where R&D is high, more trade marks come from overseas:** the Australian share of a division's trade marks falls
  with its business R&D per business (-0.635; -0.623; the filer's origin, ADR 0037).
- **Standard patents per business against business R&D** reach 0.465 in both years, which 19 divisions cannot
  separate from chance after the correction.
- **FY2025 is not a second sample:** the same 19 divisions a year later, with business R&D held at FY2024, so its
  agreement is a stability check, and the leads are a single sample of 19 units.
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** this said divisions "file" their allocated counts, read the denominator pairs as findings and
  FY2025 as a replication (audit S2 L6 R02 to R04).

observations.statement: Across 112 institutions with 100 or more works (2017 to 2023), universities win far more ARC grants per 1,000 works than medical research institutes, which have the most citations from US patents per work. observations.original:
**B44 (observational). Across institutions, the kind of institution sorts most measures; research that patents cite
goes with the institution's own patenting.** 112 institutions with 100 or more works in 2017 to 2023 (43 universities,
42 medical research institutes, 11 public research agencies) and 111 in 2010 to 2016: 32 pairs are leads (18
distinct), 8 hold in one period only.
- **Kind:** universities hold far more ARC grants per 1,000 works (a median 4.251) than medical research institutes
  (strength 0.898; 0.794 earlier), as the ARC's rules make them (U83: universities hold all ARC funding), so this is a
  mechanic of funding, not performance; medical research institutes have the most citations from US patents per work
  (0.573; 0.694) and per work generally (0.474; 0.642).
- **Research and invention together:** the share of an institution's works cited by US patents rises with its own
  provisional applications per 1,000 works (rho 0.583; 0.488) and with the citations its works receive (0.529;
  0.518). NHMRC grants per work go with standard patents per work (0.338; 0.367).
- **Size:** larger institutions hold more ARC grants per work (0.803; 0.826), largely universities against medical
  research institutes (kind is the pair's first third factor; not checked within kind), and file somewhat more standard patents
  per work (0.269; 0.225).
- The second period is mostly the same institutions seven years earlier: a stability check, not a replication
  (Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043); audit S2 L7 R03).
- **The IP detail:** 21.41% of the institutions' patents are filed with others and 10.98% with another research
  institution, against 5.69% and 3.5% of their trade marks (type × filed with others, 0.14; 0.146). How a filer was
  matched goes with whether its country is known (0.201; 0.182), as the link's design expects (ADR 0021).

later.what: Across every kind of institution, the patent-cited share goes with the institution's own patents per work with kind, size, citations and NHMRC held (2.307 and 1.644 per standard deviation).

observations.headline: Few of the US patents that cite Australian research have an Australian applicant or inventor, and the share does not consistently follow the institution's own patenting
observations.statement: For institutions with 1,000 or more works, the median share of their US patent citations that come from patents with an Australian applicant or inventor is 3.252% for works from 2017 to 2023 (82 institutions) and 5.482% for 2010 to 2016 (69). Against the institution's own patents per 1,000 works the rank [[correlation]] is 0.298, then 0.165: not consistent.

figures.label: median share of US patent citations with an Australian applicant or inventor (works from 2017 to 2023)
the same, works from 2010 to 2016

points: Against the share of the institution's works cited by patents: 0.361, then 0.082.

**What this does not show.** Most US patents have no Australian party, whatever they cite, and there is no baseline here (such as the Australian share of all US patents). A citation, often added by an examiner or an attorney, is not use. And the 2017 to 2023 works have had less time to be cited, so the two shares are not a change over time.
Where Australian research is used, and whether value from it is realised elsewhere, are questions these citations raise but do not answer ({U85}).

questions.how: Raises, without answering, where Australian research is used and where value from it is realised.
Shows what US patent citations can and cannot say about research reaching invention in Australia.

observations.original:
**B46 (observational). Few US patents citing Australian research have Australian links, and the share does not
consistently follow the institution's own patenting.** For institutions with 1,000 or more works, the median share of
their US patent citations that come from patents with an Australian applicant or inventor is 3.252% in 2017 to 2023
(82 institutions) and 5.482% in 2010 to 2016 (69). Against the institution's patents per 1,000 works: rho 0.298, then
0.165; against the share of its works cited by patents: 0.361, then 0.082. These are shares of US
patents' citations, most of which come from patents with no Australian party whatever they cite, with no baseline
here (such as the Australian share of US patents); a citation, often added by an examiner or attorney, is not use;
and the 2017 to 2023 works have had less time to be cited than the 2010 to 2016 ones, so the two shares are not a
change. Where Australian research is used, and whether value from it is realised elsewhere, are questions for Q1 and
Q4 that these citations raise but do not answer. (Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043): this read "Australian research is used mostly by
inventions owned and made elsewhere"; audit S2 L7 R01, R04.)

observations.headline: Institutions with more invention disclosures per research dollar file more patents, and those that file more earn more licence income, partly because all are divided by the same research spend
observations.statement: Across 66 institutions with $10 million or more of research spend (2004 to 2009), per $ million, invention disclosures go with standard patents at 0.617 (0.615 in 2010 to 2015), and patents with licence income at 0.593 (0.525). Patents per disclosure fell from 0.161 to 0.134.

figures.label: disclosures with standard patents, per research dollar
patents with licence income
patents per disclosure

points: Disclosures with provisionals 0.555 and 0.694; patents with licences 0.535 and 0.436; with start-ups 0.349 and 0.513; licences with income 0.555 and 0.544.

**A shared denominator.** All six measures are divided by the same research spend, so an institution whose reported spend is low is high on all six, and the correlations are partly that. Dividing by size does not remove size, and field mix is not held.
Whether patents are a sign of commercialisation is for Stage 3 to test, with research spend as an exposure rather than a divisor.

questions.how: Patenting per research dollar goes with licensing and licence income per research dollar, one possible route by which research IP produces value; the shared denominator means this is not yet a measured link.
Disclosure, patenting and licensing move together, a chain of conditions to test further.

**B62 (observational). Institutions that receive more invention disclosures per research dollar file more patents, and
those that file more patents earn more licence income; the links hold in both periods.** 66 (2004 to 2009) and 67
(2010 to 2015) institutions with $10 million or more of research spend, as ratios per $ million: disclosures with
standard patents 0.617 (strength interval 0.43 to 0.76) and 0.615 (0.42 to 0.77); with provisionals 0.555 and 0.694;
patents with licences 0.535 and 0.436; with licence income 0.593 (0.37 to 0.76) and 0.525 (0.30 to 0.72); with
start-ups 0.349 (0.06 to 0.57) and 0.513; licences with income 0.555 and 0.544. Patents per disclosure fell from 0.161 to
0.134.
- **For Stage 3:** across institutions, 2004 to 2015, patenting per research dollar goes with licensing and licence
  income per research dollar. All six measures are divided by the same research expenditure, so an institution whose
  reported expenditure is low is high on all six, and the correlations are partly that shared denominator; dividing
  by size does not remove size, field mix is not held, patents are counted by year of application (for a PCT patent,
  national phase entry) against disclosures in the year reported, and the NSRC joins the lens by name. Whether patents
  are a sign of commercialisation is for Stage 3 to test with expenditure as an exposure.

observations.headline: Patents filed without an attorney are still granted far less often once the factors settled at filing are held together
observations.statement: Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted 31.2 [[percentage-point|points]] less often than those filed with an attorney once the route, filing year, state and co-filers are [[held-together|held together]] (FY2010 to FY2019), against 35.8 points with nothing held: 87.2% of Stage 2's gap remains, and 86.2% in the earlier decade. Trade marks filed alone show the same gap for individuals and organisations alike, almost untouched by what is held.

figures.label: Australian individuals' patents filed alone, FY2010 to FY2019, held together (raw -35.8)
of the raw gap left once held together (86.2% in FY2000 to FY2009)
of the trade mark gaps left, individuals and organisations, both decades

points: **Australian organisations' patents** hold in FY2010 to FY2019 (-40.0 raw, -35.3 held together) but not in FY2000 to FY2009, where neither the raw nor the held figure is detected (+6.0, interval -18.5 to 30.6). That decade's 1,149 lone applications came from 392 filers, the ten largest filing 59.8% of them: a few heavy filers, perhaps with their own patent staff, though the data do not say who they were.
**A second reading** among applications that have a technology field, holding the field and number of classes too: -27.2 and -27.8 points. Among examined applications: -30.5 and -29.1.

**Not a few filers' doing.** The ten heaviest lone filers hold 0.8% to 10.1% of the lone filings in every group but the older organisations'; Australian individuals' 1,642 lone patent applications came from 1,370 filers.

**Not a cause.** Only what is known at filing is held. The filer's resources, experience and the merit of the invention are not in the data, and an application dropped early may never appoint an attorney, so the arrow can run backwards.

Keeps representation as a signal worth a design that separates the choice of an attorney from the outcome (the first of Stage 3's early signals).

prep.what: Decided standard patents and trade marks filed FY2000 to FY2019, filed alone or with an attorney (agents who are not attorneys left out, as in B6); trade marks capped at 200,000 a group and decade by a hash of the application number.
prep.why: Only decided applications have an outcome, and the cap keeps the models quick while the hash makes the sample the same on every run.

prep.what: Each application is grouped by its [[filers-party|filer's party]], so a filer with many applications counts as one source of evidence in the intervals ([[clustered|clustered intervals]]).
prep.why: A firm's thousand applications are not a thousand independent cases.

steps: Take Stage 2's comparison (filed alone against with an attorney) as the raw figure.

Fit one model of the yes or no outcome (granted or not) with the route, filing year, state and co-filers held together, and report the difference as an [[average-marginal-effect|average difference in points]].
Compare the held figure with the raw one, and give the outcome by Stage 3's rule (holds if at least half remains and the interval is clear of zero).
Repeat in the earlier decade, among applications with a field (holding the field), and among examined applications.
assumptions: What is settled at filing (route, year, state, co-filers, trade mark classes) is not itself caused by the choice to file alone, so holding it does not hide part of the gap.
limits: The technology field is assigned as an application is classified, and an application abandoned early may never get one, so the field is held only in a second reading among applications that have one.
The filer's resources and experience, and the invention's merit, are not in the data; they could explain the gap.
observations.next: The first of Stage 3's early signals (with {M2}): a design that separates the choice of an attorney from the outcome, such as the same filers' applications with and without one, or a change in what representation costs.

observations.original:
**M1 (observational). Standard patents filed alone are granted far less often, and most of the gap stays when the
factors settled at filing are held together, for Australian individuals in both decades; trade marks likewise for
individuals and organisations.** Difference in the share granted or registered, filed alone minus with an attorney,
in points (raw; with the route, filing year, state and founders held together), with 95% intervals clustered by the
filer:
- **Australian individuals' standard patents:** FY2010 to FY2019, raw -35.8 (-37.8 to -33.8), held together -31.2
  (-34.0 to -28.4), 87.2% of the raw gap remaining; FY2000 to FY2009, -36.8 (-38.9 to -34.8) and -31.7 (-34.5 to
  -29.0), 86.2%. **Holds** in both decades. Among applications with a field, with the field and number of classes
  held too: -27.2 (-30.5 to -23.9) and -27.8 (-31.0 to -24.7). Among examined applications: -30.5 (-35.9 to -25.1)
  and -29.1 (-34.0 to -24.2).
- **Australian organisations' standard patents** hold in FY2010 to FY2019 (raw -40.0, -45.6 to -34.4; held together
  -35.3, -40.6 to -30.0), but not in FY2000 to FY2009: raw +6.0 (-30.2 to 42.3), held together +6.0 (-18.5 to 30.6),
  **not detected either way** (the raw interval includes zero too; corrected 3 November 2026 in the review: this
  read "not detected once held", which the table's verdict does not give); among examined applications that decade, alone is granted more often (+17.2, 0.6 to
  33.8). Clustering shows why the earlier decade differs: its 1,149 lone applications came from 392 filers, the ten
  largest filing 59.8% of them, against 10.1% of the later decade's 685 (543 filers). B6's guess that these were
  firms with their own patent staff fits a few heavy filers, but the data do not say who they were.
- **Trade marks** (with the Nice class and number of classes held too): Australian individuals -24.3 raw, -22.3
  (-23.2 to -21.5) held together, then -23.2 and -22.6 (-23.8 to -21.4); Australian organisations -23.7 and -23.3
  (-24.1 to -22.6), then -21.3 and -21.3 (-22.2 to -20.4). **Holds** in both decades, 91.9% to 99.9% remaining: the
  route, class, year, state and filers' number account for almost none of it.
- Lone filing is spread thinly: the ten heaviest lone filers hold 0.8% to 10.1% of the lone filings in every group but
  the older organisations', so the gap is not a few filers' (Australian individuals' patents: 1,642 lone applications
  from 1,370 filers).
- **Not a cause.** What is held fixed is what is known at filing; the filer's resources, experience and the merit of
  the invention are not in the data, and an application dropped early may never appoint an attorney (the arrow can run
  backwards, B6). The signal for Q4 is that the gap is not explained by the route, year, place, field or co-filers.

observations.headline: Trade marks and designs with no agent before the first renewal are less often in force after it, once other factors are held
observations.statement: With no agent recorded before the first renewal, 31.7% of Australians' trade marks filed FY2010 to FY2015 were in force after 10 years, against 50.8% with an attorney. With the filer's type, class, state, route and cohort held together the gap is 14.4 points, 75.5% of the raw 19.1; within individuals and within organisations it holds more fully. Designs show the same at their five-year renewal, almost untouched by what is held.

**Designs after 5 years**, FY2010 to FY2019: 30.0% against 46.7%, -16.7 raw and -16.3 held together in the first half; 32.4% against 46.8%, -14.5 and -14.1 in the second.
B10's raw figures are reproduced (31.7% against 50.8%).

observations.original:
**M4 (observational). Australian organisations' patents reach fewer offices and are cited less within five years of
priority; the field, route, year and the rest account for much of each gap, and reach for most of the citation gap,
but neither gap goes.** Standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019, first half then second:
- **Filed only in Australia:** 40.9% of Australian organisations' against 8.2% of overseas organisations', raw +32.7
  points (28.3 to 37.0), held together +9.3 (8.3 to 10.3), 28.4% remaining; second half +32.2 and +10.2 (9.1 to
  11.2). **Weakened.**
- **Five or more offices:** 22.2% against 69.7%, raw -47.5 (-51.5 to -43.5), held together -31.9 (-34.6 to -29.3),
  67.3% remaining; second half -46.4 and -31.4 (-34.1 to -28.7). **Holds.**
- **Citations within five years** (the fixed-age window): on average 4.44 citing families for Australian
  organisations' patents against 14.22 for overseas organisations'. Rate ratio 0.312 (0.272 to 0.359) raw, 0.645
  (0.577 to 0.721) with reach held, 0.729 (0.677 to 0.784) with every factor held; second half 0.307, 0.633 and 0.700
  (0.634 to 0.774). On a log scale reach accounts for about three fifths of the raw gap (62% and 61%), and about 27%
  and 30% of it remains with every factor held: **weakened**, but about 27% to 30% fewer citations at the same reach,
  field, route and year.
- **So the three signals still disagree once held together:** fewer offices and fewer citations in the same field,
  route and year, yet more often in force at the same reach. None of them is value, private or public (A22, B8);
  they are three readings of how patents are used, to be read side by side. Reach is held only in three bands, so
  part of a gap within a band could still be reach.

observations.headline: Expedited examination's link with a longer life does not survive the filer, field and route held together; for individuals it goes with a shorter one
observations.statement: Stage 2 found expedited standard patents slightly more often in force at 10 years. Held together with the filer, field, route, cohort, co-filers and classes, that link is not detected in FY2010 to FY2016 and reverses in FY2003 to FY2009 (a [[hazard-ratio|hazard ratio]] of 1.124: more likely to end). Australian individuals' expedited patents are about a quarter more likely to end in a given year, in both periods.

observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**M5 (observational). Expedited examination's link with a longer life does not survive the other factors: pooled, it
is not detected once the filer, field, route and cohort are held (FY2010 to FY2016) and reverses (FY2003 to FY2009);
among Australian individuals, expedited patents are more likely to end, in both periods.** Hazard ratios, expedited
against not (below 1: less likely to end), to 10 years from the date of patent (raw; held together):
- **All filers:** FY2010 to FY2016, 0.958 (0.842 to 1.091) and 1.021 (0.902 to 1.156), not detected either way;
  FY2003 to FY2009, 0.782 (0.717 to 0.853) and 1.124 (1.030 to 1.228), **reversed**. The earlier period's raw
  advantage (B13's 3.7 points) is accounted for by what is held: B13 found it was not the mix of filers, and here the
  field, route, cohort, founders and classes held with the filer take it away. **Revisits B13**, whose "not a
  composition effect" held for the filer mix only.
- **Overseas organisations** (most of the patents): 0.945 (0.805 to 1.110) and 1.004 (0.863 to 1.169), then 0.598
  (0.537 to 0.665) and 0.957 (0.862 to 1.063): **not detected once held** in the earlier period.
- **Australian individuals:** 1.341 (1.086 to 1.656) and 1.264 (1.013 to 1.576), then 1.344 (1.141 to 1.582) and
  1.249 (1.053 to 1.481): **holds** in both periods, expedited patents about a quarter more likely to end in a given
  year. B13 found the same direction in shares (59.7% against 68.5%, then 55.1% against 65.0%).
- **Australian organisations:** 0.992 and 0.989 (0.836 to 1.170), not detected either way; then 1.146 (0.934 to
  1.405) and 1.285 (1.046 to 1.580), appears once held. **Overseas individuals:** 1.077 and 1.070 (0.920 to 1.244),
  not detected either way; then 1.329 (1.070 to 1.651) and 1.721 (1.378 to 2.149), holds.
- **So** expedited examination is not a sign of a patent that lasts longer, once who files, the field and the route
  are known; for Australian individuals it goes with a shorter life. One reading, to test: an individual who asks for
  speed may want a granted patent quickly (to show investors or licensees) and let it go if nothing comes of it. Since
  2014 "expedited" also includes work-sharing requests (OQ25), so the kinds of request are mixed.

observations.headline: On provisionals, organisations' inventors include more women than individuals'; on standard patents the field accounts for the gap
observations.statement: On provisional applications, Australian organisations' inventors include more women than Australian individuals' (21.19% against 16.12%, FY2013 to FY2022), and the gap holds with the year, state and co-filers held: +5.56 points, and +6.63 in the earlier decade. On standard patents the organisations' apparent advantage is the field: with the field held, their inventors include fewer women in FY2010 to FY2019 (-2.82 points).

observations.headline: Divisionals doubled within the same filers, not through a change in fields or filers
observations.statement: Divisional applications rose from 11.59% to 22.62% of Australian organisations' standard patents between FY2000 to FY2009 and FY2010 to FY2019, and from 7.08% to 15.63% of overseas organisations'. With the field, co-filers and classes held the rise holds (+10.7 and +8.8 points), it holds without the ten filers with the most divisionals, and it holds [[within-filers|within the same filers]]: +19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones.

figures.label: Australian organisations, within the same filers (1,413 filers)
overseas organisations, within the same filers (5,664 filers)
of Australian organisations' later divisionals held by ten filers

points: **Australian organisations:** +11.0 raw, +10.7 held together (96.9% left). Without the ten filers with the most later divisionals, +7.1.
**Overseas organisations:** +8.5 raw, +8.8 held together; without their ten largest +8.4. Their ten largest hold 8.51% of the later divisionals.
So Stage 2's doubling is not a change in the mix of fields or filers: the same organisations file more divisionals.
Why is not in the data. Stage 2's lead, that a divisional keeps claims pending longer, needs the dates of each divisional's parent and its examination.

revisits.what: The rise holds with the field, co-filers and classes held (+10.7 and +8.8 points), without the ten largest filers, and within the same filers (+19.18 and +10.97): the same organisations file more divisionals.

verdicts.signal: Overseas organisations

questions.how: A change in how the same organisations use the system (more divisionals), which bears on examination and on how long claims stay pending (the twelfth early signal).

prep.what: Applications with a field only, capped at 200,000 a group by the hash; the route cannot be held, because a divisional is a route.
prep.why: An application abandoned before it is classified has neither a field nor a class count, so the two would repeat each other.

prep.what: The within-filer reading takes filers with patents in both decades and removes each filer's own average first (a fixed effect for the filer).
prep.why: It says how the same filers changed, not how the mix of filers did.

steps: Compare the share of divisionals between the decades, with nothing held (raw).
Hold the field, co-filers and classes, clustered by the filer; then leave out the ten filers with the most later divisionals.
Compare within the same filers.
assumptions: A filer's party identifies the same organisation across the two decades.
limits: Why organisations file more divisionals is not in the data.

observations.headline: Inventions made in Australia and filed from overseas are, in about equal numbers, international teams' and all-Australian teams'
observations.statement: Of standard patents with an inventor in Australia, those whose teams also have inventors abroad are filed from overseas more than half the time (62.08%, then 54.20%), against about one in ten whose known inventors are all here (10.85%, then 8.57%). In FY2010 to FY2019 the two kinds of team give about as many patents filed from overseas (1,207 and 1,142). The fall between the decades holds with the team, field and reach held (-2.7 points).

figures.label: filed from overseas, teams with inventors abroad too (FY2000 to FY2009, then FY2010 to FY2019)
filed from overseas, every known inventor in Australia
the fall between decades, held together (raw -4.8)

points: 22,335 patents filed FY2000 to FY2019 with an inventor in Australia, 13.96% with inventors abroad too.
**Inventors abroad too, against every inventor here:** +51.2 points raw, +52.0 held together; then +45.6 and +47.5. Holds.
**The decade:** 19.28% to 14.51%, -4.8 raw, -2.7 held together (56.3% left). **Wide reach** (five or more offices): +4.5 held in FY2000 to FY2009, not detected once held; +5.7 in FY2010 to FY2019.
The 1,764 patents with every known inventor here that were filed from overseas came from 583 filers, the ten largest 33.0%: a parent or a buyer at filing; who they are is not in the data.

revisits.what: B16's "one in seven" is two things in about equal parts: international teams with an inventor here, filed by their owners abroad, and teams wholly here whose filer is overseas. The fall between decades holds (-2.7 points held together, against -4.8 raw).

prep.what: Standard patents filed FY2000 to FY2019 with at least one inventor in Australia (from Google Patents); "filed from overseas" means no founding applicant in Australia, as in B16.
prep.why: The same patents as Stage 2, with the team's other inventors added.

Within each decade, compare the two kinds of team and wide against narrow reach.

observations.headline: Owners did not let rights go more often at the anniversary after a renewal fee changed
observations.statement: At each right's own anniversary, owners did not let patents, trade marks or designs go more often after any of nine changes in the renewal fee from 2000 (rises of 11% to 33% and a 10% cut), once the trend either side, the anniversary, the filer, the field and the founders are held. For patents the intervals rule out more than about 1.4 [[percentage-point|points]] either way: a precise null.

figures.label: of the nine fee changes from 2000 is followed by a detected change in letting go
patents, September 2002 (+15.27%), held together (raw +1.94)
patents, October 2020 (+29.55%), held together

points: **Patents**, held together: September 2002 +0.08; March 2007 (-10%) -0.57; August 2010 (+12.92%) -0.12; July 2012 (+11.11%) +0.05; October 2016 (+10.87%) +0.43; October 2020 (+29.55%) -0.06. Not detected after any.
**The raw gaps of 2002, 2007 and 2010 are each period's trend:** anniversaries whose fee did not change in August 2010 show one too (-1.68 raw), and it goes once the trend is held (+0.72).

**Trade marks**, October 2016 (+33.33% at the 10-year renewal): -0.99 held. **Designs**, July 2012 (+16.36%) +6.24 and October 2020 (+25%) -2.49, about 11,000 and 12,600 designs: not detected, with wide intervals.
**Not a cause either way:** an owner can pay before the anniversary at the old fee, and a change announced months ahead may move decisions outside the window.

revisits.signal: Renewal fees and letting rights go
revisits.what: At each right's own anniversary no response is seen after any of nine fee changes; for patents within about 1.4 points either way. B49's cessations beyond every placebo month are not seen at the anniversary ({M34} reads the national series again).

held: a straight-line trend either side of the change

verdicts.signal: Patents, six fee changes from September 2002 to October 2020
verdicts.detail: held together from -0.57 to +0.43 points; every interval includes zero

verdicts.signal: Trade marks, October 2016 (+33.33%)
Designs, July 2012 and October 2020
verdicts.detail: +6.24 and -2.49 held together, with wide intervals

questions.how: At this design's power, owners' decisions at the anniversary did not respond to these fee changes, so renewal fees look a weak lever on letting rights go (the fourteenth early signal).
A precise null for patents that any projection of a fee change's effect would have to respect.

prep.what: For each change in renewal fees from 2000, every right whose changed anniversary fell in the 12 months before or after the change, granted before it and not ended before it, is a row; October 2024 is too recent to have its year after.
prep.why: Compares owners deciding just before and just after the change, at the same kind of anniversary.

prep.what: A right is [[let-go|let go]] if it ceased at that anniversary (for patents, a cessation dated 3 to 12 months after it, since cessations are dated at the end of the six-month grace period).
prep.why: The register dates a lapse at the end of the grace period, not at the anniversary.

steps: Compare the share let go at anniversaries after the change with those before (raw).
Hold a straight-line trend with its own slope on each side, the anniversary number, the filer, the field or class and the founders together, clustered by the filer.
Check the method on anniversaries whose fee did not change (August 2010 and October 2016), which should show nothing once the trend is held.
assumptions: Owners deciding just before and just after a change are alike in every way but the fee.
limits: An owner can pay before the anniversary at the fee then in force, so this tests the decision at the anniversary, not the price each owner paid.
A change announced months ahead may move decisions outside the window.
observations.next: The fourteenth early signal: owners' payment dates (early payment at the old fee), and the fee's share of a patent's cost of keeping, to read fees as a lever.

observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**M28 (observational). At the anniversary after a change in its renewal fee, rights were not let go more often than at
the anniversary before, after any of nine changes from 2000 (rises of 11% to 33% and a 10% cut); for patents the
intervals rule out more than about 1.4 points either way.** Difference in the share let go at the anniversary, after
the change against before, in points (raw; with the trend either side, the anniversary, the filer, the field and the
founders held), clustered by the filer:
- **Patents:** September 2002 (a median +15.27% over 14 anniversaries) raw +1.94 (1.17 to 2.71), held together +0.08
  (-0.82 to 0.98); March 2007 (-10%) -1.19 and -0.57 (-1.27 to 0.12); August 2010 (+12.92%) -2.35 and -0.12 (-1.23
  to 1.00); July 2012 (+11.11%) +0.01 and +0.05 (-0.79 to 0.90); October 2016 (+10.87%) -0.03 and +0.43 (-0.55 to
  1.41); October 2020 (+29.55%) -0.44 and -0.06 (-0.84 to 0.72). **Not detected** after any. The raw gaps of 2002,
  2007 and 2010 are each period's trend: the anniversaries whose fee did not change in August 2010 show one too (-1.68
  raw), and it goes once the trend is held (+0.72, -0.20 to 1.64).
- **Trade marks**, October 2016 (+33.33% at the 10-year renewal): raw +0.50, held together -0.99 (-2.78 to 0.80).
  **Designs**, July 2012 (+16.36%) +6.24 (-0.74 to 13.21) and October 2020 (+25%) -2.49 (-9.29 to 4.32), about 11,000
  and 12,600 designs: not detected, with wide intervals.
- **For Q4 and Q5:** at this design's power, owners' decisions at the anniversary did not respond to these changes in
  the fee to keep a right. **Revisits B49**, which found cessations beyond every placebo month after three changes in
  the national series: at each right's own anniversary none is seen (M34 reads the series again). Not a cause either
  way: an owner can pay before the anniversary at the old fee, and a change announced months ahead may move decisions
  outside the window.

observations.headline: Asking for examination before being directed goes with patents more likely to end, not less, against IP Australia's commissioned study
observations.statement: IP Australia's commissioned study counts a request for examination made before the Commissioner directs one as a way of speeding examination up, and reports that applicants who speed up are more likely to renew their patents. Built from the open data, the same measure covers 41.39% of granted patents (the study: 41.9%). But with the filer, field, route, cohort and expedited examination held together, those patents are more likely to end in a given year after grant, in both periods ([[hazard-ratio|hazard ratios]] 1.276 and 1.383).

figures.label: of granted standard patents, 2004 to 2016, asked for examination before any direction (the study, 41.9%)
all filers, FY2010 to FY2016, held together (raw 1.214): more likely to end
all filers, FY2003 to FY2009, held together (raw 1.366)

points: **The measure reproduces the study's share:** 303,486 standard patents with a date of patent in 2004 to 2016, divisionals left out, of which 191,477 granted; 41.28% were never directed. The share rose between the periods: overseas organisations 0.273 to 0.5148, Australian organisations 0.2357 to 0.4602.

**By filer, held together:** overseas organisations 1.282, then 1.388; overseas individuals 1.298, then 1.340; Australian organisations 1.005 (not detected either way), then 1.587; Australian individuals 1.169 (not detected once held), then 1.486.

**Why it may differ from the study:** its outcome ("the lifetime over which the applicant renews the patent") and its controls are not in IP Australia's report. Here each patent is followed from its grant, so the comparison is among patents alive at the same age.

**One reading, to test:** applicants who wait use the years to drop weak applications before grant, the study's own point about delay as an option, so the granted patents of those who were directed are already filtered.

revisits.signal: Speeding up examination and staying in force
revisits.what: On IP Australia's commissioned study's wider measure, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents), the link with a longer life is not found either: those patents are more likely to end, held together (1.276 and 1.383).

verdicts.signal: All filers, FY2010 to FY2016
verdicts.detail: 1.214 raw, 1.276 held together (more likely to end)

verdicts.signal: All filers, FY2003 to FY2009
Australian organisations, FY2010 to FY2016
Australian individuals, FY2010 to FY2016

questions.how: Asking for examination sooner does not mark a patent that is kept longer, on either the narrow measure (M5) or IP Australia's study's wider one.
Bears on how IP Australia reads its own study; the difference from the study is a question for IP Australia about its model.

prep.what: A request is unprompted if IP RAPID's first request for examination is dated before any direction to request examination (its exam_direction_to_request_exam events), as the study defines early and unprompted requests. Granted standard patents with a request, divisionals left out as the study left them, cohorts by the date of patent as in {M5}.
prep.why: The audit against IP Australia found that {M5} tested only expedited requests, a few per cent of patents, while the study's measure covers 41.9% of granted patents.

steps: Check that the measure gives the study's share of granted patents.
Compare unprompted with directed requests as a hazard ratio, raw, then with the filer, field, route, cohort, co-filers, classes and expedited examination held together.
Fit the same model within each filer group, and give each outcome.
assumptions: A request made before any direction is the applicant's own choice; a direction is IP Australia's, to manage its workload.
limits: The study's model and outcome are not published in the report, so this tests its measure, not its result.
observations.next: Ask IP Australia how the study measured the renewal lifetime and what it held (with the owner's request), and read M40 beside {M5} in the third early signal.
observations.section: 1.11 Early, unprompted requests for examination and staying in force (C3; added 4 November 2026)
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**M40 (observational). Early, unprompted requests for examination go with patents more likely to end, not less: the
open data do not repeat the link IP Australia's commissioned study reports, on the study's own measure, in either
period, with the filer, field, route, cohort and expedited examination held together.** Added at the owner's decision
(OQ27, A36).
- **The measure reproduces the study's share:** of standard patents with a date of patent in 2004 to 2016,
  divisionals left out (303,486, of which 191,477 granted), 41.39% of the granted had examination requested before any
  direction, against the study's 41.9% (of 316,077 patents; it does not say how it counted them); 41.28% were never
  directed. The share rose between the periods, as a share of the sampled patents: overseas organisations 0.273
  (FY2003 to FY2009) to 0.5148 (FY2010 to FY2016), Australian organisations 0.2357 to 0.4602, Australian individuals
  0.3585 to 0.517.
- **All filers:** hazard ratios, unprompted against directed (above 1: more likely to end in a given year), to 10
  years from the date of patent (raw; held together): FY2010 to FY2016, 1.214 (1.116 to 1.321) and 1.276 (1.172 to
  1.389); FY2003 to FY2009, 1.366 (1.252 to 1.490) and 1.383 (1.286 to 1.487). **Holds**, in both periods, and in
  the opposite direction to the study's finding.
- **By filer, held together:** overseas organisations (most of the patents) 1.282 (1.171 to 1.404), then 1.388 (1.281
  to 1.503); overseas individuals 1.298, then 1.340; Australian organisations 1.005 (0.856 to 1.180), **not detected
  either way**, then 1.587 (1.235 to 2.038); Australian individuals 1.169 (0.907 to 1.505), **not detected once held**
  (raw 1.427), then 1.486 (1.217 to 1.815).
- **So** a patent whose applicant asked for examination before being directed is about 28% (FY2010 to FY2016) and
  38% (FY2003 to FY2009) more likely to end in a given year after grant than one examined after a direction, with who
  filed, the field, the route, the cohort and expedited examination held. This is the study's measure, not its
  model: its outcome ("the lifetime over which the applicant renews the patent") and its controls are not in IP
  Australia's report, so the difference may lie there. Here each patent is followed from its grant, so the comparison
  is among patents alive at the same age. One reading, to test: applicants who wait use the years to drop weak
  applications before grant (the study's own point about delay as an option, ipr-2025 p11), so the granted patents of
  those who were directed are already filtered. **Revisits B13** (and M5): on the study's wider measure, too, asking
  for examination sooner does not go with a patent kept longer.

observations.headline: Among R&D claimants, older firms, higher spenders and public companies more often have a standard patent linked, held together; the city gap does not replicate
observations.statement: Among 17,514 active R&D Tax Incentive claimants, claimants 20 years or more on the record are 23.1 points more likely to have a filing linked than those of 3 to 10, with spend, company form, state and postcode advantage [[held-together|held together]]. Spending above the median and being a public company go with having a standard patent (about 4 to 5 and 8 to 9 points held together), but much less with any filing. A city address goes with filing in one half only.

figures.label: any filing linked, 20 years or more against 3 to 10, held together (first half)
a standard patent, R&D spend above the median, held together
a standard patent, public against private company, held together

points: **Age:** any filing linked +24.2 raw and +23.1 held together; +22.9 and +22.4. A standard patent +13.0 and +10.5; +12.0 and +9.0. Holds. Age is on the record at the build date, so an older firm has had longer to file: part of this is time, not kind.

**R&D spend above the median** ($326,125, the median average claim): a standard patent +6.2 and +4.3, holds; any filing +6.0 and +2.4, weakened. The form and age of high spenders account for more than half of their higher filing.
**Public against private company** (969 public, 16,510 private): a standard patent +15.5 and +8.0, holds (51.5% and 59.5% left); any filing +13.0 and +5.9, weakened.
**Major city against elsewhere:** any filing +5.2 raw and +5.6 held in the first half, +2.2 and +0.5 in the second. It does not replicate.

Among claimants, age holds (+23.1 and +22.4 points for any filing) and public form holds for a standard patent (+8.0 and +9.4); a city address does not replicate (+5.6, then +0.5).

observations.headline: Followed by cohort, about two thirds of firms that file both kinds filed a trade mark before their first standard patent
observations.statement: Following firms by the year of their first public registration, rather than a window of filings, 64.04% to 69.48% of firms that have filed both a trade mark and a standard patent filed the trade mark first: a little less than Stage 2's 72.86%, and least in the cohort followed longest. points: **2001 to 2005:** 64.04% of 762 and 66.09% of 752 firms; a median 4.04 and 4.85 years between the two first filings. **2006 to 2010:** 68.01% and 68.30%; 3.61 and 2.96 years. **2011 to 2015:** 68.68% and 69.48%; 2.79 and 2.92 years.

observations.headline: A name match to the business register recovers most missing business numbers accurately, and changes no firm finding
observations.statement: Matching Australian organisations' rights that have no filer's ABN to the ABR's and ASIC's names recovers a known ABN for 66% to 85% of rights where the ABN was hidden for a test, with 1.1% to 4.8% of matches naming another ABN. Applied to rights with no ABN it links 17.7% to 35.3% of them. It closes most of the recent fall in standard patents linked to an ABN, and moves concentration and the claimants' figures by less than a point.

figures.label: of standard patents' hidden ABNs recovered, FY2010 to FY2019 (2.06% of matches another ABN)
standard patents with a filer's ABN, FY2024 to FY2026; 89.43% to 89.20% with the matched links
of standard patents filed by the top 1% of firms, by ABN and with the matched links

points: **The test:** standard patents FY2010 to FY2019, 83.41% matched and 81.70% recovered; FY2020 to FY2026, 68.95%, 67.85% and 1.60% another ABN. Trade marks 78.89%, 76.59% and 2.91%. Designs filed FY2000 to FY2009 are the weakest, 9.84% another ABN. A "wrong" ABN can be a related company of the same group.
**With the postcode as well**, 42.62% to 46.04% matched, with 2.34% to 4.71% another ABN: it halves the matches for no gain in accuracy, so it was dropped.

**Rights with no ABN, FY2000 to FY2026:** 3,217 of 9,104 standard patents matched (35.34%), 20,845 of 117,531 trade marks (17.74%), 6,183 of 18,317 provisionals, 2,171 of 8,275 designs; none of 3,220 plant breeder's rights.

**Firms with a first observed linked standard patent:** 660 (FY2020) to 542 (FY2026) by the filer's ABN, 675 to 616 with the matched links: about half of U45's later fall is linking (an 18% fall becomes 9%).
**R&D claimants with no filing linked** fall from 48.48% to 47.70%; every signal of {M8} keeps its direction and verdict. Adopting the matched links into the counts is the owner's decision (OQ26).

prep.what: The filer's name is matched to the ABR's main names and ASIC's company names (current and former), and a match is kept only if exactly one ABN has the name and is registered in the filer's state (`name_matched_abn`, ADR 0045 and 0047).
prep.why: A name shared by several ABNs, or found in another state, is too likely to be the wrong firm.

prep.what: The match is tested on rights whose ABN is known, with the ABN hidden.
prep.why: Shows how often the match is right before it is used where the ABN is missing.

steps: Run the match on rights with a known ABN, hidden, and measure the share recovered and the share naming another ABN.

assumptions: An organisation's name as filed, in its state, picks out one business.
limits: A "wrong" ABN can be a related company of the same group, which the test cannot tell.

observations.next: For the owner (OQ26): whether to adopt the matched links into the counts. The gaps it leaves are the ABNs IP RAPID leaves out (OQ7) and trading and business names (ASIC's business names register).

observations.original:
**M12 (descriptive). A name match to the ABR and ASIC recovers a known ABN for 66% to 85% of Australian
organisations' rights, with 1.1% to 4.8% of matches naming another ABN (older designs 9.8%); applied to the rights
with no ABN it links 17.7% to 35.3% of them, and it changes no firm finding: it closes most of the recent fall in
standard patents linked to an ABN, and moves concentration and the claimants' figures by less than a point.**
- **The test** (ABN hidden on rights that have one; the state must agree): standard patents FY2010 to FY2019, 83.41%
  matched and 81.70% recovered, 2.06% of matches another ABN (1.84% to 2.31%); FY2020 to FY2026, 68.95%, 67.85% and
  1.60% (1.37% to 1.88%). Trade marks: 78.89%, 76.59%, 2.91%; then 79.61%, 77.40%, 2.78% (2.71% to 2.85%). Designs
  filed FY2000 to FY2009 are the weakest, 9.84% another ABN; every other type and decade is 1.14% to 4.83%. A
  "wrong" ABN can be a related company of the same group, which the test cannot tell.
- **With the postcode as well** (ADR 0045's first rule): 42.62% to 46.04% matched, with 2.34% to 4.71% another ABN, so
  it halves the matches for no gain in accuracy (ADR 0047).
- **Rights with no filer's ABN, FY2000 to FY2026:** 3,217 of 9,104 standard patents matched (35.34%), 20,845 of
  117,531 trade marks (17.74%), 6,183 of 18,317 provisionals (33.76%), 2,171 of 8,275 designs (26.24%); none of 3,220
  plant breeder's rights (IP RAPID gives none of them an ABN, so the match cannot be tested on them).
- **U45 again:** standard patents with a filer's ABN fall from 88.68% (FY2024) to 83.85% (FY2026); with the matched
  links, 89.43% to 89.20%, so most of the recent fall closes. Trade marks 92.34% to 90.94% become 93.01% to 92.91%;
  designs 92.27% to 89.34% become 92.76% to 90.72%. Firms with a first observed linked standard patent: 660 (FY2020)
  to 542 (FY2026) by the filer's ABN, 675 to 616 with the matched links, so U45's later fall in first patent filers
  is about half a matter of linking (an 18% fall becomes 9%).
- **U44 again:** the top 1% of firms file 55.31% of standard patents by the filer's ABN and 55.06% with the matched
  links (23,971 and 24,595 firms); trade marks 25.66% and 26.02%.
- **M8 again:** R&D Tax Incentive claimants with no filing linked fall from 48.48% to 47.70% (first half) and from
  47.94% to 47.15% (second), 69 claimants gaining a filing by name in each half; every signal of M8 keeps its
  direction and verdict (age +23.8 and +23.2 held together, against +23.1 and +22.4).
- **For the owner** (ADR 0045, point 5): the matched links are reliable enough to read beside the counts, not to
  replace them. Adopting them into the counts is the owner's decision.

observations.headline: Places' characteristics repeat each other; one dimension, advantage, carries half of how areas differ
observations.statement: Across 2,525 postal areas, the measures of advantage, income and education can largely be predicted from one another. Summarised as [[principal-components|components]], the first, an advantage gradient on which every advantage measure rises together, carries 49.5% of the variation; the first four carry 82.3%. So Stage 2's single indicators (income, education, advantage) are mostly one measure: none should be read as the one that matters.

points: **[[variance-inflation|Variance inflation]]:** IRSAD 86.0, IRSD 32.1, IEO 25.0, median household income 19.6, IER 13.0, the share with a degree 11.4: all above 10. Businesses per person (1.6) and R&D claimants per 1,000 businesses (1.3) are not.
**The second component** (14.5%) rises with median age and businesses per person and falls with household size: older areas of small households and many businesses.

**The third** (11.3%) rises with economic resources and household size and falls with R&D claimants and the degree share: its low end is areas with more degrees and R&D claimants than their resources alone suggest.
**The fourth** (6.9%) rises with rent and age and falls with businesses per person.

observations.original:
**M13 (descriptive). Places' characteristics repeat each other: one component, advantage, carries half of the
variation across postal areas, and the advantage measures can largely be predicted from one another.** 2,525 areas
with every characteristic:
- **Variance inflation:** IRSAD 86.0, IRSD 32.1, IEO 25.0, median household income 19.6, IER 13.0, the share with a
  degree 11.4: all above 10, so each is largely predictable from the others. Businesses per person (1.6) and R&D
  claimants per 1,000 businesses (1.3) are not.
- **Components:** the first carries 49.5% of the variation, the first four 82.3% (14.5%, 11.3% and 6.9% for the
  second to fourth). The first loads on every advantage measure together (IRSAD +0.38, household income +0.36, IEO
  +0.35, IRSD +0.33, the degree share +0.33): it is the **advantage gradient**. The second rises with median age
  (+0.52) and businesses per person (+0.46) and falls with household size (-0.47): older areas of small households
  and many businesses. The third rises with economic resources (IER +0.53) and household size (+0.41) and falls with
  R&D claimants per 1,000 businesses (-0.46) and the degree share (-0.36): its low end is areas with more degrees and
  R&D claimants than their resources alone would suggest. The fourth rises with rent (+0.52) and age (+0.46) and
  falls with businesses per person (-0.51).
- **So** B27's and B28's single indicators (income, education, advantage) are mostly one measure. Read one at a time,
  each stands for the whole gradient; none should be read as the one that matters.

  (weakened). Designs 1.863 and 1.186 (1.025 to 1.372); 2.054 and 1.205 (27% and 26%); provisionals 1.652 and 1.247;
  1.960 and 1.313 (44% and 40%): **weakened**.
- **The other dimensions, held together** (standard patents): the second component (older areas, small households,
  many businesses) 1.446 (1.312 to 1.593) and 1.219 (1.092 to 1.361); the third 0.731 (0.674 to 0.792) and 0.663

observations.headline: Postal areas do not fall into distinct kinds; one group of 288 advantaged city areas holds more than half the patents
observations.statement: Grouping postal areas by their four components gives at most a weak structure: the best grouping, five groups, has a [[silhouette|silhouette]] of 0.269, short of clear segments (0.5 or more). Read as a description, one group of 288 advantaged, educated city areas files 3.14 standard patents a year per 10,000 people and holds 13,993 of the 24,879 patents placed (56%); the rest is a continuum.

points: Silhouettes for two to eight groups run from 0.232 to 0.269.

**288 areas** (4,451,909 residents; 95% of their people in major cities; median IRSAD 1,088), high on advantage (1.36) and low on the third component (more degrees and R&D claimants than their resources): 50.13 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.
**713 areas** (11,871,712 residents, the most), above average on advantage (0.78): 0.59 patents and 13.37 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.
**The other three groups** (260, 539 and 725 areas) are below average on advantage and file 0.37 to 0.48 patents and 8.76 to 10.63 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.

observations.original:
**M16 (descriptive). Postal areas form at most a weak structure: the best grouping, five kinds, has a silhouette of
0.269, and one group of 288 city areas holds more than half of the patents placed.** Silhouettes for two to eight
groups run from 0.232 to 0.269 (corrected 3 November 2026 in the review: this gave 0.231; the lowest is 0.2316); the best, five groups at 0.269, is "some structure" under ADR 0046, short of clear
segments (0.5 or more). Read as a description, not kinds of place:
- **288 areas** (4,451,909 residents; 95% of their people in major cities; median IRSAD 1,088), high on advantage
  (1.36) and low on the third component (-1.66: more degrees and R&D claimants than their resources), file 3.14
  standard patents a year per 10,000 people and 50.13 trade marks: 13,993 of the 24,879 patents placed (56%).
- **713 areas** (11,871,712 residents, the most), above average on advantage (0.78): 0.59 patents and 13.37 trade
  marks a year per 10,000 people.
- The other three groups (260, 539 and 725 areas) are below average on advantage (-0.80, -0.30 and -0.80), file 0.37
  to 0.48 patents and 8.76 to 10.63 trade marks a year per 10,000 people, and differ on the second and fourth
  components and in how many of their people live in major cities (49%, 1% and 7%).
- **So** the concentration of filing in a minority of advantaged, educated, city areas is the clearest structure in
  the places lens; the rest is a continuum.

observations.headline: Across OECD members the indicators spread over several dimensions; Australia is low on manufacturing and exports, high on education and new businesses
observations.statement: Across 35 OECD members, eleven indicators that are not IP measures spread over several dimensions rather than one: the first [[principal-components|component]], income and research output, carries 24.7% of the variation and the first four 73.4%. Australia sits at an edge of the second: little manufacturing and exporting, much tertiary education and many new businesses. On these indicators its nearest members are Norway, New Zealand and Sweden.

figures.label: Australia's score on the second component (manufacturing and trade against education and new businesses)
the members closest to Australia on the first four components (distances 1.21, 1.76 and 1.82)

points: **Less repetition than among places:** variance inflation is under 10 for every indicator (journal articles 8.3, GDP per person 6.5, the rest 1.4 to 4.1).

**The first component** is income and research output (GDP per person +0.53, journal articles +0.53, business R&D +0.30); **the second** is manufacturing and trade (manufacturing +0.56, exports +0.34) against education and new businesses (advanced education -0.39, new business density -0.34).

**Australia on single indicators**, in standard deviations from the members' mean: manufacturing -1.57, exports -1.06, business R&D -0.35; tertiary enrolment +1.78, new business density +1.75, journal articles +0.96, GDP per person +0.64.

Then Denmark (2.44) and the United Kingdom (2.46). These are the natural first set for comparisons of Australia with similar economies; they are similar on these eleven indicators, not on the IP system.

observations.headline: Across OECD members, patenting at home follows business R&D at the same income and size; income adds nothing once R&D is held
observations.statement: Across OECD members, residents' patenting at home goes with business R&D with income and population held (a [[partial-correlation|partial rank correlation]] of 0.715 in 2016 to 2020, 0.623 in 2006 to 2010), while income adds nothing detectable once business R&D is held. Abroad, richer members file more at the same business R&D. Trade marks go with income rather than R&D, and only in the later period. Australia's patenting is near what business R&D and income together predict.

points: **Patents filed worldwide by residents:** with business R&D 0.910 raw and 0.811 held; 0.903 and 0.818. With income 0.827 and 0.637; 0.757 and 0.502. Both hold.

**Australia:** 104.9% of the patenting business R&D alone predicts (Stage 2's figure), 111.9% with income too, in 2016 to 2020; 55.22% and 53.76% in 2006 to 2010, also inside wide intervals. With 36 members, Australia's position cannot be told from the line.
**Changes from 2006 to 2010 to 2016 to 2020** (34 members): patents against the change in business R&D 0.165 raw and 0.130 with the change in income held: not detected either way, as Stage 2 found.

Seasons are strong for Australians' trade marks (0.799) and provisionals (0.753). Once trend and season are removed, different series move together only moderately (0.239 to 0.325).

observations.headline: Raising the Bar's rush, and Australians' lower level of patents after it, hold with trend and season held; the Designs Act's step does not stand apart
observations.statement: Read as an interrupted time series with each series' trend and season held, Raising the Bar (April 2013) brought a rush of Australians' standard patents (0.605 in logs) and a lower level after it (a step of -0.334, about 28% fewer a month), which then recovers; its controls were quiet but for one small series. The Designs Act 2003's step for overseas applicants (June 2004) does not stand apart: Australians' trade marks, a control, stepped too.

figures.label: Australians' standard patents, step after Raising the Bar (about 28% fewer a month)
Australians' standard patents, the rush before it (in logs)
Australians' trade marks, a control, stepping with the Designs Act (0.391 for overseas designs)

points: **Raising the Bar:** a slope of +0.089 a year after the step, a lower level that then recovers. **Overseas applicants:** a rush of 0.352, no step detected (-0.047).

**Its controls:** Australians' designs, rush 0.049 and step -0.077, quiet; plant breeder's rights, rush 0.206, a small and noisy series. Stage 2's reading holds, with the plant breeder's rights' rush as a caution.

**The Designs Act 2003:** overseas applicants' designs step 0.391; but Australians' designs step too (0.162), and so do Australians' trade marks (0.251), while Australians' standard patents do not (0.036).
A linear trend over ten years is a simple counterfactual; Stage 2's placebo months remain the check on how often a step this size appears by chance.

revisits.what: Raising the Bar's rush and lower level hold for Australians' standard patents with trend and season held (rush 0.605, step -0.334); the Designs Act's overseas step (0.391) is not shown to be the Act's, since a control steps too (0.251).

A natural experiment for estimating what a policy change did, with its controls set out.

prep.what: Each series' log monthly count over ten years (five either side), with a linear trend and the month of the year held, plus a rush, a step and a change in slope after the change.
prep.why: Stage 2 measured each break against placebo months; Stage 3 holds the trend and season, which a break could otherwise be confused with.

steps: Fit an [[interrupted|interrupted time series]] to each series with a rush, a step and a change in slope.
Fit the same to control series the change should not have moved.
Read a behavioural break only where the series moves and its controls do not.
